beats.modern: told Tom the truth flat out: I'm stealing a man out of slavery and it's Miss Watson's Jim. braced for the whole sermon about how low-down it is. his eye lit up and he said I'll help you steal him. chat I let go all holts like I was shot. most astonishing speech I ever heard, and I'm bound to say Tom Sawyer fell considerable in my estimation.
beats.quote: “I’ll help you steal him!”

beats.title: Tar And Feathers
beats.modern: we were too late to warn them. crowd came up the street with torches and tin pans and horns and the king and the duke riding a rail, tarred and feathered, not looking like anything human in this world. just a couple of monstrous big soldier-plumes. and I couldn't feel any hardness against them any more. they earned every bit of it and I still felt sick. human beings can be awful cruel to one another.
beats.quote: Human beings can be awful cruel to one another.

beats.title: But The Books Say
beats.modern: there's a loose board on the window. Jim could be out in nine seconds. Tom says that's the infant-schooliest way of going at a thing. the correct method per the best authorities is: saw the bed-leg off, SWALLOW the sawdust, rope ladder to the battlements, break your leg in the moat. he wanted to dig a moat. he weighed sawing Jim's leg off, because some of the best authorities have done it, and ruled against it on grounds of insufficient necessity.
beats.quote: There ain’t necessity enough in this case;

beats.title: A Prisoner's Got To Have A Pet
beats.modern: Tom informs Jim that a prisoner of style is required to keep a rattlesnake. tame it, he says. every animal is grateful for kindness. it'll sleep with you and let you put its head in your mouth. Jim says he'd wait a powerful long time before he ASKED for that favor. they negotiated down to garter snakes with buttons tied on their tails, plus rats. Jim, quietly: I never knowed before it was so much bother and trouble to be a prisoner.
beats.quote: I never knowed b’fo’ ’t was so much bother and trouble to be a prisoner.”

beats.title: Tom Was The Gladdest Of All
beats.modern: fifteen men with guns in the shed. we went out the hole and over the fence and Tom's britches caught a splinter and snapped it. somebody yelled answer or I'll shoot. we ran, they shot, the dogs turned out to be OUR dogs and just said howdy and kept going. got to the raft and told Jim he's a free man again. we were all glad as we could be. Tom was the gladdest of all, because he had a bullet in the calf of his leg.

beats.title: Not Without A Doctor
beats.modern: Tom wants to keep running with a bullet in him. Jim, one bend of the river from actually being free, says no. asks it plain: if it was Mars Tom being set free and one of the boys got shot, would he say go on and save me, never mind about a doctor? you bet he wouldn't. well then is Jim going to say it? no sir. not if it's forty year. and he sat down in the open and waited to be taken.

beats.title: The Doctor's Statement
beats.modern: they have got Jim chained hand and foot to a staple in the floor on bread and water, and some of them wanted to hang him as an example. then the doctor spoke. said he could not cut the bullet out alone, and this man crawled out of nowhere and offered, and did it well, and stayed all night, risking his own freedom. best nurse he ever saw. so they agreed Jim deserved reward, and locked him back up. the reward: they promised not to cuss him any more.

beats.title: He Was Free The Whole Time
beats.modern: Tom sits up in bed and says it: he ain't no slave, he's as free as any creature that walks this earth. Miss Watson died two months ago, was ashamed she ever meant to sell him, and freed him in her will. so Aunt Sally asks the only question that matters. then what did YOU want to set him free for. and Tom says he wanted the ADVENTURE of it. weeks of rope ladders and rattlesnakes and a bullet in the leg. for a man already free.
beats.quote: he ain’t no slave; he’s as free as any cretur that walks this earth!”

beats.title: The Man In The Floating House
beats.modern: I said pap has probably been back and drunk up my six thousand by now. Jim says, kind of solemn, he ain't coming back no more. I ask why. he won't say. I keep at him. so he says: remember the house that floated down the river, and the man in there, covered up, that I went in and uncovered and wouldn't let you look at? your money is safe. that was him. he carried that the whole way down so I wouldn't have to.
beats.quote: Well, den, you kin git yo’ money when you wants it, kase dat wuz him.”

beats.title: Light Out For The Territory
beats.modern: Tom's got the bullet on a watch-chain around his neck and checks it constantly. Jim got forty dollars and told me he always knew he'd be rich again, signs is signs. and now Aunt Sally's fixing to adopt me and sivilize me. so that's my exit queued. I got to light out for the Territory ahead of the rest. I been there before. gg chat, stream's over, and if I'd knowed what a trouble it was to make a book I wouldn't have tackled it.
beats.quote: I got to light out for the Territory ahead of the rest,

beats.title: The Actor Problem
beats.modern: chat my sister is seventeen, straight out of boarding school, and she fell for an ACTOR she saw in a play. I intercepted one of his letters, went to find the man, and it escalated fast. so now I'm on a health-spa roadtrip with a gout-ridden uncle and an aunt who is a walking debuff. new arc. buckle up.

beats.title: Pistols At Dawn, Cancelled
beats.modern: we met at the city gate, priming pistols. then my uncle, a man who cannot walk, comes hobbling out from behind a house with the mayor's constables and ends the whole thing. the mayor threatened to jail the actor as a vagrant. I gave my word not to pursue it just so he wouldn't be dragged off to hard labour. he thanked me. weirdly the most respect I've felt for anyone this week.

beats.title: The Stink Doctor
beats.modern: there is a doctor at the wells who just gave a full lecture proving that bad smells are a social construct. he says he'd drink ditchwater. he told my uncle he looks dropsical and offered, when they tap him, to drink whatever comes out of his abdomen. then he casually mentioned he confirms his pox cures by sleeping with the patient three times. every woman in the room got up and started spitting.
beats.quote: if I should be present when you are tapped, I will give you a convincing proof of what I assert, by drinking without hesitation the water that comes out of your abdomen.’--The

beats.title: The Wart
beats.modern: he swore the wart on his nose was nothing and made me feel it to prove the bone underneath was sound. I felt it VERY thoroughly. he sneezed, tears down both cheeks, and my uncle laughed for the first time since I met him. so the doctor went home and burned the wart off with acid. his entire face is now one enormous nose.

beats.title: Twenty Pounds
beats.modern: caught my uncle sneaking a woman into a private parlour and posted up at a crack in the wall like a proper degenerate. he handed her twenty pounds. she's a widow whose daughter is dying. she fainted from gratitude and he panicked and started flinging water in her face. then aunt Tabby kicked the door in screaming about his morals and would not accept the truth. chat, I stood there crying at a wall.
beats.quote: charity.--Who gives twenty pounds in charity?--But you are a stripling--You know nothing of the world.

beats.title: Sir Ulic Upstairs
beats.modern: the ceiling started BOUNCING so I went up and found a one-eyed lame dancing master coaching a sixty-year-old Irish knight in a nightcap. I said the noise was preposterous. he girded on a long iron sword, marched downstairs, apologised to my uncle at enormous length, and then hugged me so hard I couldn't breathe and told me he loves me like his own soul.

beats.title: The Horns On The Stairs
beats.modern: two Black servants owned by a Creole colonel practise the French horn on the staircase, ten feet from our door. uncle sends a man to ask them to stop. the colonel sends back that the stairs are common ground and anyone who dislikes it can find other lodgings. uncle takes his cane, walks out, and beats them both. no gout that morning. the colonel never came for satisfaction.

beats.title: We Are Drinking The Bathwater
beats.modern: first thing uncle sees in the King's Bath is a child covered in open sores being carried through the water. he leaves. then he works out the pump probably draws off the bath, meaning everyone in the Pump-room is sipping the runoff of twenty diseased bodies. so he tries the other spring instead. that one drains through the abbey burial ground. bath is over for this man.

beats.title: The Sweetmeat Riot
beats.modern: a rich idiot threw a tea party with sweets on every table and a bell to signal open season. chat it was carnage. grabbing, screaming, china in pieces, nosegays torn out of women's dresses, ladies pulling each other's caps off. he had his horns sound a charge to hype them up and it only made everyone realise what they'd become. the two biggest offenders were a baroness and a knight's widow.
beats.quote: ‘I bless God (said he) that Mrs Tabitha Bramble did not take the field today!’

beats.title: The Ghost Of Gimlet
beats.modern: my aunt cornered the greatest actor in England, called him the wrong name, asked him to perform the ghost from Gimlet (she means Hamlet), and then asked where she could buy a rooster of the same breed as the one that crowed onstage, because she'd like one at home to wake the maids. he said: dunghill. she did not stop.
beats.quote: the Ghost of Gimlet is laid, never to rise again’--

beats.title: Forty Years Ago
beats.modern: uncle found his oldest friends in a coffeehouse full of wrecked men. one is a bust of a person in a wheeled chair. one is bent double like a mounted telescope. the admiral recognised him, hugged him, and in the process jammed his spectacles into uncle's eye and put a wooden leg on his gouty toe. uncle cried for real. he says it's the happiest day he's had in twenty years.
beats.quote: ‘Ha! Matt, my old fellow cruizer, still afloat!’

beats.title: Chowder Gets Punted
beats.modern: my aunt's dog walked into the assembly rooms like he pays a subscription. the master of ceremonies tried to shoo him out, got shown a full set of teeth, and then Sir Ulic gallantly booted the dog across the room without knowing whose it was. she has excommunicated him. he is DELIGHTED. turns out he'd been fed wrong numbers on her fortune, six thousand pounds wrong, and needed an exit.

beats.title: Uncle Drops At The Ball
beats.modern: he got talked into watching my sister dance a minuet. two hours packed shoulder to shoulder watching people trace the same dull figure on a patch of floor. then the benches got moved for country dances, the whole room stood up at once, and the accumulated air of Bath hit him in the face. he went down. flat. out cold on the floor. we're leaving.

beats.title: The Coach Goes Over
beats.modern: coach flipped into a rut on the Downs. I gallop back and all I can see through the window is the maid's legs kicking in the air. then uncle shoots out headfirst, using her backside as a step. I pulled my aunt out last, wigless and feral, and she did not ask about her brother once. she screamed for the DOG. dog was fine. dog bit uncle's leg, then bit the footman to the bone.
beats.quote: ‘Chowder! Chowder! my dear Chowder! my poor Chowder is certainly killed!’

beats.title: Enter Humphry Clinker
beats.modern: my aunt filed a formal complaint that our replacement postilion had no shirt and had exposed his backside to her. uncle summons him: yellow, starving, in rags, hasn't eaten in a day. workhouse kid, orphan, apprenticed to a blacksmith who died, sick six months, sold everything he owned to survive. uncle sentences him for the crime of being poor, then puts a guinea in his hand. name's Humphry Clinker.
beats.quote: offender--You stand convicted of sickness, hunger, wretchedness, and want--But,

beats.title: The Job Interview
beats.modern: uncle asks what he's actually good for. Humphry: can read, write, shoe a horse, bleed it, and there's not a man in Wiltshire who can geld a pig better. also hog's puddings, hob-nails, mending kettles. also single-stick, psalms, jew's harp, Welsh jig, and he'll wrestle anyone his own size. hired on the spot. first assignment: go apologise to my aunt for the tail incident.
beats.quote: I can make hog’s puddings and hob-nails, mend kettles and tin sauce-pans.’--Here

beats.title: Him Or Me
beats.modern: Humphry spilled custard on my aunt, trod on the dog, smashed the dish, then heard her shout kill it at once and grabbed a knife to go do exactly that. box on the ear. she gives uncle an ultimatum: the boy goes or she does. uncle gives her one straight back, the dog or him. chat she FOLDED. sat down in a corner. then hugged him. the dog is being rehomed in London.
beats.quote: Either discard your four-footed favourite, or give me leave to bid you eternally adieu--For

beats.title: Our Footman Is Preaching
beats.modern: walked out of the palace and there's a crowd of servants at the foot of the stairs with OUR FOOTMAN up on a stool holding forth. he wasn't selling anything. he was telling the lackeys of London to stop swearing. uncle grilled him at dinner and Humphry mildly noted that if the poor gave up swearing there'd be nothing left to tell their conversation from their betters'. uncle changed colour.

beats.title: The Whole Family Was In There
beats.modern: followed a crowd into a Methodist meeting to see the famous preaching footman. it's Humphry. mid-psalm, doing the graces. and sitting in the congregation: my aunt, my sister, the maid, lady Griskin, and Barton. all of them singing along with strong marks of devotion. uncle ordered him down out of the pulpit and marched us into a hackney coach while the entire room sat in silence.

beats.title: No Light But What Pays Taxes
beats.modern: uncle's ruling on the new light of grace: you're a knave or a lunatic, pick one, and if it's the second there's a room with clean straw waiting in Bedlam. Humphry, on his knees, works it through out loud: I know I'm not a knave, therefore I must be mad, therefore please get me treated. uncle couldn't keep his face straight. aunt, however, is furious he didn't martyr himself.
beats.quote: I will have no light in my family but what pays the king’s taxes,

beats.title: Aunt Tabby Proposes
beats.modern: Barton came to ask permission to marry into the family. my aunt announced that she had decided to abandon the single life and vest him with a legal title to her person and fortune. Barton, who meant my SISTER, developed an immediate vertigo and left the building. Liddy turned him down anyway. then aunt and lady Griskin curtsied at each other so low and so long that somebody should have painted it.

beats.title: They Arrested Our Footman
beats.modern: constables in the house with a warrant. a postilion swore point-blank that Humphry robbed a chaise on Blackheath back in March. nothing in his box, no bail possible, straight to Clerkenwell in irons. the gentlest man I have ever met is in a cell for highway robbery and the crowd outside the courtroom agreed his face looked villainous.

beats.title: Say You're Innocent
beats.modern: uncle in open court, desperate: in the name of God, if you're innocent SAY SO. Humphry: God forbid I call myself innocent while my conscience is burdened with sin. the justice immediately tried to have that written down as a confession. and the sharp young gentleman arguing hardest for him? the constable told me afterwards that's Martin, and Martin is the man who actually did the robbery.
beats.quote: God forbid that I should call myself innocent, while my conscience is burthened with sin.’

beats.title: He Ruined The Prison
beats.modern: the turnkey at Clerkenwell is furious with us. nobody's buying beer. nobody's buying wine. hardened road-men who'd have gone to the cart like true-born Englishmen have been blubbering all night. our footman is running a revival in the chapel with the gaoler's wife in the front row, and the felons have already held their own trial and acquitted him.

beats.title: The Highwayman Escort
beats.modern: two men waiting at the end of a lane for our coach. uncle reaches for his pistols and gets dogpiled by three screaming women. then Martin, the actual working highwayman, gallops up, tells the ladies to compose themselves, and takes Humphry off to charge the ambush with him. the pair scattered. he then rode with us to dinner and my aunt found him charming and well-bred.

beats.title: The Ear
beats.modern: uncle went sea-bathing at six in the morning. he yelped from the cold. Humphry heard it, decided his master was drowning, ran into the sea fully clothed, knocked over the guide, reached him, and dragged him BY THE EAR naked up the beach in front of the entire town. uncle punched him. then apologised. then left Scarborough forever.
beats.quote: he seized me by one ear, dragged me bellowing with pain upon the dry beach,

beats.title: Ah, Jacob
beats.modern: coach broke eight miles from anywhere. we found a forge, but the blacksmith had died days before and his widow had just given birth and lost her senses. Humphry lit the fire and started hammering. she heard the anvil, got up, ran into the smithy, threw her arms round his neck and asked how he could leave her like this. nobody laughed. he hammered the iron and wept at the same time.
beats.quote: ‘Ah, Jacob (cried she) how could you leave me in such a condition?’

beats.title: Lismahago's Origin Story
beats.modern: the Scotch lieutenant we picked up was taken prisoner in Canada. they marked his friend for the stake and handed him the bride instead. a finger sawn off, a toe crushed between stones, teeth dug out with a nail, gunpowder packed into his calves. he stood at the fire and sang his friend's death song with him. then he married, was made a chief, had a son, and lost her to a fever. my aunt is enthralled.

beats.title: Aunt Tabby Locks On
beats.modern: she has decided the lieutenant is the prettiest gentleman she ever saw. uncle, asked directly, said the man's face is hard-favoured and forbidding and he cannot in good conscience agree. she does not care. and the lieutenant, doing the arithmetic on a half-pay pension against an old maid with money, has started returning fire: snuff, compliments, and a woven purse his late wife used to carry shot in.

beats.title: Win Gets Poached
beats.modern: my valet Dutton fought Humphry for the maid's affections and won on presentation alone: French snuff, tooth powder, Paris hairdo, dancing lessons. he walked her to the theatre in a bag wig with a sword swinging, her hair seven inches high and her face painted from chin to eyes. on the way there people assumed they were actors. on the way back the town had worked out they were servants and pelted them home.

beats.title: Cold Iron
beats.modern: Dutton challenged him to swords. Humphry's position: I know as much about swordplay as he knows about making a horseshoe, I'm not having any man's blood on my conscience, but I'll give him a good drubbing free of charge. the lieutenant egged him on to try steel anyway. Humphry declined, provoked Dutton into swinging first, and beat him until he asked for quarter.
beats.quote: ‘Cold iron (cried Humphry) I shall never use against the life of any human creature;

beats.title: Dutton Exits
beats.modern: chat you'll never guess. Dutton eloped. before dawn, with a pawnbroker's heiress who'd come north with an Irishman to get married, after quietly telling her the Irishman was a tailor. post-chaise to Coldstream, married before breakfast. the Irishman woke at six, found the bird flown, tore the favour off the postilion's cap and beat him with it. I have lost a valet. he has lost five thousand pounds.

beats.title: The Sheep's Head
beats.modern: we asked for the national dishes and regretted it immediately. first a singed sheep's head. then haggis: minced lights, liver, suet, oatmeal, onions and pepper, all cooked inside the sheep's stomach. my aunt visibly changed colour. our host clocked our faces and had the whole thing removed with a single nod. I am not yet Scotchman enough.

beats.title: The Lord Who Dismissed Us
beats.modern: dined with a lord who'd invited a dozen strangers purely so he'd have something to shine on. three toasts, one bumper, then he wished us good afternoon, which is house code for get out. everyone obeyed. uncle did not move. lord orders the gentleman's carriage brought round. uncle leaves a guinea on the table like it's an inn and says he won't leave the county until he can thank his lordship in person.

beats.title: The Horse-Pond
beats.modern: uncle sent the lieutenant to deliver a formal challenge. a commoner challenging a PEER set the whole house off like a fire bell. footmen disarmed him, put his sword through a close-stool and him through the horse-pond. so he came back and challenged UNCLE instead. my aunt physically got between them. final settlement: three days of us riding armed past the gates until his lordship apologised, and his valet begging pardon on his knees. the lieutenant kicked him in the face.
beats.quote: ‘What! a commoner send a challenge to a peer of the realm!--Privilege!

beats.title: Buried In The Country
beats.modern: uncle's oldest friend Baynard married for money, then gently suggested they live within it. she went silent, then said: so I am to be buried in the country. eight-hour fit. aunt in tears. he apologised on his knees. then a neighbour turned out to keep two more servants than him, she skipped supper, had another fit, and the family plate got sold for scrap to fund a fashionable one. he has never won since.
beats.quote: ‘So (said she) I am to be buried in the country!’

beats.title: Fire!
beats.modern: three in the morning, cry of FIRE, torches in the yard, the back stair burning. the lieutenant is locked in upstairs, can't find his clothes in the dark, and the servants are shouting that robbers took everything and set the house alight. he runs round the room naked like a squirrel in a cage. then comes down a ladder in his shirt and nightcap by torchlight while the entire household watches. it was a bit. our host staged all of it.

beats.title: A Mad Dog
beats.modern: next afternoon our host is dozing in his chair, feet wrapped in flannel, crippled with gout. the lieutenant kicks the door open screaming MAD DOG and dives out the window. our host, who has not walked unaided in years, went through that window like an arrow from a bow and stood up to his middle in his own new fishpond. then the lieutenant leaned out and started calling for warm blankets.
beats.quote: ‘A mad dog! a mad dog!’

beats.title: The River
beats.modern: a mill-head burst as the coach was crossing the ford. the whole thing floated, then turned over, in the middle of the stream. my aunt hung round the lieutenant's neck like a millstone and nearly took them both down. I pulled my sister out by the hair. then I realised uncle hadn't come up. Humphry dived into a coach full of water and brought him out looking dead, carried him ashore like a baby, howling, and bled him with a horse-fleam. he opened his eyes.
beats.quote: she hung about his neck like a mill-stone (no bad emblem of matrimony),

beats.title: Keep Your Money
beats.modern: uncle offered him the purse, thirty guineas and a ring, for fishing him off the riverbed. Humphry refused it. said he'd have done the same for the lieutenant, for Macalpine, for the most worthless creature on earth, so how could he take payment for doing it for HIM. uncle settled thirty pounds a year on him anyway and made us witness it. the lieutenant is still sore about being ranked with the sinners.

beats.title: Stand Forth, Matthew Loyd
beats.modern: the gentleman who took us in recognises uncle from Oxford under a name I have never heard him use: Matthew Loyd. Humphry drops a coal scuttle on the lieutenant's foot and starts CAPERING round the room. then pulls out an old wooden snuff-box: a seal, a direction in uncle's own handwriting, a baptism certificate. his mother was a barmaid at Chippenham, dead. chat. our footman is my uncle's son.
beats.quote: ‘Stand forth, Matthew Loyd--You see, gentlemen, how the sins of my youth rise up in judgment against me--Here

beats.title: Sister, Meet Your Nephew
beats.modern: uncle presents him to my aunt as a poor relation and a crab of his own planting from the days of hot blood. she eyes him sideways, flirts her fan, holds out her hand to be kissed, informs her brother he has been very wicked, and then decides the boy has uncle Loyd's nose and the governor's long chin. her only instruction: change his name and change his LIVERY. nobody with our blood wears that coat.
beats.quote: the rogue proves to be a crab of my own planting in the days of hot blood and unrestrained libertinism.’

beats.title: Wilson Is The Son
beats.modern: the son of the house walks in, sees my sister, and freezes in the doorway. it's Wilson. the actor. the man I twice tried to shoot. except he is the heir to this estate, his parents already approve, and he has been riding round England looking for us to make a formal offer. Liddy managed to say that it was a very surprising, providential something, and would he please assume she had said whatever was agreeable.

beats.title: The Whole Wilson Bit
beats.modern: full explanation, finally. he ran from Cambridge to dodge a marriage he hated, worked as a stroller in the country until the girl chose someone else, then went home and told his father about Liddy. the horseman I saw through the inn window and challenged? that was him, hunting for us. the man who actually turned up in the field with pistols? the real Mr Wilson, his father's neighbour, whose name he'd borrowed.

beats.title: Humphry Gets Married Too
beats.modern: my new cousin has formally petitioned, through me, to marry the maid. uncle's response: he'd rather the boy had stayed out of this scrape, but the girl's already having fits of despondence, so he may go ahead and play the fool in imitation of his betters. aunt consented with terrible grace. she cannot have Matthew Loyd's wife handing her the soup.

beats.title: Three Couples, One Church
beats.modern: they married all three pairs at once. Dennison and my sister, plainly dressed, doing everything with their eyes. my aunt in a gown from 1739 under a sable cloak worth eighty guineas, walked up the aisle while the lieutenant advanced in military step in a coat ending mid-thigh, a campaign wig beyond description, and a distinctly ironical leer. ring was two hundred years old. and then Humphry and Win.

beats.title: The Cat
beats.modern: wedding night. somebody shod a cat with walnut shells and let it loose in the newlyweds' room. Win screamed and vanished under the bedclothes. Humphry, convinced Satan had come to buffet him in person, laid aside all carnal thoughts and began praying at volume. the cat, more frightened than either of them, jumped into the bed and howled. he got up, opened the door, let it out, and double-bolted it.

beats.title: GG From Win
beats.modern: last word goes to the maid, who signs herself Loyd now and reports that three couples were chined by the grease of God. she says madam Lashtniheygo's head was fintastical, that one guest called the captain a monkey-bank and the old butler swore he was the born image of Titidall. she has been removed to a higher sphere and would like everyone below stairs to keep a proper distance. stream's over, chat.

beats.title: Amazons Only Server
beats.modern: chat I'm back in Cranford and you need to understand the demographics here. every house above a certain rent? a woman. men who move in just... evaporate. either scared to death at their first card party or permanently "away with his regiment." nobody's mad about it. the ladies of Cranford are, and I quote, quite sufficient.
beats.quote: he is either fairly frightened to death by being the only man in the Cranford evening parties,

beats.title: The Cow In Grey Flannel
beats.modern: a local cow fell in a lime pit and lost ALL her hair. town is in mourning. Captain Brown, the only man here, gives his verdict: flannel waistcoat, flannel drawers, or put her down. chat she picked the flannel. there is now a cow walking to pasture in a full grey outfit and not one person in this town finds that strange.
beats.quote: “Get her a flannel waistcoat and flannel drawers, ma’am, if you wish to keep her alive.

beats.title: Boz Versus Dr Johnson
beats.modern: Captain Brown reads out a bit of the new Dickens and half the room actually laughs. Miss Jenkyns does not laugh. Miss Jenkyns sends me to fetch Rasselas, reads a scene aloud in her big church voice, and then declares herself the winner of a competition nobody entered. chat she is ratioing a man over a serialised novel and she thinks she's won.
beats.quote: “I must say, I don’t think they are by any means equal to Dr Johnson.

beats.title: The Down Train
beats.modern: the carter can barely say it. Captain Brown's on the platform, nose in a book, waiting for the down train. a little girl gives her sister the slip and toddles onto the line. he looks up, sees her, goes, grabs her, throws her clear to her mother — and his foot slips. she has one bruise on her shoulder. that's the whole trade he made and he made it in about a second.
beats.quote: he darted on the line and cotched it up, and his foot slipped, and the train came over him in no time.

beats.title: Poor Dear Infatuated Man
beats.modern: the county paper runs the full account. says the gallant gentleman was deeply engaged in a number of Pickwick when it happened. Miss Jenkyns makes me read it out, shakes her head long and slow, and sighs: poor, dear, infatuated man. chat she is not talking about the train. she is STILL talking about Dickens.
beats.quote: “Poor, dear, infatuated man!”

beats.title: Though He Slay Me
beats.modern: his eldest is dying and nobody has told her her father is already dead. she's whispering apologies for being selfish, begging her sister to tell him how much she loved him. so Jessie tells her: he's gone on ahead. he knows now. and the last thing that woman says isn't about herself, it's: but you will be alone, Jessie. and Jessie can't answer for a minute. then she puts her hands together, lifts them, and says it.
beats.quote: us—“Though He slay me, yet will I trust in Him.”

beats.title: The Most Proper Place
beats.modern: a man turns up with a card. turns out he proposed to Jessie years ago, she said no because she couldn't leave her dying sister, he took it as coldness and left the country. he read about the funeral in a paper in Rome and came straight back. Miss Matty walks in SCANDALISED — there's a gentleman with his arm round Miss Jessie's waist — and Miss Jenkyns, strictest woman alive, just goes: correct. most proper place in the world for it.
beats.quote: “Deborah, there’s a gentleman sitting in the drawing-room with his arm round Miss Jessie’s waist!”

beats.title: Call Me Matilda
beats.modern: Miss Jenkyns is dead and her little sister just asked me, very carefully, holding my hand, to stop calling her Matty. Deborah never liked it. she says she did many a thing Deborah didn't like, and now she's gone. so we all switch to Matilda. and we all fail within a fortnight. she was always going to be Miss Matty, chat.
beats.quote: but I did many a thing she did not like, I’m afraid—and now she’s gone!

beats.title: I Should Not Have Known You
beats.modern: we're in the draper's arguing about silk when a tall Don Quixote-looking farmer hears her name and crosses the shop in two strides. that's him. that's the man she nearly married forty years ago, the one her family decided wasn't gentleman enough. and what he says, delighted, no filter, over and over: I should not have known you. she goes to her room. doesn't come down till tea. eyes red.
beats.quote: I should not have known you.

beats.title: I Saw I Imitated I Survived
beats.modern: dinner at his farm. ducks and green peas. the forks have TWO PRONGS. Miss Pole gives up and leaves hers on the plate untouched. Miss Matty is spearing peas one at a time like a boss fight. I look up and our host is shovelling them in wholesale with his knife. so I did too, chat. I saw, I imitated, I survived.
beats.quote: I saw, I imitated, I survived!

beats.title: Black As Ash-Buds
beats.modern: he's striding ahead of me quoting poetry at trees, forgetting I exist. then he wheels round and demands to know what colour ash-buds are in March. sir I do not know. "I knew you didn't. no more did I, an old fool that I am, till this young man comes and tells me." BLACK. jet-black, madam. then off he goes down the field vibrating over one line of Tennyson.
beats.quote: Black as ash-buds in March.

beats.title: Any Commands For Paris
beats.modern: he sits with his hands on his knees, whistling, then jumps up: any commands for Paris? he's seventy. he's never been. says if he doesn't go now he never will. on his way out he pulls a book of poems from his coat — the ones she liked — hands them to her and says good-bye, Matty. take care of yourself. Matty. like it's thirty years ago and none of it happened.
beats.quote: “good-bye, Matty! take care of yourself.”

beats.title: Not Widows Of Course
beats.modern: Miss Pole comes round and says he's dead. Paris finished him. Miss Matty doesn't cry, doesn't say his name, never says his name again. she just quietly asks the milliner for caps a bit more like Mrs Jamieson's. and the milliner says, ma'am, those are widows' caps. "oh! I only meant something in that style." the book he gave her sits next to her Bible for the rest of her life.
beats.quote: “But she wears widows’ caps, ma’am?”

beats.title: Please Ma'am There's Jem Hearn
beats.modern: same week she hears he's dead, she calls the maid back after prayers and says: Martha, you're young. if you ever meet a young man you like, tell me, and he can come once a week. God forbid I should grieve any young hearts. and Martha, instantly, zero pause, fully loaded: please ma'am there's Jem Hearn, he's a joiner on three and six a day and he's six foot one in his stockings and he can come tomorrow night.
beats.quote: there’s Jem Hearn, and he’s a joiner making three-and-sixpence a-day, and six foot one in his stocking-feet,

beats.title: We Must Burn Them
beats.modern: sixty years of family letters on the table and we're reading them out to each other before destroying them. her father the terrifying rector wrote his girl-bride letters that are basically desperate. she looks at me and says, we must burn them, I think. no one will care for them when I am gone. and in they go. one at a time. she watches every single one catch and go grey up the chimney.
beats.quote: “No one will care for them when I am gone.”

beats.title: The Pillow Baby
beats.modern: so her brother Peter decides the funniest possible bit is dressing in their sister's clothes, making a pillow into a baby, and pacing the garden walk cooing at it where the whole town can see through the railings. twenty people watching by the time their father comes up the street. the rector tears the clothes off him, throws the pillow over the fence, and flogs him in front of everybody. worst way a bit has ever ended.
beats.quote: he cuddled his pillow, just like a baby, and talked to it all the nonsense people do.

beats.title: God Bless You For Ever
beats.modern: Peter walks into the store room where his mother is making cowslip wine. doesn't smile. doesn't explain. says he's come to say God bless you for ever, holds her like he doesn't know how to stop, and he's out the door before she can get a word out. she asks what he meant. he's gone. chat that was a goodbye and she didn't know it yet. she never made cowslip wine again.
beats.quote: ‘I am come to say, God bless you for ever.’

beats.title: Shall We Drag The Ponds
beats.modern: they've searched the house, the garden, the hayloft, ten times each. it's dark. old Clare comes to Matty — she's a girl, she's the one holding this whole night together — and says very gently: I've borrowed the nets from the weir. shall we drag the ponds tonight, or wait for morning. she stares at him until she works out what he's actually asking. then she laughs. she says she can still hear that laugh.
beats.quote: Shall we drag the ponds to-night, or wait for the morning?’

beats.title: Too Late
beats.modern: he'd walked to Liverpool and signed onto a king's ship. the captain's letter gets delayed somewhere. and it's racetime, so every post-horse in Cranford is at the races. his parents take their own gig and drive all night. they get there and the ship is gone. his last letter says he hopes they go into battle, but he has to see her first. "and she was too late," Matty says. "too late."
beats.quote: I hope we shall, and lick those French: but I must see you again before that time.”

beats.title: The Shawl From India
beats.modern: his mother doesn't last the year. the day AFTER she dies, a parcel arrives from India. from him. a big soft white shawl with a little narrow border, exactly the thing she'd have chosen. their father takes it, feels it, and says she'll be buried in it — Peter shall have that comfort. she wanted one like it when she got married and never got it. she gets it now.
beats.quote: It was a large, soft, white Indian shawl, with just a little narrow border all round;

beats.title: Just A Leetle Glass
beats.modern: our retired milliner hostess brings out cherry-brandy after the oysters — just a little, leetle glass, ladies. we all shake our heads like a row of mandarins. then Mrs Jamieson caves and the whole table follows. Miss Pole, setting her empty glass down: I do believe there's spirit in it. hostess, serene: only a drop, to make it keep. I often feel tipsy from eating damson tart.
beats.quote: us—“just a little, leetle glass, ladies; after the oysters and lobsters, you know.

beats.title: We Are Not To Call
beats.modern: Mrs Jamieson has a titled sister-in-law staying and comes round IN PERSON, very slowly, to let us know we're not to call on her. we're not county enough. Miss Pole comes back from checking the Peerage absolutely glowing with rage: widow of a Scotch baron who never even sat in the Lords, poor as Job, fifth daughter of some Mr Campbell. also Miss Pole had already ordered a new cap. that's the real wound.
beats.quote: I wish I had thought of something very sharp and sarcastic; I dare say I shall to-night.

beats.title: The Lace And The Cat
beats.modern: Mrs Forrester's irreplaceable lace was soaking in milk, as you do, and the cat DRANK IT. so she sends the maid to the surgery to borrow one of the doctor's top-boots, stuffs the cat in it feet-first so it can't scratch, feeds it currant jelly with an emetic hidden in it, and lays a clean towel on the floor. half an hour later she has her lace back. boiled it, dried it on a lavender bush. you'd never guess.
beats.quote: would he be kind enough to lend me one of his top-boots for an hour?

beats.title: Turbans Are Worn
beats.modern: curtain finally goes up on the conjuror and there's a magnificent man in full Turkish costume with a beard down his chest. Miss Pole announces LOUDLY that this is not Signor Brunoni because the one she met had no beard. he stares her down over the beard. and Miss Matty turns round to me with total quiet devastation and says: you see, my dear, turbans are worn. she wanted the turban. I bought her the sensible cap.
beats.quote: “That’s not Signor Brunoni!”

beats.title: The Penny Ball
beats.modern: town's convinced there's a robbery gang so we're all confessing our fears. mine is eyes watching me out of flat wooden surfaces. Miss Matty's is that since she was a girl she's been sure someone under the bed will catch her by the last leg. so she rolls a penny ball under there every night. comes out the other side, we're clear. doesn't come out, hand goes to the bell-rope and she calls for John and Harry — two menservants who do not exist.
beats.quote: now she rolled this ball under the bed every night:

beats.title: His Name Is Sam
beats.modern: the terrifying foreign conjuror we decided was a French spy running a burglary ring is lying in a roadside inn with internal injuries from a cart accident, six weeks now, nursed by his wife, out of money. Miss Pole goes from suspicious to fully mobilised in about ninety seconds. and his real name? Samuel Brown. Sam. we kept calling him the Signor anyway. it sounded better.
beats.quote: his wife said his proper name was Samuel Brown—“Sam,”

beats.title: Six Children
beats.modern: his wife tells me about India. she was a sergeant's wife out there and she lost six children. she says it plainly, because it's just a fact she carries. when the seventh was coming she told him she'd go mad if this one died too — so she WALKED. station to station, village to village, all the way to Calcutta with the baby on her breast. strangers brought her rice and milk. she got her home. Phoebe is alive because her mother refused to stop walking.
beats.quote: but, ma’am, I’ve lost six children,”

beats.title: The Aga Jenkyns
beats.modern: and then she mentions, casually, the kind Englishman who took them in when the baby fell ill upcountry. his name was Aga Jenkyns. chat. CHAT. everyone here says poor Peter is dead. some say he became Great Lama of Thibet. Miss Matty says she still hears his step in the street and it always goes past. I am writing a letter and I am telling nobody.
beats.quote: could the Aga Jenkyns be the lost Peter?

beats.title: Marry! Madness!
beats.modern: Miss Pole arrives before twelve, which never happens, hands in the air, too big for words. Lady Glenmire is marrying Mr Hoggins. the SURGEON. the man who says "Jack's up" and whose boots smell of the stable. marry! we said. marry! madness! and the part actually killing Miss Pole is that she heard it in a grocer's shop, out loud, in the hearing of shopmen. her heart stopped while you might have counted twelve.
beats.quote: Where feminine delicacy is gone to, I don’t know!

beats.title: Five Sovereigns For A Note
beats.modern: a farmer tries to pay for his wife's shawl with a five-pound note and the shopman won't take it — that bank's about to go. it's HER bank. she doesn't understand finance. she understands one thing: she's a shareholder, so his loss is partly her doing. so she puts down her five sovereigns, the ones saved for the first dress she's ever chosen for herself, and takes his worthless paper. it's only going without my gown a few days longer.
beats.quote: I would rather exchange my gold for the note, if you please,”

beats.title: Thirteen Pounds A Year
beats.modern: bank's gone. she sits with the account book, then comes over in the dark, takes my hand and says the number out loud: a hundred and forty-nine pounds thirteen shillings and fourpence a year, gone. thirteen pounds left. five shillings a week. and then she says the thing that finishes me — that she's glad her sister didn't live to see it, because Deborah could never have borne to come down in the world.
beats.quote: I shall only have thirteen pounds a year left.”

beats.title: I'll Not Listen To Reason
beats.modern: I try to explain to Martha, gently, that there is no money to keep a servant. she says, and I'm quoting: reason always means what someone else has got to say. she's got savings, she's got clothes, she is not leaving, not if Miss Matty gives her notice every hour of the day. then she goes and buys the ingredients for a pudding out of her own teapot money because a good dish on the table helps.
beats.quote: “Reason always means what someone else has got to say.

beats.title: A Twentieth Of Everything
beats.modern: the ladies hold a secret meeting. green card-cloth, pens, cowslip wine. every one of them writes down what she can give annually, signs it, seals it, and Miss Matty is never to be told a penny of it came from them. then Mrs Forrester takes me aside, shaking like she's confessing a crime, to admit how little she actually lives on — terrified I'll think her number means she loves Matty less. it's more than a twentieth of everything she has.
beats.quote: Every lady wrote down the sum she could give annually, signed the paper, and sealed it mysteriously.

beats.title: Licensed To Sell Tea
beats.modern: the rector's daughter is opening a shop. tea in bright green canisters, comfits in tumblers, floor scrubbed white, a strip of oilcloth for customers to stand on. and the sign — Matilda Jenkyns, licensed to sell tea — is deliberately tucked up under the lintel where nobody can see it. she also walked down to the other shopkeeper first to check she wouldn't be taking his business. he started sending her customers.
beats.quote: “Matilda Jenkyns, licensed to sell tea,”

beats.title: Can You Be Peter
beats.modern: a weathered brown man with snow-white hair comes into the shop and doesn't buy anything. just looks at her, drumming his fingers on the table exactly the way her sister used to. he panics and orders a whole pound of almond comfits to buy time. she looks up to warn him about the indigestion, sees something in his face, and says: it is — oh, sir! can you be Peter? and then he's round the table with his arms round her, crying the tearless cries of old age.
beats.quote: “It is—oh, sir! can you be Peter?”

beats.title: Peace To Cranford
beats.modern: Peter's telling Mrs Jamieson about the Himalayas, each peak taller than the last, until he mentions he once shot a cherubim up there. she's appalled. surely that's sacrilege. he apologises with a completely straight face. then he tips me a wink and explains the whole thing: keep her awake, keep her sweet, get her in a room with the Hogginses, because the feud upsets Matty. he walks in that night with one on each arm. town's been friendly ever since. gg.
beats.quote: to find that he had shot a cherubim!

beats.title: The Tenant Won't Leave
beats.modern: some soft southern gentleman rents my OTHER house and then rides four miles to my gate to thank me for it. I said walk in through my teeth, chat. even the gate didn't move. he took it as an invitation. he's decided we're the same because we both hate people. buddy. we are not the same.

beats.title: Something At The Window
beats.modern: the tenant sleeps ONE night in the old oak bed and a hand comes through the broken pane and grabs him. a kid's voice on the moor side of the glass. twenty years a waif, she says. TWENTY YEARS. and he pulls her wrist across the glass to get free and piles books against the hole. chat. he shut the window on her.
beats.quote: “Let me in—let me in!”

beats.title: Come In
beats.modern: soon as he's out of the room I'm on that bed wrenching the lattice open, sobbing into the snow like an animal. hear me THIS time. and nothing. wind, snow, candle out. eighteen years I've asked and she shows up in a stranger's dream instead.
beats.quote: “Come in! come in!”

beats.title: Picked Up In Liverpool
beats.modern: origin story, chat. old man walks sixty miles to Liverpool, promises his kids a fiddle and a whip, comes back at eleven at night with ME in his coat instead. the fiddle got crushed on the road. the whip got lost. the wife wants me thrown out the door. the little girl spits at me. I get washed, handed a dead son's name, and left on the landing.

beats.title: The Old Man Goes Quiet
beats.modern: she's singing him down to sleep with her head on his knee and his fingers just stop holding hers. she's the one who finds out. she screams that he's dead and grabs for me. and then we sat up all night building each other a better heaven than the parson ever managed. that's the last kind night this house ever has.

beats.title: The Dog Got Her
beats.modern: the son's back from college and I'm staff now, so we spend our nights on the moor. we go laugh at the rich kids through their window and their bulldog takes her ankle in the dark. I get a stone and try to jam it down its throat. they carry her in to the fire and the cakes and the warm water. me they drag out the gate as a thief. same crime, chat. two verdicts.

beats.title: She Came Back A Lady
beats.modern: five weeks in that house and she comes home in silk with curls and a feathered hat. she runs at me, kisses my face eight times, then backs up and LAUGHS. how black and cross you look. then she checks her dress for dirt where I touched it. fine. I'll be as dirty as I please. I'll be dirty forever actually. chat I never got over this one, and I mean never.

beats.title: Apple Sauce Incident
beats.modern: edgar linton says one thing about my hair so I grab the nearest object and put an entire tureen of hot apple sauce in his face. it was Christmas. I got hauled upstairs and beaten red for it. chat I would do it again tomorrow.

beats.title: Planning It Out
beats.modern: nelly asks what I'm thinking about, sat there sick by the fire with my chin in my hands. I'm working out how I pay Hindley back. I don't care how long it takes. I just need him not to die before I get to him. it's the only thing that stops it hurting.
beats.quote: I don’t care how long I wait, if I can only do it at last.

beats.title: I Caught The Baby
beats.modern: the drunk is dangling his own toddler over the banister to prove a point, hears a noise, forgets what's in his hands. kid falls. and I catch him. REFLEX. chat I looked up and understood what I'd just done. I caught my own revenge in two hands and stood it back on its feet. worst play of my life.

beats.title: It Would Degrade Me
beats.modern: I'm sat behind the settle while she tells the housekeeper she's marrying linton. and then she says it. it would DEGRADE her to marry me. so he shall never know how I love him. chat I didn't stay for the second half of that sentence. I stood up, walked out the gate, and disappeared off the map for three years.
beats.quote: It would degrade me to marry Heathcliff now; so he shall never know how I love him:

beats.title: The Part I Didn't Hear
beats.modern: here's what she said after I walked. that loving edgar is leaves on a tree, seasonal, it changes with the weather. that loving me is the rock the whole moor sits on: no visible delight, just necessary, always there. and then, flat out: nelly, I AM heathcliff. eight words. I was already at the gate.
beats.quote: My love for Heathcliff resembles the eternal rocks beneath: a source of little visible delight, but necessary.

beats.title: Gone In The Storm
beats.modern: she stood at the wall in the rain calling my name till midnight, and the storm took a tree down onto the roof and half the chimney into the kitchen fire. she caught a fever off it. she nearly died off it. I was already miles gone. no VOD of those three years, chat. don't ask where. don't ask how I got the money.

beats.title: Back, And Rich
beats.modern: three years later I'm stood in her husband's garden in the dark. tall now. black coat. money. I waited an hour before I could make a sound. nelly turns round and nearly drops her apples. go tell your mistress a person from gimmerton wants one word. one word. that's all I'm asking for.

beats.title: The Tyrant Rule
beats.modern: she wants to know how I'll take revenge on HER. I won't. that's not the build, chat. the tyrant grinds his slaves and they never turn on him, they turn on whatever's below them. she levelled my palace. now she wants to hand me a shed and be admired for the charity.
beats.quote: You are welcome to torture me to death for your amusement, only allow me to amuse myself a little in the same style,

beats.title: The Lamb Threw Hands
beats.modern: the milk-blooded husband actually swung on me. straight at the throat, while I was choking, then out the back door to go fetch men and pistols. I told her I'd crush his ribs like a rotten hazelnut. she'd already thrown the key in the fire to make him fight me. chat everyone in this kitchen is unwell.
beats.quote: “By hell, no! I’ll crush his ribs in like a rotten hazel-nut before I cross the threshold!

beats.title: Pigeon Feathers
beats.modern: three days locked in her room without food and now she's tearing the pillow open, sorting feathers by bird out loud. turkey. wild duck. pigeon. THAT'S why she can't die, chat, there's pigeon feathers in the pillow. then she finds a lapwing's, and remembers the nest full of little skeletons because I set a trap over it and the parents couldn't get back. she made me promise never again. that promise I kept.

beats.title: Married At Midnight
beats.modern: while she's upstairs raving about feathers, I'm at a blacksmith's two miles out of gimmerton at one in the morning, paying a sovereign for a horse's shoe, holding both bridles. edgar's sister is on the other horse with her hood up. yes chat, I married her. no I do not like her. she was never for that.

beats.title: Is He A Devil
beats.modern: my wife's first letter home. she has two questions for the housekeeper. one: how did you stay a human being living in this house. two: is mr heathcliff a man, is he mad, or is he a devil. she asks for someone to visit and bring her something from her brother. chat she's been married about a fortnight.
beats.quote: If so, is he mad? And if not, is he a devil?

beats.title: No Pity
beats.modern: the housekeeper asks if I've ever felt pity in my life. no. the more the worms writhe the harder I want to grind. it's teething, chat, it's just teething. then I tell her the terms: let me in that house or I walk in over her master's body. six hours in his garden last night. I'll be there again tonight and every night.
beats.quote: The more the worms writhe, the more I yearn to crush out their entrails!

beats.title: You Have Killed Me
beats.modern: I got in while they were at church. five minutes of holding her and I already know she's not coming back from this. and the first thing she says: you and edgar broke my heart and now you both want pity. you have killed me and thriven on it. how many years do you mean to LIVE after I'm gone. she's asking me to swear I'll be wretched forever. easiest promise of my life.
beats.quote: You have killed me—and thriven on it, I think.

beats.title: You Broke It First
beats.modern: why did you despise me. why did you betray your own heart. nothing could have parted us, not God, not the devil, not death, and YOU did it, of your own free will, for a poor fancy. I did not break your heart. you broke it, and breaking it broke mine. and she just says: I forgive you. forgive me. chat what am I supposed to do with that.
beats.quote: I have not broken your heart—you have broken it; and in breaking it, you have broken mine.

beats.title: Now You Are Mine
beats.modern: the drunk finally locked himself in and drank himself to death in one night, and it turns out he'd mortgaged every yard of this land to ME. so his son inherits a job. I lifted the boy onto the table before the funeral and told him: now, my bonny lad, you're mine. we'll see if one tree won't grow as crooked as another, with the same wind to twist it. he played with my whiskers, chat. he thought it was a nice speech.
beats.quote: “Now, my bonny lad, you are mine!

beats.title: Delivery Of My Property
beats.modern: my wife died down south and posted me a son. thirteen years old, white as milk, cries at the weather. I was afraid I'd have to come down and fetch my property myself. I looked at it and laughed in its face, chat. I don't need to love it. it only has to stay alive long enough to marry the right girl.

beats.title: The Wrong Boy
beats.modern: the girl walks into my house, calls me uncle, and kisses my face. so now I'm building a marriage: my dying son plus the grange heiress equals both estates in one hand. and chat, the sick joke of it. twenty times a day I look at the OTHER boy, the one I turned into a servant, and I know I'd have loved him if he'd been anyone else's.
beats.quote: Hareton!—Do you know that, twenty times a day, I covet Hareton, with all his degradation?

beats.title: The Door Locked Behind Them
beats.modern: got them both inside and turned the key in my pocket. the girl came at me for it and bit my hand, so I pulled her onto my knee and slapped her head from both sides till she couldn't stand. she stood there afterwards touching her own ears like she wasn't sure they were still on. I'm your father tomorrow, I told her. and her real one is dying four miles away and she is not getting back in time.

beats.title: I Opened The Coffin
beats.modern: eighteen years, chat. yesterday I paid the man digging the next grave to take the earth off her lid and I opened it. her face is still her face. I'd have stayed down there, he had to pull me out. so I knocked one side of the coffin loose, covered it back up, and paid him to slide mine out the same way when I'm laid in. by the time her husband gets down there nobody will be able to tell which is which.

beats.title: The Night I Took A Spade
beats.modern: the day they buried her it snowed. I went up at dusk with two yards of loose earth between us and I dug. hit the lid, went at the screws with my hands, nearly had it. and then a sigh, right at my ear. warm breath in a sleet wind. I knew there was nothing alive up there and I knew it was her, not under me, ON the earth with me. I filled the grave back in and walked home consoled. and she has not left me alone since.
beats.quote: myself—‘I’ll have her in my arms again!

beats.title: His Life Isn't Worth A Farthing
beats.modern: the girl came down asking for a doctor for my son. his life is not worth a farthing and I won't spend a farthing on it. act the nurse or lock him up and leave him. so she nursed him alone in that room, night after night, crying on the stairs where the servants could hear and chose not to. he signed everything over to me first, chat. then he went.

beats.title: She Kissed Him
beats.modern: and then the two kids I ruined start reading together by MY fire. she snaps his pipe, tells him he's her cousin and he'll own her, and when he won't shake her hand she just kisses his cheek. he couldn't work out where to look for a full minute. chat. they have the same eyes. they have HER eyes.

beats.title: An Absurd Termination
beats.modern: nobody warned me about this part. I won. levers, mattocks, the strength to pull both roofs down, every deed in my hand, nobody left who could stop me. and I get there and I find I can't be bothered to lift a slate. my enemies didn't beat me. I've just lost the taste for it. too idle to destroy for nothing.

beats.title: She's In Everything
beats.modern: I can't look down at the floor without her face in the flagstones. every cloud. every tree. the air at night. strangers' faces. MY OWN FACE mocks me with the resemblance. the whole world is one enormous pile of notes saying she existed and I lost her. that's the wallpaper now, chat. that's every single frame.
beats.quote: day—I am surrounded with her image!

beats.title: Three Feet To Go
beats.modern: they keep asking why I won't eat, where I go at night, why I'm smiling like that. last night I was on the threshold of hell. today I'm within sight of my heaven. I have my eyes on it. hardly three feet between us. now go away and stop prying and you won't see anything that frightens you.
beats.quote: To-day, I am within sight of my heaven. I have my eyes on it: hardly three feet to sever me!

beats.title: The Window Stayed Open
beats.modern: rain came in all night through the lattice. they found me on my back, soaked through, one hand grazed on the sill, eyes open and fixed and pleased. she tried to close them and they would not shut. four days without food, chat, and I wasn't doing it on purpose. I just kept forgetting. I had somewhere to be.

history-of-tom-jones.title: History of Tom Jones, a Foundling
history-of-tom-jones.author: Henry Fielding

beats.title: There Is A Baby In My Bed
beats.modern: chat I have been gone THREE MONTHS. I get home, say my prayers, pull back the covers to get into my own bed and there is a BABY in it. asleep. not mine. no note. and I am standing there in my shirt holding a candle like an absolute clown when the housekeeper walks in and nearly faints at the sight of my knees.

beats.title: Deborah Has Notes
beats.modern: my housekeeper's plan for the surprise infant: basket, churchwarden's doorstep, it's only a bit rainy, two to one it lives till morning. and if it doesn't, she reckons that's arguably the better ending for it. ma'am. MA'AM. meanwhile the baby has got hold of my finger and out-argued her without saying a word.
beats.quote: it is, perhaps, better for such creatures to die in a state of innocence, than to grow up and imitate their mothers;

beats.title: They Pin It On Jenny
beats.modern: the parish runs an investigation, meaning two women list every girl who ever acted above her station. they land on Jenny Jones. her crimes: reading Latin and owning one silk gown. she confesses immediately, no fight. the whole village piles on and she takes it flat. then one woman insults her face, and THAT is where the patience finally runs out.

beats.title: The Study Sermon
beats.modern: the parish wants her whipped at a cart's tail. I take her into my study and give her a talking-to instead. yes. a talking-to. she left the child where he'd be safe rather than in a ditch, so I'm reading that as love, not malice. the village is FURIOUS I didn't ruin her. they wanted content.

beats.title: The Keyhole Guild
beats.modern: my sister has a keyhole in my study door she has been working for YEARS. she and the housekeeper are crouched at it eating the whole scene raw. then she stands, smooths her dress, and delivers a speech about how she personally would never pry into other people's affairs. mask on so tight it is load bearing. remember this woman. remember her.

beats.title: Captain Blifil Runs The Numbers
beats.modern: a captain turns up and falls passionately in love with my sister. correction: with the house. and the gardens. and the lands, tenements and hereditaments. this man would have married the deed. the book says outright he'd have taken the witch of Endor if she came bundled with the estate. green flag behaviour, chat, absolutely.

beats.title: Eight Months
beats.modern: wedding was eight months ago. baby arrives today. midwife announces he was simply born a month early and everyone at the table goes yes, of course, a month early, absolutely. chat do the arithmetic with me one time. one time.

beats.title: Speedrun Denied
beats.modern: the captain has put YEARS into this. bought every book on how long people live. drew up renovations for a house he doesn't own. all of it waiting on one event: my death. and then, mid-daydream about my funeral, alone on his evening walk, he drops dead of a stroke. measured out exactly as much ground as he actually needed. six by two.

beats.title: I Sold The Horse
beats.modern: Thwackum wanted to beat the answer out of me. my guardian just asked. so I told him: the gamekeeper's kids were starving because of MY poaching, so I sold the horse he gave me and handed that family every penny. he went quiet a long time. then he cried. enjoy this beat, chat, it's the only time being good works out for me.
beats.quote: I sold the horse for them, and they have every farthing of the money.”

beats.title: He Let The Bird Go
beats.modern: Sophia has one bird. she loves this bird. Blifil asks to hold it for one second, gets it in his hand, and immediately slips the string and throws it at the sky. she screams. I'm off with my coat and up the tree after it. branch snaps. I go head first into the canal. that's Blifil. that is who he is, day one, aged about eleven.

beats.title: Blifil Gives A Statement
beats.modern: and then the little psycho holds a PRESS CONFERENCE. he was moved by the poor creature's longing for liberty. caging things is against nature and frankly unchristian. and oh, by the way, while Jones was busy drowning, a hawk got it. sir you workshopped this. Sophia's father says if that were his son he'd flay him.

beats.title: Molly Versus The Parish
beats.modern: the whole village jumps Molly Seagrim in a graveyard for the crime of wearing a nice dress. she drops the ringleader with one punch, picks a SKULL up off a fresh grave and throws it, then grabs a thigh bone and goes through the crowd like a raid boss. the narrator starts naming the fallen like it's the Iliad. a hundred of them. one of her. she was winning.

beats.title: Broke My Arm, Worth It
beats.modern: her horse bolts, I catch her coming off it, and my arm takes the entire landing. she's screaming BROKE YOUR ARM and I'm going ma'am, please, I've still got a right hand, let me walk you home first. then her father rides up, sees she's unhurt, and says: if Tom's broke his arm we'll get a joiner to mend un. thanks squire. love that for me.
beats.quote: If Tom hath broken his arm, we will get a joiner to mend un again.”

beats.title: What Fell Out Of The Curtain
beats.modern: I'm in Molly's room mid-argument and the rug she's nailed across the rafters comes down. behind it, folded into a hole in the ceiling, wearing HER nightcap, is Square. the philosopher. the man who lectures me weekly on the eternal fitness of things. staring directly at me. chat I could not have written it.

beats.title: He's Going To Live
beats.modern: the doctor comes down and says he's out of danger. out of DANGER. chat I was drunk on joy before the wine got anywhere near me, and then I hit the wine too. kissed the doctor. told him he deserves a statue at public expense. Thwackum sniffs that at least the old man lived long enough to cut me out of the will, and I said let the earth swallow every acre, I'd still take him alive.
beats.quote: D--n me if I don't love him better than my own soul.”

beats.title: Carving Her Name
beats.modern: so I'm out in the grove, hammered, monologuing SOPHIA ALONE SHALL BE MINE, penknife out, about to carve her name in a tree. I turn round. it is not Sophia. it is Molly Seagrim holding a pitchfork. fifteen minutes of conversation later we're in the trees. narrator's explanation: I reckoned one woman beat none and she reckoned two men beat one. and Blifil is watching from the stile.
beats.quote: Jones probably thought one woman better than none, and Molly as probably imagined two men to be better than one.

beats.title: Her Father Finds Out
beats.modern: her aunt rats us out in a single sentence. Western has genuinely never once considered his daughter could love a poor man, it was outside his physics. he comes down the hall roaring, swearing he'll kill me, kicks the door in. and stops dead, because Sophia has fainted in my arms. every scrap of rage leaves him instantly. he's screaming for water.

beats.title: Turned Out
beats.modern: he doesn't shout. that's the worst part. he tells me he raised me like his own son, hands me a sealed paper, says he will never speak to me again on any account. and then adds that the thing he resents most is how badly I treated Blifil. chat. BLIFIL. that one went in like a knife. paper had five hundred pounds in it and the whole county still says he threw me out naked.

beats.title: The Pocket Book
beats.modern: I tore my own pockets out by the brook during a breakdown, including five hundred pounds I never even opened. Black George helps me search. we go over every tuft of grass in that meadow. we do not check the only place they are, which is HIS POCKET, because he found them first and put them away for his own use. and he does it while genuinely being fond of me. that's the part that gets me.

beats.title: Midnight, Bag Packed
beats.modern: they want me married to Blifil TOMORROW. my father screamed at me until I said something that wasn't quite yes, he took it as yes, and then he kissed me and cried and handed me a bank bill for trinkets. so: maid dismissed on purpose, meeting place chosen, twelve o'clock sharp. I am leaving my father's house tonight.

beats.title: Cupid Kicks It Over
beats.modern: for about ten minutes I genuinely talked myself into it. the martyr version. obedient daughter, sacrifices herself, makes her father the happiest man in England, very holy, very moving, I was getting emotional about my own performance. then one thought of Jones walked in and kicked the entire thing over like a puppet show. so much for the saint arc.

beats.title: Say Her Name Again
beats.modern: joined the army heading nowhere. I toast Sophia Western at dinner and an ensign called Northerton informs the table he knows her, that half of Bath has had her. I tell him he is the most impudent rascal on earth. he replies with a full bottle to my temple. lights out. I come round in blood while everyone argues about whether I'm dead.

beats.title: Human Nature Is The Same Everywhere
beats.modern: met a hermit on a hill who has read everything and hates everyone. I ask what he learned from all those different countries. he says don't bother travelling, just go to carnival in Venice, you'll see every court in Europe at once, same fraud in different outfits. he walked through the entire world holding his nose. sir you TOUCHED grass and it made you worse.

beats.title: The Garter In The Wood
beats.modern: heard something in the trees. woman half stripped, man with a garter round her neck hauling her toward a branch. I asked zero questions, went in with the stick, and kept swinging until SHE told me to stop. then I tie his hands with that same garter, roll him over, and it's Northerton. bottle guy. chat, fortune has a sense of humour and it is not a kind one.

beats.title: Three Pounds Of Ox
beats.modern: we reach the inn at Upton and I want to be precise about the order of events here. Mrs Waters is across the table running an entire silent campaign of eye contact at me. and I notice none of it, for one reason: I have not eaten in twenty four hours and I am putting away roughly three pounds of beef. plate clear, attention available. she did not have to work hard.

beats.title: She Leaves The Muff
beats.modern: I rode all night. I got to Upton. he is upstairs with another woman. I don't scream and I don't go up. I take off the muff he once put his hands in, the one I've carried every day and slept with every night since he left, I pin my NAME to it in pencil, and I pay the maid to put it in his empty bed. then I get back on my horse.

beats.title: Here Lies The Muff Of One Of Them
beats.modern: Partridge is telling me he thinks we've slept in a bawdy house, that two wenches tried to get into my room, and oh, here lies the muff of one of them on the floor. I ask to see it. pinned to it, in her handwriting: Sophia Western. she was HERE. in this building. tonight. while I was in the wrong room.

beats.title: A Beggar Sells Me Her Name
beats.modern: a lame beggar offers to sell me something he found in a field. it's a little gilt pocket book. first page, her own handwriting: Sophia Western. I am kissing a book in front of witnesses. then a paper falls out of it, hundred pound bank bill. Partridge's eyes light up. mine don't. she's out there with nothing and I'm holding all of it.

beats.title: The Mask Comes Off
beats.modern: London. masquerade. I follow the domino I'm certain will lead me to Sophia. into a coach, into a house, into a warm room at two in the morning. finally get her to unmask and it is not Mrs Fitzpatrick. it is Lady Bellaston. we talk until six. the deal: she finds Sophia for me, and in exchange I stop seeing her. chat I want to flag that I agreed to that.

beats.title: Fifty Pound Note
beats.modern: I hand Partridge a fifty pound note to change and his eyes go bright, then dark, because the only explanation he can reach for is that I robbed someone. and honestly the reader can't do better either, unless the reader guesses the truth. which is that I am being kept. that's the word for it. she pays, and I'm paid.

beats.title: Lord Fellamar Shuts The Door
beats.modern: I'm alone reading a tragedy, crying at the ring scene, and a lord walks in uninvited and starts describing his own behaviour as a frenzy that I caused. he takes my hand. says if he owned the world he'd lay it at my feet. I told him I'd spurn his world and its master with equal contempt. and then I found out he was not planning to let me leave the room.
beats.quote: “I promise you, sir, your world and its master I should spurn from me with equal contempt.”

beats.title: Propose To Get Fired
beats.modern: I want out and I can't afford out. Nightingale's plan: propose marriage to her. she'll drop me on the spot, apparently a lad he knew tried it in earnest and was binned the same day. I said what if she says YES, then I'm caught in my own trap forever. he said relax, I can get you her letters. so my exit route from being kept is a fake engagement. this goes great.
beats.quote: propose marriage to her, and I would venture hanging upon the success.”

beats.title: I Have Satisfaction Enough
beats.modern: Fitzpatrick hits me first and draws. I have never had a fencing lesson in my life, so I just went straight at him and half my sword ended up inside him. he steps back, leans on his own blade, and says: I have satisfaction enough, I am a dead man. men rush in. I don't resist. I ask them to see to him first. constable has me by nightfall.
beats.quote: “I have satisfaction enough: I am a dead man.”

beats.title: Partridge Says It Out Loud
beats.modern: I'm in a cell for killing a man and Partridge comes in shaking. was that the woman from Upton. yes. did you go to bed with her. you know I did. and he says the Lord have mercy on your soul: that was your mother. chat. chat I can't. every single thing that has gone wrong in my life I did myself, and this is the bill arriving.
beats.quote: as sure as I stand here alive, you have been a-bed with your own mother.”

beats.title: The Letter With The Postscript
beats.modern: her letter arrives. she has met a gentleman, she has learned something about me that surprises and affects her, she cannot write it down yet, and that one day at Upton is going to embitter the rest of her life. I couldn't hold the paper. Partridge read it off the floor. then, at the very bottom, a postscript: Fitzpatrick lives. so whatever else I am, I am not a murderer.

beats.title: Square Writes From His Deathbed
beats.modern: the philosopher is dying and he writes to my guardian. says nothing sits heavier on his conscience than what he did to me. says on the word of a dying man that I'm innocent of the thing I was thrown out for, that when the old man lay dying I was the only person in that house who actually cared, and that the rest came from another person's baseness. he doesn't name Blifil. doesn't need to.
beats.quote: on the word of a dying man, he hath been basely injured.

beats.title: Your Sister Was The Mother
beats.modern: she tells me she has to say who really paid her. she says the woman was a near relation of mine. I said a relation? and she says: you had a sister. and then she says it out loud. my sister was the mother of the child I found in my own bed. the boy I raised out of pity and threw out of my house was my nephew the entire time.
beats.quote: “your sister was the mother of that child you found between your sheets.”

beats.title: The Message He Buried
beats.modern: the lawyer cracks. he says my sister took his hand on her deathbed, gave him a letter, and said: tell my brother, Mr Jones is his nephew, he is my son. bless him. then she fell back and died within minutes. and the letter went to Blifil. who said he'd delivered it. who then watched me throw my own sister's son out of the house and kept the paper.
beats.quote: Tell my brother, Mr Jones is his nephew--He is my son.--Bless

beats.title: O My Child
beats.modern: he picks me up off the floor and holds me and says: how have I been to blame, how have I injured you, what amends can I ever make. and I'm going sir, look at me, I've already been repaid ten times over. then he lays out every single thing Blifil did, one after another, and keeps apologising, and I keep telling him the wisest man alive would have been fooled exactly the same way.

beats.title: Look In The Glass
beats.modern: she says repentance earns pardon from someone who can actually judge sincerity, and she is not that someone. she says prove it with time. I said I've got better security than my word. took her hand, walked her to the mirror, told her the proof is standing in it. she blushed, half smiled, forced the frown back on, and said my image will leave his heart the moment I leave the room. brutal. also correct.

beats.title: A Twelvemonth, Perhaps
beats.modern: I beg her to name a date. any date. she says: a twelvemonth, perhaps. I told her she'd just named an eternity. and she goes, perhaps something sooner, I will not be teazed. and then, quietly: indeed sir, that day is in your own power. chat that's a yes. that's a yes with terms attached. I kissed her like I'd never dared before.
beats.quote: love.”--“A twelvemonth, perhaps,”

beats.title: Everyone At One Table
beats.modern: final scene. everyone who spent this entire book screaming at each other is sat at one table. Western already forgave her, hugged her before she could finish kneeling, and is now singing wedding songs so filthy my uncle has to say Fie, Mr Western, out loud, twice. Sophia and I are the quietest people in the room, because the biggest joy doesn't talk much. we were married that morning. five people in the chapel.

beats.title: GG From The Foundling
beats.modern: final stats, chat: the bastard nobody would name is the heir. the two men who spent this whole book calling me a reprobate are dead or exposed. Blifil got exactly the ending he built for himself. and every servant, tenant and neighbour on that estate blesses the day I married Sophia. from a baby in a stranger's bedsheets to that. stream's over. go outside.

beats.title: The River Stat Line
beats.modern: chat we are doing a river today and it is not a small river. four thousand three hundred miles. drains twenty-eight states. carries more water than the Rhine twenty-five times over. the drainage basin is bigger than England plus France plus Spain plus Germany plus Italy stacked together. this is not a body of water, this is a continent's plumbing and I'm about to learn every inch of it by heart.

beats.title: De Soto Logs Off
beats.modern: so the first European to see this river takes one look, dies, and gets buried IN it. then nobody comes back for a hundred and thirty years. Shakespeare was born, lived, died, and had been in the ground half a century before white guy number two showed up. imagine finding a whole continent's river and going 'nah.' these days we'd send fifteen expeditions: one for the creek and fourteen to look for each other.

beats.title: The Corpse-Maker Monologue
beats.modern: chat this raftsman just stood up and cut the most unhinged promo I have ever heard. he claims his dad was a hurricane. he eats nineteen alligators for BREAKFAST. he says his glance splits rock. then he cracked his heels together three times and screamed that he's the bloodiest son of a wildcat alive. no notes. absolute mic drop energy from a man standing on a pile of logs.
beats.quote: Sired by a hurricane, dam'd by an earthquake, half-brother to the cholera, nearly related to the small-pox on the mother's side!

beats.title: Snake As Big As A Cow
