beats.modern: balloon's built, whole city is watching, Oz is in the basket with his hand out for me. and Toto runs off to bark at a KITTEN. I go get him. I'm three steps away when the ropes snap. he calls down that he can't come back. chat the only man who knows the way out of here is now a dot in the sky and my ride home went with him.

beats.title: Region Locked Monkeys
beats.modern: scarecrow thinks so hard the pins come out of his head and produces a plan: use the cap, have the monkeys fly me over the desert. so I call them. the King bows, listens, and says no. they belong to this country and cannot leave it. there has never been a Winged Monkey in Kansas. chat I burned a wish to find out that monkeys are region locked.

beats.title: The Trees Have Bouncers
beats.modern: first row of trees in this wood is ALIVE. the scarecrow walks up and gets picked up and thrown back at us. tries a different tree, thrown again. so the tin man walks over and chops the arm off the one that did it, the tree shakes like it's in pain, and we all stroll under. Toto got grabbed and shaken until he howled and got cut free the same way. chat the trees were just security.

beats.title: The China Country
beats.modern: over the wall is an entire country made of CHINA. people no taller than my knee, houses the size of a footstool, cows that break. I chased a princess and she yelled don't chase me, if I fall I break. I asked if she'd come home and stand on Aunt Em's mantel. she said out there our joints stiffen and all we can do is look pretty. on the way out the Lion smashed a china church with his tail.

beats.title: The Coward Kills A Spider
beats.modern: whole forest is being eaten by a spider the size of an elephant with legs like tree trunks. the animals beg the Lion for help. he asks if they'll make him King if he handles it, walks over alone, notices the monster's head sits on a neck as thin as a wasp's waist, and takes it off in one swing while it's asleep. chat the coward has a kingdom now.

beats.title: Heads On Springs
beats.modern: a hill full of short armless men who fire their HEADS at you on a stretchy neck. the scarecrow tries to walk past and gets launched down the hill by a flying skull. the Lion charges and comes back down like a cannonball. his review: it is useless to fight people with shooting heads. so we spent our last monkey wish flying over the entire problem.
beats.quote: “It is useless to fight people with shooting heads; no one can withstand them.”

beats.title: The Exit Was On My Feet
beats.modern: Glinda tells me the silver shoes I looted off a dead witch on day one can carry me anywhere in the world in three steps. I could have gone home the FIRST DAY. the witch, the monkeys, the poppies, the kitchen, all of it optional. and then my friends said no wait, then I'd still be on a pole, I'd have rusted in that forest forever, I'd have been a coward my whole life. chat they were glad it didn't work.
beats.quote: “If you had known their power you could have gone back to your Aunt Em the very first day you came to this country.”

beats.title: Three Clicks
beats.modern: hugged the Lion. kissed the tin man, who immediately started crying in a way that is genuinely dangerous for him. hugged the scarecrow instead of kissing him because his face is paint. picked up my dog. clicked my heels three times and said take me home to Aunt Em. chat I'm crying, they're crying, the one with no heart is crying hardest.
beats.quote: “Take me home to Aunt Em!”

beats.title: Home Again
beats.modern: three steps, the wind stops, and I'm rolling across grass. Kansas. new farmhouse, Uncle Henry milking, Toto already sprinting for the barn. I stand up in my stocking feet: the silver shoes fell off somewhere over the desert, gone forever, so I have zero proof any of it happened. Aunt Em is watering the cabbages. she asks where in the world I came from. from the Land of Oz. chat I have never been so glad to see a gray farm. gg.
beats.quote: And oh, Aunt Em! I’m so glad to be at home again!”

beats.title: The Coffee-Pot Cam
beats.modern: I'm stood on the hearth-rug holding a client's forgotten walking stick doing my best detective impression, and Holmes, facing the other way, eyes nowhere near me, goes "well, Watson, what do you make of it?" I ask how he possibly knew. he says he has a well polished silver coffee pot in front of him. bro is running screen capture off the breakfast set.
beats.quote: “I have, at least, a well-polished, silver-plated coffee-pot in front of me,”

beats.title: Conductor Of Light
beats.modern: he tells me I may not be luminous myself but I am a conductor of light, and I'm sat there GLOWING, first compliment in years, might frame it. then he takes the stick, runs a lens over it, and calmly explains that most of my conclusions were wrong, he just triangulates the truth off my bad takes. love being the tutorial NPC.
beats.quote: It may be that you are not yourself luminous, but you are a conductor of light.

beats.title: He Covets My Friend's Skull
beats.modern: our client walks in, meets the most famous detective in England, and opens with: any objection to me running a finger along your parietal fissure. then says a cast of the skull would be an ornament to any museum. then clarifies he would rather have the original. sir. you have not told us the case yet.
beats.quote: It is not my intention to be fulsome, but I confess that I covet your skull.”

beats.title: Hugo Sells His Soul
beats.modern: 1742 lore drop, read to us off the actual manuscript. ancestor Hugo grabs a farmer's daughter, locks her upstairs, gets loud drunk with the lads below. she goes out the window down the ivy and runs three leagues home across the moor. Hugo finds the empty room, jumps on the dinner table scattering plates, and offers his body and soul to hell if he can catch her tonight. then he unkennels the pack.

beats.title: The Thing In The Goyal
beats.modern: the drunk posse rides down into the hollow and stops dead. the girl is lying in the grass, dead of fear and exhaustion. Hugo is dead beside her. and standing over him with its jaws in his throat is a black beast shaped like a hound and bigger than any hound alive. it turns and looks at them. one of the three died that same night. the other two were broken men for the rest of their lives.

beats.title: Footprints Of A Gigantic Hound
beats.modern: the doctor saved the real thing for last. no wound on the old man. face so twisted he could hardly swear it was his own friend. the butler told the inquest there were no marks around the body. except the doctor looked twenty yards further out. and chat, he found prints. he drops his voice to a whisper to tell us whose.
beats.quote: “Mr. Holmes, they were the footprints of a gigantic hound!”

beats.title: Devonshire In Spirit
beats.modern: come home, can't see the furniture. the room is one hundred percent tobacco smoke and Holmes is a silhouette inside it with a black clay pipe. he has not moved from that chair all day: two pots of coffee, an ordnance survey map of the moor, and he announces he has been to Devonshire. in spirit. king does location scouting from an armchair and charges for it.

beats.title: He Was Running
beats.modern: the inquest decided the old man strolled down his own garden path on tiptoe. Holmes: nobody tiptoes. that is not a stroll, that is a man SPRINTING in the dark. he ran until his heart burst and went face first into the gravel with his fingers dug into the ground. from what, chat. from what.
beats.quote: “He was running, Watson—running desperately, running for his life, running until he burst his heart—and fell dead upon his face.”

beats.title: Keep Away From The Moor
beats.modern: the heir gets post at his hotel. words snipped out of a newspaper and gummed onto a half sheet: keep away from the moor. one word written in ink because they couldn't find it in print. Holmes reads the typeface like a barcode, names the paper, the page, the leading article on free trade, and clocks that the cutter used nail scissors and was in a hurry. somebody is watching this man. somebody is also warning him.
beats.quote: As you value your life or your reason keep away from the moor.

beats.title: Lost Him In Regent Street
beats.modern: we tail the man tailing our client. bushy black beard, piercing eyes, watching us out of a cab window. he clocks us, screams at his driver, and the cab is gone down Regent Street before Holmes can grab another one. my friend comes out of the traffic panting, white with vexation, and tells me to write this one up too and file it next to the wins. fine. it's in the VOD.

beats.title: Now It's An Old Black One
beats.modern: day one someone stole one of his brand new boots at the hotel. never even worn. today they took an OLD BLACK one. he is stood in the corridor holding a single shoe, accent going full frontier, threatening to walk out of the den of thieves. and here's what nobody is saying out loud: whoever is doing this does not want new boots. they want a worn one. one that smells like him.

beats.title: The Fare Gave His Name
beats.modern: Holmes tracks down the cabman who drove the bearded man and asks who the fare was. cabman says the gentleman gave his name, actually. Holmes leans in like the case is over. the name was Mr. Sherlock Holmes. I have never seen my friend so completely blindsided in my life. he sat in silence and then laughed. we are being ratioed by someone who knows exactly who we are.
beats.quote: “His name,” said the cabman, “was Mr. Sherlock Holmes.”

beats.title: There Is A Murderer Out There Too
beats.modern: we get to Devon and there are soldiers with rifles stood on the hills watching every road. the driver explains: a convict broke out of the prison three days ago and they cannot find him. not an ordinary one either. Selden, the Notting Hill murderer, alive only because a court decided he might be too insane to hang. so that's out there in the dark with us. cool. cool cool cool.
beats.quote: “It is Selden, the Notting Hill murderer.”

beats.title: Someone Is Crying In This House
beats.modern: first night at the Hall. I pull the curtain: black moor, half moon through racing cloud, wind chewing the trees. can't sleep. and then in the dead of the night, inside this house, clear and unmistakable, a woman sobbing. the strangled kind you cannot fake. I sat up and listened for half an hour. nothing came back but the clock and the ivy.

beats.title: The Mire Eats A Pony
beats.modern: the naturalist neighbour points at the pretty green patches and explains that it is a bog which swallows anything that steps on it. mid sentence a pony wanders in. we watch the neck come craning up out of the mud, we hear it scream, and then the moor is quiet again. two in two days, he says, cheerful as anything. then he mentions he personally can walk to the very heart of it and come back alive. hold that thought, chat.
beats.quote: “A false step yonder means death to man or beast.

beats.title: Go Back To London Instantly
beats.modern: a woman comes running up the moor path and tells me to leave tonight. get away at all costs, never set foot here again. will not say why. then she hears her brother coming and flips mid sentence into cheerful small talk about orchids like nothing happened. and here's the part that's kept me up, chat: she thought I was Sir Henry. that warning was never meant for me.
beats.quote: Go back to London! Start tonight! Get away from this place at all costs!

beats.title: The Wooing Gets Interrupted
beats.modern: our baronet finally gets her alone on the moor and I am watching from a hill like an absolute creep. he puts an arm round her. and then her brother comes SPRINTING across the broken ground with the butterfly net flapping behind him, gesticulating, screaming in his face. white with fury over a rich man proposing to his sister. that is not protective. that is something else.

beats.title: The Convict Is Her Brother
beats.modern: the butler has been creeping to a window at two in the morning holding a candle against the glass, and we finally catch him mid signal. he will not talk. his wife does. the light is not a plot against anyone. the starving man out on the moor eating their leftovers is HER LITTLE BROTHER. the Notting Hill murderer is the housekeeper's curly headed baby brother and she will lose the job before she lets him starve.
beats.quote: “The escaped convict, sir—Selden, the criminal.”

beats.title: It Was The Cry Of A Hound
beats.modern: we're out hunting the convict and Sir Henry jokes about that line in the legend, the hour of darkness when the power of evil is exalted. the moor answers him. a long deep mutter, a rising howl, a sad moan dying away, again and again, the whole air throbbing with it. he asks what the country folk call that sound. I tell him. he says feel my hand. it was cold as a block of marble.
beats.quote: “They say it is the cry of the Hound of the Baskervilles.”

beats.title: The Man On The Tor
beats.modern: chase blown, sat on rocks getting our breath back, and I look up. a man is standing on the tor against the moon. tall, thin, arms folded, head bowed, absolutely still, like the moor grew him. I turn to grab Sir Henry's arm and point and when I look back he is gone. not the convict. not anyone I have met down here. somebody ELSE is out here with us.

beats.title: Burn This Letter
beats.modern: the butler owes us now, so he pays up. he knows why the old man was stood at that gate at ten at night. he was meeting a woman. she asked him to burn the letter and he did, but months later the wife found the ashes in the back of the grate and one strip of it still legible. please, as you are a gentleman, be at the gate by ten. signed with initials. L. L.
beats.quote: ‘Please, please, as you are a gentleman, burn this letter, and be at the gate by ten o clock.

beats.title: I Never Went
beats.modern: found L. L. quoted her own burned letter back at her across her typewriter and watched every bit of colour leave her face. yes she wrote it. yes she asked to meet him at that gate at that hour on that night. and then she swears on everything she holds sacred that she never went, something stopped her, and no she will not tell me what. she is lying about something. I just can't work out which part.

beats.title: Dr Watson Has Gone To Coombe Tracey
beats.modern: tracked the stranger to a prehistoric stone hut on the hillside. empty. blankets, a bucket, empty tins, a loaf. and under the food bundle, a sheet of paper with one line of pencil on it. Dr. Watson has gone to Coombe Tracey. it is not Sir Henry being watched, chat. it's me. every step I have taken on this moor has been reported to somebody.
beats.quote: “Dr. Watson has gone to Coombe Tracey.”

beats.title: A Lovely Evening My Dear Watson
beats.modern: I'm in the darkest corner of that hut with the pistol cocked, waiting to meet whatever lives here. boot on stone. closer. closer. a shadow falls across the doorway. and the voice says it is a lovely evening and I would be more comfortable outside. HOLMES. he has been on this moor the whole time. he has been reading my reports out here. I have been streaming to a man I thought was in London.
beats.quote: “It is a lovely evening, my dear Watson,”

beats.title: She Is Not His Sister
beats.modern: Holmes says it flat, like weather. the sister is his wife. has been the whole time. our friend has been falling in love with a married woman as bait in a trap, and the husband made very sure it never actually went anywhere. and the mild little bug collector with the straw hat and the green net turns, right there in front of me, into infinite patience, a smiling face, and a murderous heart.
beats.quote: The lady who has passed here as Miss Stapleton is in reality his wife.”

beats.title: The Scream On The Moor
beats.modern: mid conversation a scream tears out of the dark. then again, nearer. then a second sound underneath it, a deep rolling rumble like the sea. Holmes shouts THE HOUND and runs. one more despairing yell, a heavy thud, and then absolutely nothing. the man of iron put his hand to his forehead and stamped his feet in the heather.
beats.quote: “He has beaten us, Watson. We are too late.”

beats.title: The Ruddy Tweed Suit
beats.modern: we find him on the rocks. face down, head folded under him at an angle bodies do not go, shoulders hunched like he was mid somersault. Holmes strikes a match and it lights his own clotted fingers and the pool spreading from the crushed skull. and then the suit. that ruddy tweed suit. the one he wore the first morning we met him in Baker Street. I left him alone for one day.

beats.title: A Beard! The Man Has A Beard!
beats.modern: Holmes bends over the body and then he is DANCING. laughing. wringing my hand in the dark. a beard, he keeps saying, the man has a beard. it isn't the baronet. it's the convict, wearing the old clothes the butler handed down to help him escape. the hound was set on that scent. those hand me down clothes are what killed him. I have never been so glad about a dead man in my life.
beats.quote: “A beard! A beard! The man has a beard!”

beats.title: The Face In The Portrait
beats.modern: Holmes holds a bedroom candle up to the 1647 portrait of wicked Hugo, the ancestor who started all of this, and curves his arm over the plumed hat and the ringlets to blank them out. I actually shouted. it's Stapleton's face. our neighbour is a Baskerville. he is not haunted by the family curse, he is standing in the inheritance queue, and he has been quietly deleting the men in front of him.
beats.quote: The face of Stapleton had sprung out of the canvas.

beats.title: Walk Home Across The Moor
beats.modern: the plan, chat. Holmes tells our friend to go eat dinner alone in the murderer's house, send the trap home, and then walk back across the moor in the dark, the exact one thing we have spent a month telling him never to do. and he says fine. asks nothing. does not even want the reason. that man's nerve is the bravest thing in this whole case.

beats.title: Out Of The Fog
beats.modern: a thin crisp patter somewhere inside the fog bank. and then it comes out. a coal black hound the size of a small lioness with FIRE pouring off its mouth and its eyes and its muzzle. Lestrade screamed and threw himself flat. I froze with my hand on a pistol I forgot I was holding. it went straight past us after our friend, and Holmes outran me and emptied five barrels into its flank at full sprint.

beats.title: Phosphorus
beats.modern: I put my hand on the dead thing's muzzle and my own fingers came up glowing in the dark. phosphorus. it was PAINT. some bastard starved a bloodhound mastiff cross, painted it to look like hell itself, and pointed it at an old man's heart. there was never a curse on this family. there was a man with a tin of luminous mixture and a claim on the estate.
beats.quote: “Phosphorus,” I said.

beats.title: The Woman Tied To The Post
beats.modern: we kick the locked door open expecting the villain and instead there's his butterfly museum, glass cases everywhere, and lashed to the roof post with sheets, gagged with a towel, a pair of dark eyes staring back at us. it's his wife. we cut her down and the FIRST thing she asks is whether Sir Henry is safe. second, is the hound dead. there's a whip weal across her neck and bruises up both arms.

beats.title: The Mire Takes Him
beats.modern: she shows us the wands the two of them planted together to mark the safe path, and we go in at first light, thigh deep, the mud pulling at our heels like a hand. one trace of him the entire way: Sir Henry's stolen black boot sticking out of the slime where he flung it running. past that, nothing. no prints, no path, no man. the bog he used as a fortress closed over him.

beats.title: Poor Mortimer's Spaniel
beats.modern: on the island in the heart of the mire we find the kennel. a staple, a chain, a heap of gnawed bones, and a small skeleton with brown curly hair still stuck to it. Holmes clocks the breed in one look: curly haired spaniel. it's the doctor's little dog that wandered onto the moor and never came home. I did not need this part.
beats.quote: “By Jove, a curly-haired spaniel.

beats.title: He Has A Box For The Opera
beats.modern: and that's the case. two men dead, a murderer somewhere under the bog, a baronet on a boat round the world getting his nerves back. Holmes closes the file, asks whether I have heard the De Reszkes, and mentions he has a box for the opera and we can stop at Marcini's for dinner on the way. half an hour, Watson. stream's over. he's already bored.

the-man-who-was-thursday.title: The Man Who Was Thursday: A Nightmare
the-man-who-was-thursday.author: G. K. (Gilbert Keith) Chesterton

beats.title: The Poet Of Order
beats.modern: some red haired guy at a garden party thinks being an anarchist is a personality. bro. the train GOES to Victoria. every single time. do you know how insane that is? a man says a word and a station appears. chaos isn't deep, chat. chaos is just lag.
beats.quote: Chaos is dull; because in chaos the train might indeed go anywhere, to Baker Street or to Bagdad.

beats.title: Revolt Is Just Vomiting
beats.modern: he says rebellion is poetry. no. rebellion is being sick. sometimes necessary, never art. chat, the most poetical thing in the entire world is not throwing up. put it on a shirt.
beats.quote: Revolt in the abstract is—revolting.

beats.title: A Very Entertaining Evening
beats.modern: he ambushes me outside in the dark after the party and makes me swear on God I won't tell the police whatever he's about to show me. and what do I get for the vow? his exact words: a very entertaining evening. I took the deal. obviously I took the deal.
beats.quote: “I will promise you a very entertaining evening.”

beats.title: The Pub With A Trapdoor
beats.modern: ordered lobster mayonnaise in the grimmest pub in London purely as a bit. they BROUGHT the lobster. then the table starts spinning, the floor drops like a lift with the cable cut, and we land in a tunnel walled with rifles. chat I did not put my cigar down. not once.
beats.quote: “it’s a kind of screw.”

beats.title: Abolish God
beats.modern: asked him what the actual goal is. expected tax policy. he says: abolish God. not the government. God. right and wrong, deleted, patch notes blank. this is the guy who was doing poetry bits at a garden party ninety minutes ago.
beats.quote: “To abolish God!”

beats.title: Dress Up As An Anarchist
beats.modern: he tried disguising as a bishop, got clocked. tried a millionaire, defended capitalism so well everyone knew he was broke. tried a major, shouted BLOOD like a man ordering wine, clocked. so the boss tells him: dress as an anarchist, you fool, nobody expects an anarchist to actually do anything. he preached murder for a year and those women let him push their prams.
beats.quote: ‘Nobody will ever expect you to do anything dangerous then.’

beats.title: I Am A Police Detective
beats.modern: he made me swear first, which means he's locked into his oath too, so I just tell him: mate, that costume trick of yours? Scotland Yard has known it for years. I am a police detective. and right on cue I can hear his friends coming down the corridor.
beats.quote: “I am a police detective.

beats.title: We Are Executioners
beats.modern: they were about to elect a guy whose entire pitch was be nice and honesty is the best policy. so I stood up in a room built out of bombs and cooked him in front of his own cult. we are the enemies of society. we are not murderers, we are executioners. I am not a man, I am a cause. chat they were CHEERING.
beats.quote: We are not murderers, we are executioners

beats.title: The Man Who Was Thursday
beats.modern: Gregory finally breaks. on his knees in front of his whole branch: kill me, but obey me, do not elect this man. he can't say why, because why means admitting he walked a cop in here himself. they vote anyway. I'm Thursday now. I take his sword stick, his cloak, his boat, and I salute him from the deck. he did promise me an entertaining evening.
beats.quote: Strike, but hear me! Kill me, but obey me! Do not elect this man.”

beats.title: The Man In The Dark Room
beats.modern: the recruitment office is a room with zero light. can't see him, just know he's massive and facing away. I say I have no experience. he says nobody has experience of Armageddon. I say I'm unfit. he says willingness is the only test, that's the martyr trade, I am condemning you to death, good day. that was my job interview.
beats.quote: I am condemning you to death.

beats.title: Too Big To See
beats.modern: there is a thing on that balcony I didn't notice at first because it was too large to see. the President. head wrong size, ears wrong size, scaled up like a statue meant for a temple. the second I clock him the other five terrorists shrink into children at a tea party.
beats.quote: He had not seen it literally because it was too large to see.

beats.title: Bacon, Eggs, And A Bomb
beats.modern: they're doing this over breakfast. on a public balcony. sunshine, coffee pot, bacon and eggs, and they have just calmly settled how the Czar and the French President both die. the Marquis is carrying the bomb. the waiter downstairs thinks they're comedians.
beats.quote: over their bacon and eggs upon their sunny balcony these beaming gentlemen had decided how both should die.

beats.title: The Balcony Temptation
beats.modern: there is a policeman standing directly under this balcony. one shout and it's over, I go home, I sleep, I live. but I swore to Gregory I wouldn't. so I'm doing moral arithmetic with my hand on cold stone while the enormous man watches me with eyes I can't get away from. he knows. he absolutely knows.
beats.quote: He had promised not to jump over that balcony and speak to that policeman.

beats.title: The Barrel Organ
beats.modern: then a barrel organ starts up in the street, cheap jangly nothing tune, and something in me locks in. that's the sound of ordinary people walking into work. I'm not a cop right now, I'm their ambassador. so I go downstairs to die for people who will never learn my name, and under all the trumpets of the pride of life I can hear the drums of the pride of death.
beats.quote: He found himself filled with a supernatural courage that came from nowhere.

beats.title: There Is A Spy At This Table
beats.modern: he stands up and announces there's a spy in this room. a traitor at this table. hand on my revolver, I'm about to sell my life expensive. his name is... GOGOL. the hairy one. three men jump his throat and I fold into my chair like wet laundry. I have never been so happy to watch a stranger get grabbed.
beats.quote: “there is a spy in this room. There is a traitor at this table.

beats.title: Chased By A Dead Man
beats.modern: the corpse shaped professor is following me. I speedwalk across London, he's in the teashop ordering milk. I sprint a hundred yards and jump a moving bus, and thirty seconds later I hear wheezing behind me and there's the top hat rising up the steps. a man who moves by inches ran down a bus. explain the physics, chat.
beats.quote: the old man could only walk like a snail, and Syme had walked like the wind.

beats.title: That's A Pity, Because I Am
beats.modern: he corners me in a dockside tavern and asks it flat out: are you a police detective. I say no. I say it like a man standing on the trapdoor. he leans back, goes soft and kindly, and says, that's a pity, because I am. then lays an identical blue card on the table.
beats.quote: “That’s a pity,” he said, “because I am.”

beats.title: Strike Upwards
beats.modern: three of the seven are cops. I get cocky, three hundred of us against four? he says no. not three hundred against Sunday. so I swear to God I'll hunt down the one man I'm actually scared of and hit him in the mouth, because nobody should leave anything in the universe that they fear. he says Sunday is a fixed star. I said you'll watch him fall.
beats.quote: no man should leave in the universe anything of which he is afraid.”

beats.title: Arrested For Not Being Himself
beats.modern: so he's not a professor, he's an actor who parodied a famous philosopher so perfectly that the real philosopher got thrown out of the room for impersonating HIM. then a copper taps his shoulder in the street: sir, I am arresting you on the charge of not being the celebrated anarchist Professor de Worms. best sentence ever spoken out loud.
beats.quote: I am arresting you on the charge of not being the celebrated anarchist, Professor de Worms.’

beats.title: Poetry Over Morse Code
beats.modern: we built a finger tapping code so we can talk in front of the guy who might kill us. I use it to inform my ally I'm having a poetic intuition. he taps back: sit on it. I tap, it's like the smell of the sea inside deep woods. he taps: extraordinary rot. I tap: I am a poet. he taps: you are a dead man. then simply, go to hell.
beats.quote: Syme said, “I am a poet.” The other retorted, “You are a dead man.”

beats.title: Take Off Your Spectacles
beats.modern: so I bet my entire life on a vibe and politely asked the scariest man in the room to remove his glasses. underneath the black discs is a cheerful lad with hazel eyes who looks like he files paperwork. the goggles were the whole devil. I threw my police card down. he laughed and flicked his own card back at me.
beats.quote: Would you be so kind as to take off your spectacles?”

beats.title: Permit Me To Pull Your Nose
beats.modern: I need the bomber to miss the 7.45 to Paris, so I walk up, bow, and say permit me to pull your nose. then I invent an insult to my aunt out of thin air. she played Wagner badly, it's a painful subject, we're always being mocked about it. he challenges me. duel at dawn. train missed.
beats.quote: “Permit me to pull your nose.”

beats.title: The Sword That Draws No Blood
beats.modern: he hears the train coming and goes berserk, and that's when I land it. clean. I feel my sword bend inside his body. I look at the blade like an idiot. no blood. none. so I go for the throat and the cheek and still nothing marks him. chat I think I am fencing the devil.
beats.quote: Syme’s sword actually bent under the weight of the Marquis’s body, which it had pierced.

beats.title: The Nose Comes Off
beats.modern: mid duel the man throws down his sword and BEGS me to pull his nose, urgently, he has a train to catch. so I do it. it comes off in my hand. pasteboard. then he offers the colonel his left eyebrow, free, in case it comes in useful one day.
beats.quote: You wanted to do it, do it! You can have no conception of how important it is to me.

beats.title: Everybody Was A Cop
beats.modern: the Marquis peels his entire face off and he's Inspector Ratcliffe. so every man on the Supreme Anarchist Council was a detective except the President and his secretary. Sunday put all his enemies on one board and had us watch each other while he quietly bought the trains, the cables, the world. we were babies playing blind man's buff and he built the game.
beats.quote: Every born man was a detective except the President and his personal secretary.

beats.title: The Whole Town Turns
beats.modern: the kind rich doctor who lent us his car just fired twice at Bull. Bull walks back with two holes in his hat still insisting people are basically good. then I look up the hill and the sweet white haired innkeeper who waved us off is riding down at us with a sword. the morning star has fallen. every single person in this country wants us dead.
beats.quote: “The morning star has fallen!”

beats.title: The Lantern On The Pier
beats.modern: the colonel shoots my sword in half so I take the iron lantern off the wreck and put him down with it. then I hold the flame up at the Secretary and tell him: you didn't make this lamp, you didn't light it, you can make nothing, you can only destroy. and I threw the last Christian lantern into the sea so his people could never find it. no I was not normal about it.
beats.quote: You can make nothing. You can only destroy.

beats.title: There Never Was Any Council
beats.modern: cornered on a jetty, mob howling, we charge out to die, and the Secretary rips off his mask and ARRESTS me. in the name of the law. Scotland Yard. there never was any Supreme Anarchist Council. it was six policemen watching each other, and the townsfolk shooting at us thought we were the bombers. Bull is going ashore to buy everyone a drink.
beats.quote: “There never was any Supreme Anarchist Council,”

beats.title: I Am The Man In The Dark Room
beats.modern: six of us go up to ask him what he is. he rises like a wave about to break and says you'll understand the sea before you understand me, you'll know what the stars are and still not know what I am. kings and churches have hunted me forever, never caught me. then he swings over the balcony, hangs by his chin, and drops the line: I'm the man in the dark room. I made you all policemen.
beats.quote: You will understand the sea, and I shall be still a riddle; you shall know what the stars are, and not know what I am.

beats.title: The Elephant And The Balloon
beats.modern: he jumped onto a passing fire engine. then he went over the Zoo railings and stole an ELEPHANT. keeper says an elephant has run off with an old man. no mate. the old man has run off with the elephant. he rides it out the gates like a bus. we lose him at Earl's Court, and then the captive balloon stops being captive. he's in it, floating off like a soap bubble.
beats.quote: He has run away with the elephant.

beats.title: The Back Of The World
beats.modern: we're chasing a balloon across Surrey in rags and every one of us describes him differently, and every one of us compares him to the universe. when I first saw his back I knew he was the worst thing alive. then I came round the front and his face was good, and that scared me far more. that's the secret, chat. we have only ever seen the back of the world. everything is stooping and hiding a face.
beats.quote: We see everything from behind, and it looks brutal.

beats.title: I Am The Sabbath
beats.modern: the Secretary asks it straight. who and what are you. and without moving he says, I am the Sabbath. I am the peace of God. and the Secretary stands up shaking, because that is the exact thing he can't forgive. I can forgive God his anger, he says, even when it destroyed nations. I cannot forgive him his peace.
beats.quote: “I am the Sabbath,” said the other without moving. “I am the peace of God.”

beats.title: I Curse You For Being Safe
beats.modern: and then Gregory walks in dressed in absolute black, the only real anarchist there ever was. he says I never hated because I never lived. you are the police, you are the Law, you have never been broken. I don't curse you for being cruel. I don't curse you for being kind. I curse you for being safe.
beats.quote: I do not curse you for being cruel. I do not curse you (though I might) for being kind. I curse you for being safe!

beats.title: Have You Ever Suffered
beats.modern: so I stand up and answer him. it is not true that we were never broken. we were broken on the wheel. we went down into hell. every one of us was alone and terrified so that a man who keeps the law can be as brave as the man who breaks it. then I turn to Sunday and ask the only question left. have you ever suffered? his face grows to the size of the sky, and everything goes black.
beats.quote: “have you ever suffered?”

beats.title: Lilac Before Breakfast
beats.modern: and then I'm just walking. country lane, dawn coming up in yellow and rose, chatting about nothing with Gregory like we're old friends. I feel weightless, like I'm carrying impossible good news. Saffron Park rises around me, and there she is behind the fence, the girl with the gold red hair, cutting lilac before breakfast. stream's over, chat. good morning.
beats.quote: He felt he was in possession of some impossible good news,

beats.title: Day One Of The Grind
beats.modern: chat I'm sixty-five and I'm writing this entire VOD out for my son. stat check on the early game: born poor, no name, no connections, barely any money. current status: rich, known, my opinions get printed. and no I'm not going to pretend I don't want you copying the build. that is literally why I'm posting it.

beats.title: Second Edition Of Me
beats.modern: would I run this life again from the start? yeah. no notes. actually correction, I'd take the notes. authors get a second edition to fix the typos in the first one, and chat, I have typos. I call them errata. get comfortable with that word, it comes up a lot.
beats.quote: were it offered to my choice, I should have no objection to a repetition of the same life from its beginning,

beats.title: The Wharf Heist
beats.modern: there's a big pile of building stones sitting next to the marsh where we fish, unguarded, overnight. so I rally the boys and we haul every single stone and build ourselves a proper wharf to stand on. workmen show up next morning like where did the— yeah. we got caught. I pleaded utility. my father's ruling: nothing is useful that isn't honest. first ban of my life.
beats.quote: though I pleaded the usefulness of the work, mine convinced me that nothing was useful which was not honest.

beats.title: Signed At Twelve
beats.modern: dad watched me read literally everything in the house and went: printer. so at twelve I sign indentures to my own brother, locked in until I'm twenty-one, journeyman wages only in the final year. nine years. my brother is now my boss. chat. tell me how you think that goes.

beats.title: Half Board, Full Library
beats.modern: read one book about not eating meat and went full vegetarian, and honestly it was the math. I ask my brother for half my board money in cash and feed myself. bread, raisins, a tart, water. everyone else leaves for a two hour dinner and I stay in the shop alone with the savings and a borrowed book. clearer head too. the whole strat was books.

beats.title: Under The Door At Night
beats.modern: my brother would never print anything with my name on it. so I disguised my handwriting and slid an anonymous essay under the shop door at night. next morning his clever friends are stood in the room reading MY piece out loud, complimenting it, guessing which local scholar wrote it. I am sitting right there. setting type. saying nothing.

beats.title: The Warrant
beats.modern: the paper printed something the Assembly hated and they jailed my brother for a month because he wouldn't name the author. dragged me in too. I gave them nothing and they let me go, figuring an apprentice keeps his master's secrets. so I ran the paper myself and took shots at the government while he sat inside. then they banned him from printing it at all, so the masthead just says Benjamin Franklin now. loophole. paper never stopped.

beats.title: Erratum Number One
beats.modern: we fight again and I walk out, betting he can't show anyone the secret indentures without confessing the whole scheme. he can't. that was not fair of me and I'm logging it as erratum number one. he goes to every print shop in Boston and blacklists me, so I sell my books, get smuggled onto a sloop, and wake up in New York. seventeen. no contacts. almost no money.

beats.title: Three Puffy Rolls
beats.modern: I walk into Philadelphia filthy, no sleep, pockets stuffed with my own shirts and socks, and ask a baker for three pennies of bread. he hands me three enormous rolls. no pocket space, so I'm going up Market Street with a roll under each arm eating a third one. and THAT is the exact moment my future wife sees me for the first time, from her father's doorway. she thought I looked ridiculous. correct.

beats.title: The Governor Buys Madeira
beats.modern: the actual governor of the province walks across the street toward our shop. Keimer sprints downstairs assuming it's for him. it is not for him. the man apologises to ME for not meeting sooner, takes me to a tavern for the good Madeira, and offers to set me up in my own printing house. and Keimer's face, chat. the text says he stared like a pig poison'd.
beats.quote: and Keimer star'd like a pig poison'd.[30]

beats.title: The Boston Flex
beats.modern: went home to Boston in a genteel new suit with a watch and five pounds of silver in my pocket, walked into my brother's shop, and let his workers ask me about the new country. spread the silver on the bench so they could look at it. showed them the watch. tipped them a piece of eight for drinks. left. he told our mother he could never forgive that. he was wrong, but he did say it.

beats.title: Row, Or Swim
beats.modern: Collins is drunk in the boat and refuses to take his turn rowing. says he'll be rowed home. I say he won't. he comes at me swinging so I get a hand under him and put him head first into the Delaware. then every time he reaches the boat we pull a few strokes out of his reach. will you row? no? okay. fished him out eventually. he was also spending money I was only holding for someone else, and I never saw him or it again.

beats.title: If You Eat Each Other
beats.modern: principles fully locked in, no animal food, until they haul cod on deck and fry it and it smells incredible. I stand there arguing with myself for a while. then I remember seeing little fish inside the big fish when they're opened. so: if you eat one another, I don't see why we mayn't eat you. it is SO convenient being a reasonable creature. you can find a reason for anything you already decided to do.
beats.quote: "If you eat one another, I don't see why we mayn't eat you."

beats.title: Half-Starving My Boss
beats.modern: Keimer wants to found a religion with me. he preaches, I destroy all objectors. fine, I said, keep your beard and your Saturday sabbath, but the doctrine includes no meat. the man is a legendary glutton and I was fully in it to watch him suffer. three months of boiled potatoes and rice later he cracks, orders a roast pig, invites me and two women to dinner, and eats the entire pig before we arrive.

beats.title: The Letters Were Never Real
beats.modern: the governor promised me letters of credit and introductions to buy a press in London. said they'd be in the ship's bag. we reach the Channel, I open the bag, and there is nothing in there with my name on it. one letter I try to deliver gets me told the sender is a known rascal. I'm nineteen, on the wrong continent, sponsored by a man who was never sponsoring anything. he wanted everyone happy and had nothing to give, so he gave expectations.

beats.title: The Water-American
beats.modern: fifty pressmen in this London shop and every one of them is drinking beer from before breakfast until they clock out. my press partner does six pints a day and pays four or five shillings back out of his wages every Saturday. I drink water and carry two forms of type up the stairs while they carry one, so they start calling me the Water-American. the strength is in the grain of a penny loaf, not the pint. he drank on anyway. these poor devils keep themselves always under.

beats.title: Chelsea To Blackfriars
beats.modern: taught two lads to swim in about two sessions, so on the boat back the whole party wants a demo. I strip, go in the Thames, and swim the three miles from Chelsea to Blackfriars doing every trick I know on the surface and under it. crowd loved it. chat I came genuinely close to opening a swimming school in London instead of ever going back to America.

beats.title: She Married Someone Else
beats.modern: eighteen months in London and I wrote her exactly one letter, and the letter said I probably wasn't coming back. so her friends married her off to a potter. he already had a wife somewhere, ran up debts, skipped to the West Indies and died there. she refused to live with him or use his name. that one is on me and I'm logging it.

beats.title: Mind Your Business
beats.modern: big commotion by the courthouse so I put my head out the window to see. Keimer is down in the street and screams up at me in front of every neighbour to mind my business, then comes upstairs still going. he offers me the quarter's notice our deal requires. I told him not to bother waiting, took my hat, and walked out the door that instant.

beats.title: First Five Shillings
beats.modern: press barely bolted together, every penny of cash already spent, and a countryman walks in off the street looking for a printer. five shillings. chat I have earned crowns since and not one of them landed like that first five did. I've been soft on young beginners ever since, purely because of the friend who walked him through my door.

beats.title: A Sheet A Day
beats.modern: one sheet a day of that folio, no exceptions. one night I've locked up the forms, work's done, and one breaks and two pages fall into complete disorder on the floor. so I set them again before bed. meanwhile the merchants' club has us written off as the third print shop in town that fails, until Dr. Baird tells the room what he sees walking home at night.
beats.quote: I see him still at work when I go home from club, and he is at work again before his neighbors are out of bed."

beats.title: Taking Her To Wife
beats.modern: we couldn't marry cleanly. the potter might be alive somewhere, and if he was dead I might inherit his debts. we did it anyway, first of September, 1730. not one of the disasters we braced for happened. she folded pamphlets, minded the shop, bought old rags for the papermakers, and we got there together. best erratum I ever corrected.

beats.title: The Subscription Library
beats.modern: the club kept quoting books that only one of us owned, so: fifty subscribers, forty shillings each to start, ten a year after. import the books, open one day a week, lend on a note promising double the value if you don't bring it back. now a tradesman reads what a gentleman reads. every subscription library in North America came out of that room.

beats.title: The China Bowl
beats.modern: breakfast was bread and milk in a twopenny earthen bowl with a pewter spoon, for years. then one morning it arrives in a China bowl with a SILVER spoon. my wife bought them behind my back, twenty-three shillings, and her entire defence was that her husband deserved a silver spoon as much as any of the neighbours. first plate in the house. chat, it did not stay the last.

beats.title: Moral Perfection Speedrun
beats.modern: new project: live without committing any fault at any time. I know what's right, so logically I just always do that. turns out that is not how a human runs. you guard one fault and another one walks in behind it, habit exploits every lapse in attention, and inclination beats reason on a bad day. so I wrote out thirteen virtues, one line of rules each, and decided to farm them.

beats.title: The Spot Book
beats.modern: built the tracker. little book, one page per virtue, seven columns for the days, thirteen red lines down the page. every evening I go back through the day and put a black dot on every virtue I broke. week one you only guard Temperance and let the rest ride, then you add a line, thirteen weeks for a full course, four courses a year. yes I gamified my own soul.

beats.title: A Speckled Ax Is Best
beats.modern: Order absolutely destroyed me. papers everywhere, never learned the habit young, relapsed constantly, nearly quit and accepted being a mess. like the man who wanted his whole ax polished as bright as the edge, turned the grindstone until his arms died, and decided actually he likes a speckled ax best. and my brain kept helpfully suggesting that a perfect character would only get me envied, and that a decent man leaves a few faults in to keep his friends comfortable.
beats.quote: "No," said the smith, "turn on, turn on; we shall have it bright by-and-by; as yet, it is only speckled."

beats.title: Proud Of My Humility
beats.modern: had twelve virtues until a Quaker friend informed me, with examples, that I come off arrogant. so Humility gets added. never actually acquired the thing. got extremely good at the appearance of it though: no certainly, no undoubtedly, just I conceive, it appears to me, if I am not mistaken. fifty years and nobody's heard a dogmatical word out of me. pride is the one you cannot kill. if I ever thought I'd beaten it, I'd be proud of my humility.

beats.title: Poor Richard Ships
beats.modern: started an almanac under a fake name and it moves ten thousand a year, in basically every house in the province. these are people who buy no other book all year, so I filled every empty space between the calendar dates with proverbs about working hard and not spending. then I collected the best ones into one old man's speech at an auction, and that thing got reprinted everywhere, pasted on walls, translated twice into French, handed out free by the clergy.

beats.title: Francis, Four Years Old
beats.modern: I lost a son to smallpox in 1736. he was four. I hadn't inoculated him. I meant to. parents skip it because they think they could never forgive themselves if the child died under the operation, and mine died the other way instead. I regretted it bitterly then and I still do. if you're weighing it: the regret is identical either way, so take the safer one.

beats.title: The Book Loan
beats.modern: new member in the House makes a long speech against me, and he's got money, education, and a real future in that room. I don't grovel. instead I write asking to borrow a very rare book from his library. he sends it. I return it in a week with a warm thank you. next time we meet he speaks to me for the first time ever, and we were friends until he died.
beats.quote: "He that has once done you a kindness will be more ready to do you another, than he whom you yourself have obliged."

beats.title: Gold And All
beats.modern: Whitefield wants his orphan house built in Georgia instead of here, which is logistically stupid, so I refused to donate. then I'm at the sermon and I can feel a collection coming, and I have decided this man gets nothing from me. he preaches. okay, he can have the coppers. he keeps going. fine, the silver. he finished so admirably that I emptied the whole pocket into the dish, gold and all.

beats.title: Eighteen Cannon By Madeira
beats.modern: sent to New York by the association to borrow cannon for our new battery. Governor Clinton refuses us flat, peremptorily, no. then we sit down to dinner with his council and the Madeira starts going round. he softens by degrees and says six. a few more bumpers, ten. by the end, very good-naturedly, eighteen. eighteen-pounders with carriages. and yes I stood my own nightly watch on that battery like any other soldier.

beats.title: Other Grain Is Gunpowder
beats.modern: the Assembly can't buy gunpowder, that's an ingredient of war, principles. so when New England needs powder they vote three thousand pounds to the governor for the purchase of bread, flour, wheat, or other grain. the council tries to get him to refuse it as not the thing he asked for. he declines to play along.
beats.quote: "I shall take the money, for I understand very well their meaning; other grain is gunpowder,"

beats.title: No Patent On The Stove
beats.modern: invented an open stove that heats a room on less fuel by warming the incoming air. gave the model away to a friend with an iron furnace, wrote the pamphlet, demand went vertical. the governor offered me a patent, sole right to sell them for years. declined. we all live off other people's inventions, so when you land one you hand it over freely. then a London ironmonger reprinted my pamphlet as his own, made the machine slightly worse, patented it there, and made a little fortune. sure.

beats.title: The Rum At Carlisle
beats.modern: treaty at Carlisle. we forbid selling them any liquor while business is going, and promise them plenty of rum the moment it's done. they stay sober, the treaty concludes well, and then we hand over the rum we promised. that evening there's a bonfire in the middle of the square and a hundred men and women fighting by firelight, and we stand there looking at what we did, and then we go back to our lodging. midnight they're pounding on our door for more. we don't answer.

beats.title: The Conditional Clause
beats.modern: country members won't fund the hospital. it only helps the city, let the city pay, and they doubt the citizens even want it. so I write the bill so the two thousand pounds releases ONLY if the contributors first raise a matching stock themselves. suddenly the men who opposed the grant vote for it, since now they get to look charitable for free. then I tell every donor their money is doubled. clause worked both ways. no political manoeuvre ever pleased me more.

beats.title: The Plan Nobody Wanted
beats.modern: drew up a plan on the road to Albany: all the colonies under one government for defence, a president-general from the crown, a grand council elected by the assemblies. congress amends it slightly and passes it unanimously. then the colonial assemblies kill it for having too much crown in it, and England kills it for being too democratic. both sides hating it for opposite reasons makes me think it was exactly right. united like that we'd have defended ourselves, needed no troops from England, and skipped the pretext for taxing us and the bloody contest after.

beats.title: One Hundred Fifty Waggons
beats.modern: Braddock's whole campaign is stalled because he has twenty-five waggons and needs a hundred and fifty. I made the mistake of saying every farmer in Pennsylvania has one, so it instantly became my problem. eight hundred pounds from the general, another two hundred of my own on top, and in two weeks a hundred and fifty waggons and two hundred and fifty-nine horses are marching to camp. the owners didn't trust the general's promise, so they made me personally bond for every horse. remember that.

beats.title: Impossible They Should Make Any Impression
beats.modern: he's telling me Fort Duquesne holds him three or four days max, then Niagara, then Frontenac. I say the one danger is ambush, because his line will be four miles long in cut woods and can be sliced like a thread. he smiles at my ignorance and explains that natives may trouble raw militia but on the king's regular troops it is impossible they should make any impression. nine miles out, fire from behind the trees, officers picked off first, men standing in a huddle being shot until two thirds are dead. then the panic, and the whole army runs.

beats.title: Eleven Farmers, Ten Dead
beats.modern: eleven farmers driven off their land ask me for guns so they can go back for their cattle. I give each of them one with ammunition. then it rains on us all day, no shelter until nightfall, and we sleep in a German's barn as wet as water could make us, our gun locks soaked. lucky nobody hit us. the same day the enemy met those eleven farmers and killed ten. the survivor said their guns wouldn't fire. the priming was wet with the rain.

beats.title: Rum After Prayers
beats.modern: chaplain complains nobody turns up to prayers. meanwhile every single man is punctual twice a day for his gill of rum. so I told him: might be beneath your profession to act as steward of the rum, but you hand it out, and you hand it out immediately after prayers. never were prayers more punctually attended. better system than flogging them for it, which is the standard military fix.

beats.title: They Shot My Lab
beats.modern: officers elect me colonel. twelve hundred well-looking men on parade, artillery firing twelve rounds a minute. first review they escort me home and salute with a few rounds outside my door, which shook down and broke several glasses of my electrical apparatus. the honour was about as sturdy: England repealed the law and every commission with it. also thirty of them once escorted me out of town with swords drawn the whole way, which the proprietor took as proof I was planning to seize the province by force.

beats.title: Laughed At By The Connoisseurs
beats.modern: wrote up every electrical experiment we ran and sent it to London. the Royal Society didn't think it worth printing in their Transactions. the paper arguing lightning and electricity are the same thing got read out to them, and word came back to me that it was laughed at by the connoisseurs. cool. noted.

beats.title: Always On Horseback
beats.modern: Lord Loudoun is holding four packet boats in New York harbour because his letters will be ready tomorrow. every day. for months. I meet a messenger in his antechamber who has come by order every single morning for two weeks for one letter. I said how, the man is constantly at his desk with a pen in his hand? he said: he's like St George on the signs, always on horseback and never rides on. Pitt eventually removed him for precisely that.

beats.title: You Must Not Think Of Persuading Us
beats.modern: I advanced over a thousand pounds of my own money supplying that army. every article gets checked against its voucher and certified correct. then Loudoun decides not to mix his accounts with his predecessor's, just exhibit them at the treasury in England and you'll be paid immediately. and when I mention I charged no commission for any of it, he tells me not to try persuading him I'm no gainer, because everyone who supplies an army fills his own pockets. I am not paid it to this day.

beats.title: As Big As A Cartwheel
beats.modern: watchman in the bow answering ay, ay with his eyes shut. midnight, every sail set, running fast before a fresh wind, our captain asleep. the ship yaws by accident and there is a light dead ahead that looked to me as big as a cartwheel. Kennedy comes up, sees it, and wears the ship round with all sails standing, which could have taken the masts off. we were running straight at the rocks the lighthouse is built on. I have been extremely pro-lighthouse ever since.

beats.title: The King Is The Legislator
beats.modern: first big room in London and the President of the Council tells me flatly that we Americans have wrong ideas about our own constitution. the king's instructions to governors aren't notes, he says, they're drafted by judges, debated in Council, signed by the king, and they are the law of the land, because the king is the legislator of the colonies. I said that's new doctrine to me, our charters say our assemblies make our laws. he assured me I was totally mistaken. I went straight back and wrote the whole conversation down.
beats.quote: "You Americans have wrong ideas of the nature of your constitution;

beats.title: Stream Cuts Out
beats.modern: Denny finally passes the act taxing the proprietors' estates like everyone else's, and they petition the king to kill it. mid-hearing Lord Mansfield pulls me into the clerk's room and asks if I'll personally engage that no injury comes to their estate. certainly. paper drawn, signed, law stands, and the assessors' own report later shows the tax was levied with perfect equity. the Penns threw Denny out and threatened to sue him, and he despised the threats, and they never— [and there the manuscript stops. that's the whole VOD, chat.]

beats.title: Late Summer, Troops Going Past
beats.modern: we're billeted in a village with the river out front and the mountains behind. troops go past all day and the dust they kick up powders the leaves off the trees. at night you can see the guns flashing up in the mountains, like heat lightning if heat lightning killed people. genuinely the prettiest map I have ever been deployed to.

beats.title: Only Seven Thousand
beats.modern: the king drives past our sector most days in a very fast little car to see how things are going. things are going very badly. winter patch notes: permanent rain, and with the rain, cholera. and I want you to hear how the report puts it, chat. ONLY seven thousand died of it. only. somebody upstairs filed that as a good month.
beats.quote: At the start of the winter came the permanent rain and with the rain came the cholera. But it was checked and in the end only seven thousand died of it in the army.

beats.title: My Roommate Rinaldi
beats.modern: back from leave. roommate wakes up, kisses me, tells me I'm dirty, demands a full debrief on every city I visited. then announces he's in love with an English nurse and will probably marry her. then borrows fifty lire off me to fund the courtship and calls me his great and good friend and financial protector. I have been in this room ninety seconds.
beats.quote: I am now in love with Miss Barkley. I will take you to call. I will probably marry Miss Barkley.”

beats.title: The Slap
beats.modern: so I lean in to kiss the English girl in the garden and she slaps me hard enough that my eyes water on reflex. earned it. then she apologizes. then she says she'd be glad to kiss me. then she's crying on my shoulder asking me to be good to her. chat I do not know what this is but she signs off with "we're going to have a strange life" and honestly? forecast accepted.
beats.quote: I leaned forward in the dark to kiss her and there was a sharp stinging flash. She had slapped my face hard.

beats.title: A Rotten Game
beats.modern: full transparency for the VOD: I do not love her. I'm running the lines because it beats the officers' house every night. it's bridge, except you say things instead of playing cards, and nobody's told me what the stakes are. then she looks right at me and says this is a rotten game we play, isn't it. she's been reading my hand the entire time.
beats.quote: “This is a rotten game we play, isn’t it?”

beats.title: Passini Debates The War
beats.modern: my driver is arguing me into the ground in a dugout. I say we have to finish the war. he says a war doesn't finish, that victory doesn't win it, one side just has to stop. I say defeat is worse. he says what's defeat, you go home. why is the mechanic in the hole the smartest man on this entire front.
beats.quote: “There is nothing worse than war.”

beats.title: Macaroni And The Trench Mortar
beats.modern: we're eating cold macaroni out of a basin with our hands because there are no forks. I pare the brick dust off the cheese with my knife. wine tastes like rusty metal. then a cough, then chuh-chuh-chuh, then a blast furnace door opens and I go out of my own body sideways. I knew I was dead. then I slid back in. turns out you don't just die.
beats.quote: I knew I was dead and that it had all been a mistake to think you just died.

beats.title: My Knee Wasn't There
beats.modern: I get my legs loose and crawl to Passini. both legs smashed above the knee. he's begging Mary to shoot him, then he stops begging. I go for his puttee to make a tourniquet and there's no point, he's already gone. then I sit up and something rolls behind my eyes and my shoes are warm and wet inside. I reach down for my knee. my knee is on my shin.
beats.quote: My knee wasn’t there. My hand went in and my knee was down on my shin.

beats.title: The Priest Explains Love
beats.modern: priest comes to my hospital bed and tells me I don't love God. correct. then he says the nights I keep bragging about aren't love either, that's just passion. love is when you want to do things for someone. sacrifice for. serve. I tell him if I ever catch it I'll let him know. chat, timestamp this one.
beats.quote: When you love you wish to do things for. You wish to sacrifice for. You wish to serve.”

beats.title: She Walks In And I'm Done
beats.modern: they shipped me to Milan. she got herself transferred to the same hospital. I hear someone in the hall and it's her, and chat, everything turned over inside of me. three weeks ago this was a bit I was running. she walked through the door and the bit was over.
beats.quote: When I saw her I was in love with her. Everything turned over inside of me.

beats.title: Six Months, They Say
beats.modern: three doctors come stand around my leg, bend the knee until I yelp, look at each other, and rule: six months before anyone opens it. six. months. so I tell them fine, cut it off, I'll wear a hook. house doctor immediately tells the room I'm joking and that I'm a very brave young man up for a silver medal. I was not joking.
beats.quote: “I want it cut off,” I said, “so I can wear a hook on it.”

beats.title: Doctor Valentini
beats.modern: second opinion walks in with his mustaches pointing at the ceiling, laughing the entire time. calls the war bloody. calls my girl lovely. offers to do all our maternity work for free. asks if she'll have supper with him. then says he operates tomorrow morning. I offer him a drink and he says a drink? certainly, I will have ten drinks. hire this man for everything.
beats.quote: “A drink? Certainly. I will have ten drinks. Where are they?”

beats.title: There Isn't Any Me
beats.modern: she asks how many girls there were before her. I lie. she tells me to keep lying, that's what she wants. then she says the line that's going to sit in my chest for the rest of the stream: I want what you want, there isn't any me any more. and she's smiling when she says it. like she's winning something.
beats.quote: “I want what you want. There isn’t any me any more.

beats.title: You're My Religion
beats.modern: I take her hair down pin by pin and it comes over both of us like being inside a tent. we've decided we got married the day she walked into the hospital and we count the months from there, because real paperwork would get her shipped home. I ask if anything worries her. only being sent away from me, she says. you're my religion, you're all I've got.
beats.quote: You’re my religion. You’re all I’ve got.”

beats.title: Afraid Of The Rain
beats.modern: she asks if I'll still love her in the rain. yes. then, flat: I'm afraid of the rain. why. because sometimes I see me dead in it. and sometimes, she says, I see you dead in it. then she takes it all back, says it's nonsense, says it twice, says she wishes she wasn't, and cries. outside it kept on raining.
beats.quote: I’m afraid of the rain because sometimes I see me dead in it.”

beats.title: Three Months Along
beats.modern: she's tight and strange all evening and won't say why. I push. she says she's going to have a baby, almost three months, and then immediately starts managing MY feelings about it. don't worry. everybody has babies. it's natural. I say you always feel trapped biologically and she goes a long way away without moving an inch.
beats.quote: “I’m going to have a baby, darling. It’s almost three months along.

beats.title: Van Campen Finds The Bottles
beats.modern: head nurse finds the empty bottles in my wardrobe and files a report that I gave myself jaundice drinking so I could dodge the front. she says I should have tried something more intelligent. so I ask if she's ever known a man to disable himself by kicking himself in the scrotum, since that's the nearest sensation to jaundice, and she leaves the room. she also takes my leave with her.
beats.quote: I should think you would try something more intelligent than producing jaundice with alcoholism.”

beats.title: The Red Plush Room
beats.modern: last night before the front. only room we can get is red plush and mirrors, the kind rented by the hour. she sees herself in it and says very quietly that she never felt like a whore before. then she calls me over and says she's a good girl again. we eat, we drink the wine, and inside an hour the room is home. we are extremely good at making homes out of rooms we have to leave.
beats.quote: “I never felt like a whore before,” she said.

beats.title: Rinaldi Comes Apart
beats.modern: my best friend is drunk at the mess, baiting the priest, telling him the meat he's eating is dead Austrian, telling the whole table to hell with the whole damn business. then it comes out sideways: he thinks he has syphilis. what if I have it, everybody has it, the whole world's got it. he calls it a simple industrial accident and pours another one.
beats.quote: What if I have it. Everybody has it. The whole world’s got it.

beats.title: Abstract Words
beats.modern: Gino says what was done this summer can't have been in vain and I just go quiet, because I can't hear those words any more. sacred, glorious, sacrifice. I've seen nothing sacred. the sacrifices were a stockyard where nobody used the meat. the only things left with any dignity are the names of the villages, the road numbers, the rivers, the dates.
beats.quote: Abstract words such as glory, honor, courage, or hallow were obscene beside the concrete names of villages,

beats.title: I Shot The Sergeant
beats.modern: ambulance is buried in mud. I order the two engineer sergeants to cut brush. they tell me I can't order them, I'm not their officer, and start walking. I say halt. they walk faster. so I open the holster, aim at the one who talked the most, and fire. Bonello asks if he can go finish him and I hand him the pistol. that's who I am now, apparently.
beats.quote: I opened up my holster, took the pistol, aimed at the one who had talked the most, and fired.

beats.title: Aymo, By Our Own Side
beats.modern: shots out of the brush by the side road. Aymo is crossing the tracks and he lurches, trips, goes down face first. through the back of the neck, out under the eye. he died while I was still plugging the two holes with my fingers. and chat, it wasn't the Germans. it was our own rear guard, scared of everything, shooting at their own retreat.
beats.quote: He died while I was stopping up the two holes.

beats.title: The Bridge Police
beats.modern: we get across the bridge and the battle police are pulling officers out of the column and shooting them by the river. they question one man loudly while they shoot the last one behind him, so nobody ever has time to move. an old lieutenant-colonel asks them to skip the questions and just do it. verdict off a notepad: abandoned his troops, ordered to be shot. and I speak Italian with an accent.
beats.quote: “please shoot me at once without further questioning. The questioning is stupid.”

beats.title: Into The River
beats.modern: they turn to look at the new prisoners and I duck, shove between two men and run for the water with my head down. shots. I go under and stay under until my lungs quit, come up for one breath, go straight back down. grab a piece of floating timber, hold on with one hand, and refuse to look at the bank. the shore was out of sight now.
beats.quote: The water was very cold and I stayed under as long as I could.

beats.title: Anger Was Washed Away
beats.modern: lying on a flatcar under canvas with a load of artillery, and here's my status: the anger went down the river with everything I owed them. it stopped being my war the second that carabiniere put his hand on my collar. I'm not against them. there are good ones and brave ones and they deserve better. I'm just out. I wish them all the luck.
beats.quote: Anger was washed away in the river along with any obligation.

beats.title: A Separate Peace
beats.modern: civilian clothes, borrowed off a friend, and I feel like a guy in a costume. the aviators in my compartment won't look at me, scornful of some healthy civilian riding trains. I've got the paper and I don't open it, because I'm not reading about the war any more. I made a separate peace. one man, one treaty, zero other signatories.
beats.quote: I was going to forget the war. I had made a separate peace.

beats.title: The World Breaks Every One
beats.modern: we're in a hotel by a lake, wrecked and happy, and I'm going to say the true thing out loud while it's good. the world breaks every one, and afterward a lot of people are strong at the broken places. the ones who won't break, it kills. the very good and the very gentle and the very brave, no order to it, no reason. and if you're none of those, it still kills you. just no special hurry.
beats.quote: The world breaks every one and afterward many are strong at the broken places. But those that will not break it kills.

beats.title: Rowing All Night
beats.modern: thirty-some kilometres of lake to row before daylight, in the rain, past customs boats. my hands blister through and keep going. she offers to row "in moderation" because apparently that's healthy for the pregnant lady. I try to sail using an umbrella, it turns inside out over my face, and she laughs so hard she can't get words out. best night I've ever had.
beats.quote: “You looked so funny holding that thing.”

beats.title: Breakfast In Switzerland
beats.modern: grab the iron ring, step up onto wet stone, and we are in Switzerland. no rolls in wartime so we take toast, jam, coffee, four eggs. a fat gray cat comes and rubs my leg. I mention they'll probably arrest us and she says fine, you won't mind being arrested after breakfast. they arrested us after breakfast.
beats.quote: You won’t mind being arrested after breakfast.

beats.title: Married When I'm Thin Again
beats.modern: she refuses to marry me until after the baby because she will not be married in this splendid matronly state. she also looked it up in an almanac: marry me, she becomes American, kid is legitimate. locked in. she wants to see Niagara Falls. no wait. the Golden Gate. San Francisco is officially on the schedule, chat.
beats.quote: I’m not going to be married in this splendid matronly state.”

beats.title: Three In The Morning
beats.modern: pains every quarter hour, so we call the doctor and get a taxi. at the desk she gives her name as Catherine Henry and says she has no religion and the woman just draws a line through the space. she's excited. she keeps telling me it'll all be over soon. I sit on a chair in the hall and pray, and I don't have a religion either.
beats.quote: “I’m so glad it’s started,” she said. “Now in a little while it will be all over.”

beats.title: What If She Should Die
beats.modern: sitting in an empty room watching it get dark and my head runs the same loop for two hours. this is what people get for loving each other. she won't die, people don't die in childbirth now. that's what all husbands think. yes but what if she should die. she can't. why would she. but what if she should die. doctor comes in and says it doesn't go. caesarean. do it now.
beats.quote: This was the end of the trap. This was what people got for loving each other.

beats.title: He Wasn't Alive
beats.modern: a doctor comes out of the operating room holding something that looks like a skinned rabbit, dangles him by the heels, slaps him, tells me he's magnificent, five kilos. I feel nothing. no fatherhood, no anything. later I take the nurse into the hall and ask what's wrong with the baby. didn't you know? he wasn't alive. cord round the neck. she thought I knew.
beats.quote: “He wasn’t alive.”

beats.title: The Ants On The Log
beats.modern: so that was it. the baby was dead. and here's the rule set, chat: you die, and you never get told what it was about. they throw you in, tell you the rules, and the first time they catch you off base they kill you. once I put a log full of ants on a campfire and watched them run to the cool end and drop off into the flames. I could have lifted the log out. I threw a cup of water on it because I wanted the cup empty for whiskey.
beats.quote: They threw you in and told you the rules and the first time they caught you off base they killed you.

beats.title: It's Just A Dirty Trick
beats.modern: hemorrhage. then another. they can't stop it. I'm in the hall bargaining with a God I don't believe in, please, anything, you took the baby, don't take her. she says I'm going to die, and then, I hate it. she says she isn't afraid, she just hates it. she asks me not to do our things with another girl. then: it's just a dirty trick. then she's unconscious, and it did not take her very long.
beats.quote: “I’m not a bit afraid. It’s just a dirty trick.”

beats.title: Good-by To A Statue
beats.modern: I put the nurses out, shut the door, turn off the light, so it can just be us one more time. it wasn't any good. it was like saying good-by to a statue. after a while I left the hospital and walked back to the hotel in the rain. that's the stream.
beats.quote: It was like saying good-by to a statue.

beats.title: You Built Him, He Ends You
beats.modern: hard rule, almost never fails: whoever makes somebody else powerful is deleting himself. France dragged the Church up and the Church drove France out of Italy. and think about why: you boosted him with either cunning or force, so now he knows for a fact you are capable of cunning and force. you are the one threat he can personally verify.

beats.title: The Landscape Take
beats.modern: some of you think a nobody has no business writing about kings. wrong. painters go down into the plain to draw the mountains and climb the mountain to draw the plain. to understand the people you have to be a prince. to understand princes you have to be one of the people. I am nobody. that IS the qualification.

beats.title: The Regime Change Cope
beats.modern: people swap rulers happily because they assume the next guy is an upgrade. that hope is what puts weapons in their hands. then they find out. the new prince has to quarter his army on them and squeeze them, because he has no choice. every revolution ships a patch that nerfs the exact people who installed it.

beats.title: Well Treated Or Crushed
beats.modern: treat a man well or finish him. there is no middle setting. men can absolutely get revenge for small injuries. they cannot get revenge for the big one. so if you are going to do damage, do it on a scale that deletes the rematch. anything less just manufactures an enemy with a grudge and a calendar.

beats.title: The Hectic Fever
beats.modern: political trouble works like a fever, chat. early stage: easy to cure, impossible to detect. late stage: impossible to miss, impossible to cure. so everyone waits for the obvious phase to act. the obvious phase is the terminal phase. Rome killed problems while they were still invisible and that is the entire trick.

beats.title: Free Cities Never Forget
beats.modern: a city that used to be free never forgets the word liberty. you can rule it kindly for a hundred years and the second you wobble that word is back on every wall. Pisa did exactly this to Florence. take a free city and refuse to destroy it, and it will destroy you. those are the only two endings.

beats.title: Aim Above The Mark
beats.modern: always walk the path the greats walked. you will not match them, but you will smell like them. clever archers do not aim AT a far target, they aim way above it, because they know their own bow. set the mark higher than your actual reach. that is how you land on the real one.

beats.title: Opportunity Plus Ability
beats.modern: Moses, Cyrus, Romulus, Theseus. luck handed each of them exactly one item: a moment. Israel enslaved. Persia sick of the Medes. Athens scattered. Romulus dumped as a baby. without the moment their ability dies unused, and without the ability the moment strolls right past. you need both, and only one of them ever shows up on its own.

beats.title: The New Order Problem
beats.modern: nothing is harder than shipping a new order. everyone who was winning under the old rules is your enemy on day one, at full aggression. everyone who would win under yours defends you at maybe twenty percent, because they have not seen it work and they do not believe in new things until they have lived in them. haters go all in. supporters wait for reviews.
beats.quote: there is nothing more difficult to take in hand, more perilous to conduct, or more uncertain in its success, than to take the lead in the introduction of a new order of things,

beats.title: Armed Prophets Only
