beats.modern: strange island, strange rules, and some helpful stranger talks Balin into swapping shields before the fight. so the red knight doesn't recognise him. they go seven wounds apiece, ground soaked red, until one of them finally asks the other his name. it's his brother. they die within hours of each other and share one grave. all of it because a man said: here, take a bigger shield.
beats.quote: "Oh! Balan, mine own brother, thou hast slain me, and I thee!

beats.title: The Table Comes With The Wife
beats.modern: I tell Merlin I want Guinevere. he asks if I'm certain and offers to find me literally anyone else. I'm certain. and the story stops right there to tell you he already knew what this marriage does to us. her father's overjoyed, sends her with a hundred knights and a round table my own father used to own. greatest wedding gift ever given. also the fuse.
beats.quote: This Merlin said, knowing the misery that should hereafter happen from this marriage.

beats.title: The Seat That Eats You
beats.modern: the archbishop blesses every chair and every knight's name comes up in gold letters on the back. and one seat has different text on it. sit here if Heaven picked you. if it didn't, you burn. so now there's a chair with a warning label at my dinner table for the next twenty years. nobody talks about it. everybody looks at it.
beats.quote: "This is the Siege Perilous, wherein if any man shall sit save him whom Heaven hath chosen, he shall be devoured by fire."

beats.title: Gawain Takes The Wrong Head
beats.modern: Gawain's on his first quest and a beaten man asks for mercy. he says no. helmet's off, sword's up, and the man's lady throws herself over him. the blow lands on her. dead instantly. and it's his own brother who says it out loud: mercy is the entire job, that's what the title means. a court of ladies sentences him to fight on women's side forever. deserved.
beats.quote: Why give ye not your mercy unto them that ask it? a knight without mercy is without worship also."

beats.title: Pellinore Rode Past His Daughter
beats.modern: Pellinore gets back and my queen says it flat: a woman screamed for help by the road and you rode past her. he says he'll regret it every day he lives. then Merlin walks in and tells him whose she was. she was his. his daughter, riding to court, and he did not stop. and the sentence is that his best friend will fail him when he needs it most.
beats.quote: for that lady was your daughter, not seen since infancy by thee.

beats.title: My Sister Swaps My Sword
beats.modern: my own sister ships Excalibur to her boyfriend and hands me a fake. so I'm in a duel bleeding out of every stroke while he takes nothing, and I'm watching my own sword open me up thinking: that's mine. that's MINE. then the fake shatters at the hilt and I fight on holding a pommel. and when I finally get my sword back in my hand I talk to it like a dog that ran off.
beats.quote: both sword and scabbard were counterfeit, brittle, and false, and the true sword Excalibur was in the hands of Sir Accolon.

beats.title: The Gift-Wrapped Mantle
beats.modern: Morgan sends an apology present: the richest jewelled cloak I have ever seen, gorgeous, stones edge to edge. and the lake lady leans in and says don't put that on, make the courier wear it first. so I do. I make her wear it. and it goes up in flame and there is nothing left of her but ash. that was for me. my sister sent that for ME.
beats.quote: "thou shalt wear it ere it go on any other person's back!"

beats.title: Tribute, Paid In Bodies
beats.modern: Rome asked me for tribute twice. so after the field I have the emperor, seventeen kings and sixty senators embalmed, boxed, and driven home in chariots with a note. the note says: here's your tribute. if you want the rest, I'll bring it personally at Christmas. chat I don't think they're going to ask a third time.
beats.quote: these dead bodies that I send them are for the tribute they have dared to ask of me;

beats.title: The Maid With The Narrow Sleeves
beats.modern: Gawain sits out a tournament and the entire castle decides he must be a merchant dodging customs. one little girl argues with a wall of adults about it. her big sister slaps her for it, hard enough to leave five fingers. so the kid walks up, grabs his leg, and formally files a complaint: fight tomorrow, for me. and he says yes. no joke in it. next day he puts her sister's favourite knight in the dirt.
beats.quote: so aid me the Lord God, for so little a girl, she hath spoken very well,

beats.title: Four Queens, One Nap
beats.modern: Lancelot takes a nap under an apple tree and four sorceress queens ride by and simply collect him. wakes up in a cold room: pick one of us to serve, or stay in here till you die. and he tells four enchanted queens to their faces that he'd rather rot. these are my knights. these people cannot be left alone for ninety minutes.
beats.quote: I will serve none of ye, for ye be false enchantresses.

beats.title: Turquine's Sixty-Four
beats.modern: the biggest man in the country has sixty-four knights in a hole, most of them mine. four hours in, both of them leaning on their swords to breathe, he offers peace and freedom for every prisoner, on one condition: as long as you're not Lancelot. it's Lancelot. and he tells him. he just tells him. Turquine has about two minutes left after that.
beats.quote: And to discover and destroy him I have slain a hundred knights, and crippled utterly as many more,

beats.title: Chapel Perilous
beats.modern: thirty enormous knights in black armour grinding their teeth at him, and they part and let him through. dead man in the chapel, he cuts a strip of the cloth and lifts the sword and the ground shakes under him. on the way out a woman asks for one kiss. he says no. and she tells him, out loud, that the kiss was the kill. she dies of the disappointment inside a fortnight.
beats.quote: "I have lost all my labor! but hadst thou kissed me, thy life's days had been all done!"

beats.title: The Kitchen Boy Cashes In
beats.modern: a year ago a kid asked me for three favours and only spent one: feed me for twelve months. Key stuck him in the kitchen and named him Fairhands as an insult. today he cashes the other two. give me this quest. and have Lancelot knight me, only Lancelot, nobody else. the damsel takes one look at the dishwasher and rides off in disgust.
beats.quote: "Shall I have a kitchen page for this adventure?"

beats.title: Forty Knights In The Trees
beats.modern: he rides up to the castle and there are forty knights hanging in the trees with their gold spurs still on. every one of them came for this same woman. there's an ivory horn on the tree: blow it and the Red Knight comes out. she says wait until noon, because until noon his strength is seven men. it is daybreak. he blows it anyway.
beats.quote: were he stronger knight than ever lived, I would not fail him.

beats.title: The Ring Slips Off
beats.modern: Gareth is dismantling my entire court in a magic ring that changes his colours every pass, so nobody can even name who's beating them. then he stops for water, hands the ring to his dwarf, and forgets to take it back. instant yellow armour. name spelled out on his helmet in gold. herald reads it aloud. and he BOLTS through the crowd shouting at a small child about the ring he personally handed over.
beats.quote: "Boy, thou hast beguiled me foully in keeping my ring; give it me again, that I may be hidden."

beats.title: Tristram Versus Marhaus
beats.modern: new kid, first fight of his life, and he's picked the one champion nobody in Cornwall would touch. half a day of it. and the last swing goes through the helmet into the skull and lodges so deep he has to pull three times to free it. a piece of the blade stays in there. Marhaus runs for his ship and dies at home with that fragment in his head. the fragment comes back later. it always comes back.
beats.quote: "I have thy sword and shield in my safe keeping,

beats.title: The Potion On The Boat
beats.modern: he is escorting her to his uncle's wedding. they get thirsty. and there's a nice little gold flask that the servants have obviously been hiding for themselves, so they help themselves. chat. that was the wedding potion. that was not for them and it does not wear off, ever, and she still has to marry the uncle at the end of the voyage.
beats.quote: they had finished drinking they loved each other so well that their love nevermore might leave them for weal or woe.

beats.title: The Dog Knows Him
beats.modern: they find a wild man in the forest and clean him up. she comes down to look at him and doesn't know his face. that's how far gone he is. then her little dog, the one he gave her when she first came, jumps on him and won't stop licking his hands. and she says his name before she can stop herself. the dog got there first.
beats.quote: "it is my own true knight, Sir Tristram."

beats.title: The Knight Of The Black Shield
beats.modern: three days and nobody can name the black shield, and he keeps taking the whole field anyway. last day Lancelot finally gets a spear into him, opens his side, and the black shield rides off bleeding. so they hand Lancelot the prize. and Lancelot refuses it in front of everyone and says the other man won it. that's why he's the one they all follow. that's the whole thing.
beats.quote: "Nay, but Sir Tristram is the victor, for he first began and last endured,

beats.title: Merlin Gets Sealed In A Tree
beats.modern: the smartest being alive teaches a girl every spell he has because she asked nicely. last one on her list: how to seal a living person inside a tree. AND HE TELLS HER. then he lies down for a nap. she walks circles around him saying the words. and my wizard, the man who saw every disaster in this story coming, is still inside that oak. he saw everything except this.
beats.quote: the damsel prayed to see all that charm whereby men might be shut up yet alive in rocks or trees.

beats.title: Galahad Sits Down
beats.modern: an old man in white walks a kid in red into my hall. no armour. empty scabbard, like he already knows what's going in it. leads him straight to the chair that burns people and lifts the silk off the letters, and the name is already written there. and the kid sits. no flame, no thunder. sits down like it's his own kitchen chair, because it is.
beats.quote: "This is the seat of Sir Galahad, the good knight."

beats.title: The Grail Comes Through The Hall
beats.modern: thunder that shakes the walls, then a light seven times brighter than daylight, and every man at my table looks better than I have ever seen him look. the Grail goes down the hall under white silk and every knight is fed the thing he loves most. then it's gone. and Gawain stands up and swears a year and a day, and man after man stands up behind him, and I'm sitting there crying because I know exactly what he's just done to us.
beats.quote: I fear me my true fellowship shall never meet together here again;

beats.title: The Dish Of Blood
beats.modern: the castle's custom is a dish of blood from every woman who passes. the three of them kill a dozen men rather than allow it. and then she volunteers anyway. she says if she dies healing someone else's body her soul comes out ahead. gives more than she can spare, and the sick woman stands up whole. then she tells her brother exactly where to bury her, and who'll be buried beside her. she was right about that too.
beats.quote: "If I die to heal another's body, I shall get health to my soul,"

beats.title: Lancelot At The Door
beats.modern: he gets to the door and it opens on its own and the light pours out. a voice tells him not to come in. and then he sees the priest struggling under the weight of it, and he can't help himself, he steps forward to help. one breath of fire and he's on the floor. twenty-four days lying there, alive, not moving a limb. best knight in the world. one step too far in.
beats.quote: I have seen marvels that no tongue can tell, and more than any heart can think."

beats.title: Galahad Logs Off
beats.modern: he heals the wounded king, carries the cup to Sarras, gets made king himself by a city that would have killed him otherwise. and then a bishop who says he's Joseph of Arimathea calls him forward. and Galahad asks to die. that was his ask. tell my father Lancelot I love him, and tell them all this world doesn't hold. then a hand comes down out of heaven and takes the cup for good.
beats.quote: "Salute for me Sir Lancelot, my father, and bid them remember this unstable world."

beats.title: The Poisoned Apple
beats.modern: a knight poisons a bowl of apples to kill Gawain, because everyone knows Gawain loves fruit. wrong man eats one. swells up, dies at the table. and because MY WIFE hosted the dinner, the whole room decides it was her. not one of them will stand for her. and I'm the judge, so I have to set the date and say the words out loud: if nobody fights for her, she burns.
beats.quote: "I made this dinner for a good intent, and no evil, so God help me in my need."

beats.title: The Barge From Astolat
beats.modern: we're at the window and a barge comes up on the tide with a body in it, dressed in her best, a letter in her hand. she asked to be steered to my court. the letter says she loved him and died of it and would he please bury her. Lancelot says he couldn't give her the one thing she wanted. and I say the truest thing I say all year: nobody can be ordered into loving you.
beats.quote: I, whom men call the Maid of Astolat, set my love upon you, and have died for your sake.

beats.title: The Trap At The Queen's Door
beats.modern: fourteen of them corner the queen's chamber while I'm out hunting, screaming traitor through the door. Lancelot has no armour in there. so he opens the door a crack, lets exactly one man in, kills him with his bare hand, takes his gear, and comes out. thirteen more. one gets away. and of course, of course, the one who gets away is Modred.
beats.quote: "Better were twenty deaths at once than this vile outcry,"

beats.title: The Blow That Ends Us
beats.modern: the rescue at the stake works and it costs everything. because in the crush Lancelot cuts down two unarmed men without ever seeing their faces, and they are Gareth and Gaheris. Gareth, who worshipped him. Gawain's little brothers. chat that blow is what ends the Round Table. not the affair. not the trial. that.
beats.quote: Sir Lancelot had unawares struck down and slain the two good knights Sir Gareth and Sir Gaheris,

beats.title: He Gives Me My Horse Back
beats.modern: we're at war and one of his own men knocks me off my horse, and Lancelot screams at him not to touch me. then he gets down, hands me his own horse, and asks me to end this because there's no honour in it for either of us. and I sit there with my eyes full thinking the thing I can never say in front of my army.
beats.quote: "My lord, I pray thee forbear this strife, for it can bring to neither of us any honor."

beats.title: Gawain's Deathbed
beats.modern: an arrow reopens the wound Lancelot gave him and that's it, that's the ending. and he says it himself while he's dying: this whole war was me. if I'd let it go you'd be at peace with him and Modred would never have dared. tell Lancelot it was my own doing. tell him to come pray at my grave. and then my nephew is gone.
beats.quote: Alas! that I have been the cause of all this war,

beats.title: One Man And An Adder
beats.modern: we have a truce. signed, agreed, both armies briefed: nobody draws unless they draw first. and one knight gets bitten in the foot by an adder and pulls his sword to kill it. that's it. that is the whole cause. both hosts see steel flash and the world ends over a snake. all day long, until there is nearly nobody left standing on either side.

beats.title: Father And Son
beats.modern: and there he is, standing alone. my son. I take the spear in both hands and drive it through him more than a fathom deep, and he pulls himself UP the shaft, hand over hand, to reach me, and puts his sword through my helmet and my skull. he dies first. I go down after him. that's the trade. that's the whole reign, right there.
beats.quote: "Traitor, now is thy death-day come!"

beats.title: Throw The Sword In
beats.modern: I'm dying and I ask for one thing: throw the sword in the water. he goes down, looks at the jewels on the hilt, hides it in the reeds, comes back and lies to my face. twice. TWICE. so I tell him what he is, a knight who'd sell out his king for a shiny grip, and promise to get up and kill him myself. third time he does it. and an arm comes out of the water, catches it, shakes it three times, and goes under.
beats.quote: Art thou called of men a noble knight, and wouldest betray me for a jewelled sword?

beats.title: The Barge To Avilion
beats.modern: three queens in black in a barge, already weeping before they see me. Bedivere carries me down the shore and lays me in it. one of them puts my head in her lap and asks why I took so long, my wound's gone cold. and he's standing there asking what becomes of him now. all I have left for him is: pray for me. I'm going to Avilion to be healed. and the barge pulls out.
beats.quote: I go to the Vale of Avilion to heal me of my grievous wound,

a-modest-proposal.title: A Modest Proposal: For preventing the children of poor people in Ireland, from being a burden on their parents or country, and for making them beneficial to the publick
a-modest-proposal.author: Jonathan Swift

beats.title: The Opening Shot
beats.modern: walked through town today chat and it is rough. moms in rags in every doorway, four to six kids trailing each one, hands out to every stranger who passes. and the kids grow up into exactly three endings: petty crime, enlist for some foreign war, or sell yourself overseas. nobody is fixing this. hold that thought.

beats.title: Statue Of Me
beats.modern: everyone agrees this is a national problem. all parties. so logically whoever finds the fair, cheap, easy fix deserves a statue. bronze. town square. no reason I bring that up. anyway I have an idea.

beats.title: The Math On A Baby
beats.modern: every other guy who has pitched a fix got the numbers wrong. here are the real ones. a baby runs on mom's milk for one solar year, total cost about two shillings, which she can absolutely beg. year one is basically free. year two is where the whole model collapses. so that is my entry point. at exactly twelve months, I take over.

beats.title: The Spreadsheet
beats.modern: pulling up the numbers, chat. million and a half people in this kingdom. two hundred thousand couples where the wife is a breeder. minus thirty thousand who can actually afford their own kids. minus fifty thousand for miscarriage and babies who die inside the year. leaves one hundred and twenty thousand surplus infants annually. that is the addressable market. I said what I said.

beats.title: Thieving Starts At Six
beats.modern: so what CAN a toddler do. cannot farm. cannot build. realistically cannot even steal until about six. I checked this. a gentleman in Cavan swore to me he has seen maybe one or two under-sixes pull off a job, and this is a county FAMOUS for producing elite thieves. before six they are just interns.

beats.title: No Resale Value
beats.modern: merchants tell me a kid under twelve is not a saleable commodity at all. even AT twelve you clear three pounds, maybe three and a half on the exchange. and you already sank four times that into food and rags. chat. the unit economics on children are catastrophic. somebody had to say it.

beats.title: The Pitch
beats.modern: okay chat here is the pitch and I want you to hear me out. I know a very knowledgeable American in London, and he assures me that a healthy one year old, well nursed, is delicious. stewed. roasted. baked. boiled. he says it holds up beautifully in a fricassee. ...why did chat go quiet.
beats.quote: a young healthy child well nursed, is, at a year old, a most delicious nourishing and wholesome food, whether stewed, roasted, baked, or boiled;

beats.title: Twenty Thousand For Breed
beats.modern: rollout plan. hold twenty thousand back for breeding, only a quarter of them male. that is a better ratio than we give sheep or swine. the other hundred thousand go to persons of quality at twelve months. advise the mother to let them nurse hard that last month so they come in plump. one child is two dishes at a dinner party, or a quarter cut when the family eats alone. leftovers keep four days. better in winter.

beats.title: Peak Season Is March
beats.modern: supply notes. in season all year, but it peaks in March. a serious French physician did the research: fish diet through Lent, everyone conceives, nine months later the market is glutted. and since Catholic births here outnumber ours three to one, there is a bonus feature baked in. fewer Papists. I am simply reading the data, chat.

beats.title: Ten Shillings A Carcass
beats.modern: pricing. two shillings a year to raise one, rags included. sells at ten. no gentleman is going to flinch at ten shillings for four dishes of excellent meat when he has a friend over. the squire becomes a beloved landlord, popular with his tenants. mom clears eight shillings net and is fit for work immediately, ready to produce the next one. everybody wins. chat is telling me everybody does not win.

beats.title: The Gloves Line
beats.modern: for the thrifty, and the times do require it: do not waste the skin. dressed properly it makes admirable gloves for ladies and summer boots for fine gentlemen. we zone slaughterhouses across Dublin, butchers will be lining up for that contract. personally I recommend buying live and dressing them hot from the knife. like a roasting pig.

beats.title: A Friend Suggests Teenagers
beats.modern: a patriot friend of mine, genuinely great guy, proposes an expansion. gentlemen have hunted out all the deer, so replace venison with twelve to fourteen year olds. I have to push back on this. my American source says teen boys go tough and lean from constant exercise, like schoolboys, and fattening them does not pencil out. the girls are worse value since they would become breeders. also, some scrupulous people might call it a little cruel. and cruelty, chat, has ALWAYS been my strongest objection to any project.

beats.title: The Formosa Story
beats.modern: in fairness to my friend, he got the idea from Psalmanaazor, a man from Formosa who turned up in London twenty years back. told him that at home the executioner sells the body afterward as a prime delicacy. a plump fifteen year old girl, crucified for trying to poison the Emperor, went to the prime minister and the court mandarins in joints off the gibbet. four hundred crowns. my friend heard that and thought: business opportunity.

beats.title: The Old And Sick Are Fine
beats.modern: people keep asking what I would do about the aged, the diseased, the maimed. honestly? not losing sleep. they are already dying and rotting of cold and famine and filth and vermin as fast as anyone could reasonably expect. young labourers, same track: too starved to work, so nobody hires them, so they starve. everyone happily delivered from the evils to come.
beats.quote: they are every day dying, and rotting, by cold and famine, and filth, and vermin, as fast as can be reasonably expected.

beats.title: Advantage One, Fewer Papists
beats.modern: benefits list. number one: fewer Papists, who we are yearly overrun by, who breed the most, and who stay home on purpose waiting to hand the kingdom to the Pretender the second enough good Protestants leave rather than pay tithes against their conscience. two problems, one solution, chat.

beats.title: Finally, Seizable Assets
beats.modern: two: poor tenants will finally own something valuable that a landlord can legally seize toward the rent, since the corn and cattle are already gone and money here is a rumour. three: national stock up fifty thousand pounds a year, plus an entirely new dish for every gentleman with refinement in taste. and the money circulates at home. buy local, chat.

beats.title: Great For Taverns
beats.modern: five: hospitality boom. vintners will race to source the best receipts for dressing it, every fine gentleman who values himself on knowing good eating will be in there nightly, and a skilful cook who wants to oblige his guests can make it cost literally whatever he likes. entire sector, unlocked.

beats.title: Fattest Child At Market
beats.modern: six: marriage rates climb. mothers get tender toward children who now come with a guaranteed settlement. you would see honest competition between wives over who brings the fattest child to market. and husbands would treat a pregnant wife as well as they currently treat a mare in foal. they would stop beating and kicking her. for the baby.
beats.quote: We should soon see an honest emulation among the married women, which of them could bring the fattest child to the market.

beats.title: Studious Of Brevity
beats.modern: more upside: export barrels, and a bacon revival, since we keep slaughtering piglets that are in no way comparable to a well grown fat yearling child, which roasted whole would absolutely headline a Lord Mayor's feast. I could go on. I am studious of brevity. projections: a thousand Dublin families as regular customers, plus weddings and christenings, puts the city at twenty thousand carcasses a year. the rest of the kingdom takes eighty thousand.

beats.title: Let No Man Talk To Me
beats.modern: only objection I can think of is that the population drops. I freely own that. it was one principal design. and let NO man come at me with the other ideas. taxing absentee landlords. using only what we grow and make ourselves. rejecting foreign luxury. curing the pride and vanity and gaming. learning to love our own country. dropping the factions. not selling our country and consciences for nothing. teaching landlords one single degree of mercy toward their tenants. do not. bring me. those.

beats.title: The Glimpse Of Hope
beats.modern: saying it again: do not bring me those until somebody shows me one glimpse of hope that anyone will ever sincerely try them. I spent years offering vain, idle, visionary thoughts. nobody moved. so I landed here. cheap, easy, entirely in our own power, and it cannot offend England, because the meat will not bear exportation and flesh is too tender to keep in salt. though I could name a country that would gladly eat this whole nation without it.
beats.quote: although perhaps I could name a country, which would be glad to eat up our whole nation without it.

beats.title: Ask The Parents
beats.modern: I am not so violently bent on my own opinion that I would reject a better idea. but whoever brings one answers two questions first. one: how do you feed and clothe a hundred thousand useless mouths as things stand. two: there are a round million creatures in human figure here whose whole subsistence, pooled, leaves them two million pounds in debt. go ask their parents whether they would not call it a great happiness to have been sold for food at a year old. go ask them, chat.

beats.title: No Skin In The Game
beats.modern: and for the record, chat, in the sincerity of my heart: I have zero personal interest here. no stake. no angle. I want trade advanced, infants provided for, the poor relieved, and the rich given some pleasure. I could not make a single penny off this if I tried. my youngest is nine. my wife is past child-bearing. stream's over.

narrative-of-the-life-of.title: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave
narrative-of-the-life-of.author: Frederick Douglass

beats.title: No Birthday
beats.modern: I do not know how old I am. There is no record of it anywhere, and asking is treated as insolence. The white children know their ages. Nobody can tell me why I should not know mine. The closest I can get is something my master let slip in 1835, that I was about seventeen. That is my whole birth certificate.

beats.title: She Came At Night
beats.modern: My mother is hired out twelve miles off. She walks that distance in the dark, after a full day in the field, lies down next to me until I am asleep, and is gone before I wake. I never once see her face in daylight. She dies when I am about seven. Nobody tells me until it is over. I take the news the way you take the news that a stranger has died. That is not a failure in me. That is the design.

beats.title: Aunt Hester
beats.modern: He ties my aunt's hands to a hook in the joist so she is standing on her toes. He strips her to the waist. Then the cowskin, until blood is running onto the floor, and the louder she screams the harder he swings. I am a small child. I hide in a closet and stay there long after it stops, certain I am next. This is the first thing I ever see of slavery. It is the door I am pushed through.

beats.title: What The Singing Is
beats.modern: People in the north hear that we sing and take it as proof we are content. I need to correct that. Those songs are made out of grief. Men sing on the road to the Great House Farm the way a person cries, because something has to get out of the body. In all my years there I sang to drown sorrow. I never once sang because I was happy.
beats.quote: Slaves sing most when they are most unhappy.

beats.title: Demby In The Creek
beats.modern: Demby runs from a whipping and stands in the creek up to his shoulders, refusing to come out. The overseer gives him three calls, raises the musket, and fires. The water goes red. Nothing happens after that. No trial, no inquiry, because the only witnesses are slaves and slaves cannot testify. The man kept his job and his good name. He is probably still living in St. Michael's, respected.

beats.title: The Corn Bag
beats.modern: No shoes, no stockings, no trousers, no bed. One coarse shirt to the knee, summer and winter. On the coldest nights I steal the sack they use to carry corn to the mill, crawl into it head first, feet sticking out, and sleep on the clay floor. My feet split open from the frost. The cracks are wide enough that the pen I am writing this with would lie down inside them.

beats.title: A Pair Of Trousers
beats.modern: I am seven or eight when word comes that I am going to Baltimore, and it is the happiest news of my life so far. I spend three days in the creek scrubbing the dead skin off my knees and feet, because Mrs. Lucretia says city people will laugh at a dirty boy, and because she has promised me trousers if I get clean. I had never owned a pair of trousers.

beats.title: The Forbidden Alphabet
beats.modern: My mistress starts teaching me letters. Her husband finds out and shuts it down in front of me. He tells her reading would ruin me, make me unmanageable, worthless to a master, unfit ever to be a slave again. He is warning her. I am standing right there hearing directions. Everything he is afraid of is the thing I want. From that moment I know exactly which way freedom is.
beats.quote: It would forever unfit him to be a slave.

beats.title: What It Did To Her
beats.modern: Hers was the first white face I ever saw with kindness in it. She fed hungry people and cried over other people's grief. Then she learns what owning a person requires of her, and it takes her apart. Within a year she is harder about it than her husband is. Nothing makes her angrier than catching me with a newspaper. She rushes me and tears it out of my hands. Slavery did that to her, and I watched it happen.

beats.title: Bread For Letters
beats.modern: So I make teachers out of the poor white boys on the street. I carry bread from the house, which I always have and they often do not, and I trade it for reading lessons. I ask them why they go free at twenty-one and I never go free at all. They have no answer for it. They just look sorry, and hope out loud that something will happen for me.
beats.quote: Have not I as good a right to be free as you have?”

beats.title: A Pit With No Ladder
beats.modern: I get hold of a book of speeches and read it until I have it by heart. It hands me words for everything I already felt, and then it ruins me. Now I can see precisely what has been done to me and to everyone I love, and there is nothing whatever I can do about it. For a stretch I want to stop thinking so badly that I envy the animals. Reading showed me the pit. It did not hand me a ladder.

beats.title: My Copybook Was A Fence
beats.modern: In the shipyard they mark timber with a letter for where it goes on the ship. L for larboard, S for starboard, F forward, A aft. I learn those four. Then I start telling any boy who can write that I write better than he does. He takes the bait every time and proves me wrong, and every time he proves me wrong I come away with another letter. My paper was board fences, brick walls and pavement. My pen was a lump of chalk.

beats.title: Ranked With The Pigs
beats.modern: My old master dies with no will, so the estate has to be counted before it is split. They line us up with the stock. Horses and men, cattle and women, pigs and children, one column, one appraisal, grey-haired women and young girls looked over exactly the same way. Then they divide us. We have no more voice in where we go than the animals standing next to us.

beats.title: My Grandmother
beats.modern: My grandmother built that family. She nursed my old master when he was an infant and wiped the sweat off his face when he died. She filled his plantation with people. When she is old and can no longer earn, the new owners walk her into the woods, throw up a hut and a mud chimney, and leave her there to feed herself. Her children, her grandchildren, her great-grandchildren, all sold off. She gropes for water in the dark, sits down by a few embers, and dies with nobody there.
beats.quote: Will not a righteous God visit for these things?

beats.title: Basket And Store
beats.modern: Four of us in that kitchen, and less than half a bushel of corn meal a week between us. So we beg and we steal, and we do not rank one above the other. Meanwhile there is food going bad in the locked smokehouse and the mistress knows it. Every morning the two of them kneel down together and ask God to bless them in basket and store.

beats.title: Henny
beats.modern: Henny fell into a fire as a small child and her hands never worked again. My master ties her up before breakfast and whips her, goes off to his store, comes back at dinner and whips her again in the places already raw. He has a verse ready to justify it. Then, because she cannot earn her keep, he puts her out to take care of herself. He is a converted man now, a class leader. He holds on to the mother and turns the crippled daughter out to starve.
beats.quote: Scripture—“He that knoweth his master’s will, and doeth it not, shall be beaten with many stripes.”

beats.title: Sent To Be Broken
beats.modern: He decides city life has spoiled me and hires me out for a year to a man whose entire trade is breaking young slaves. Everyone knows what that means. Some owners lend their people out to him for nothing, just for the training. I know all of it going in. I go anyway, almost gladly, because that man feeds his hands, and I am hungry.

beats.title: He Broke Me
beats.modern: Six months. Worked in every weather, no hour too hot or too cold or too dark. He wanted me tamed and he got it. The reading stopped. The thinking stopped. Whatever light was behind my eyes went out. I want to be exact about this, because people speak of the spirit as though it cannot be reached. It can. He reached mine.
beats.quote: Mr. Covey succeeded in breaking me. I was broken in body, soul, and spirit.

beats.title: Talking To The Ships
beats.modern: The house sits right on the bay. Sundays I stand on the bank and watch the sails go out, and they are not beautiful to me, they are ghosts. I talk to them out loud because there is nobody else. You are loose and I am chained. Then I talk myself back down. One hundred miles straight north and I am free. I will take to the water. Get caught or get clear, I will try it. There is a better day coming.
beats.quote: “You are loosed from your moorings, and are free; I am fast in my chains, and am a slave!

beats.title: The Wheat Field
beats.modern: August, one of the hottest days of the year, four of us fanning wheat. Around three in the afternoon my head goes and my legs go and I drop. He comes out and asks what is wrong. I can barely get the words out. He kicks me in the side and tells me to get up. I try and fall. He kicks me again. Then he picks up a hickory slat and opens my head with it and tells me again to get up. I stay down. Let him do his worst.

beats.title: Seven Miles Of Blood
beats.modern: I decide to walk to my master and ask for protection. Seven miles, through the woods to stay off the road, barefoot and bareheaded through bogs and briers, and partway there I fall down and lie bleeding long enough to think I will die of it. Five hours. I arrive covered in blood from my hair to my shirt. He hears the whole account, tells me I probably deserved it, says he cannot lose the year's wages, and sends me back in the morning. No supper. No breakfast.

beats.title: Sandy's Root
beats.modern: I spend the day hidden in the corn and the woods with two choices in front of me: go back and be beaten to death, or stay out here and starve. That night I run into Sandy. He takes me home, feeds me, hears all of it, and tells me to go back, but first to dig a certain root and carry it always on my right side, and then no white man will ever be able to whip me. I do not believe in the root. I carry it anyway, because he means it kindly.

beats.title: Two Hours In The Stable
beats.modern: Monday before daylight he walks into the stable with a long rope and grabs my legs. I do not know where it comes from, but something decides. I take him by the throat and stand up. He is shaking like a leaf. He calls Hughes in and I put a kick under Hughes's ribs and Hughes is finished. He calls Bill, and Bill says he was hired to work, not to help whip me, and walks away. Two hours. At the end he is out of breath, telling himself he went easy on me. He never laid a finger on me again.
beats.quote: he had used me like a brute for six months, and that I was determined to be used so no longer.

beats.title: The Turning Point
beats.modern: That fight is where my life turns over. I stayed a slave in form for four more years. I was never again a slave in fact. Only a man who has taken hold of the arm that was beating him knows what that morning felt like, and nobody else does. From then on I made sure it was understood: whoever intends to whip me had better intend to kill me.
beats.quote: It was a glorious resurrection, from the tomb of slavery, to the heaven of freedom.

beats.title: Forty Scholars
beats.modern: I keep a Sunday school in a free man's house, and I will not write his name down even now. More than forty come, mostly grown men and women. Every hour they sit in that room they are risking thirty-nine lashes. They come anyway, because they want to read. Those Sundays are the best hours I have had in my life, and I know that most of the people in that room are still exactly where I left them.

beats.title: We Are Betrayed
beats.modern: Five of us. The plan is a canoe up the bay on the Saturday night before Easter, then the north star the rest of the way. I wrote out passes for each man in another man's name. Saturday morning we are in the field spreading manure and a certainty comes over me that I cannot argue with. I turn to Sandy and say it out loud. He says the same thought had just struck him. Neither of us says another word.
beats.quote: “We are betrayed!”

beats.title: Henry Won't Be Tied
beats.modern: The constables come. They tie me. They tie John. Then they tell Henry to cross his hands and he says no. Two of them cock pistols in his face and swear they will blow his heart out of him. He tells them to shoot, that they can only kill him once, and that he will not be tied. Then he knocks both pistols out of their hands in one motion. It takes every man there to put him down.
beats.quote: “you can’t kill me but once. Shoot, shoot,—and be damned!

beats.title: Own Nothing
beats.modern: Henry asks me what to do with his pass. Eat it with your biscuit and own nothing. We pass it down the line, own nothing, and every man holds. Fifteen miles dragged behind horses to the Easton jail, and inside twenty minutes the slave traders are in the room looking us over, laughing, asking would we like them for masters. Then the others are taken home and the door closes and I am alone in a stone room. That is the part that finished me. I thought freedom was gone.

beats.title: Four Of Them
beats.modern: Four of the white apprentices come at me at once with sticks, stones and handspikes. One in front, one on each side, and the one behind me swings a handspike into the back of my head. I go down and a boot comes into my left eye until it bursts. Fifty white carpenters are standing in that yard watching it happen. Not one of them says a word, except the ones shouting to kill me for striking a white man.

beats.title: No Warrant On My Word
beats.modern: Master Hugh is genuinely furious and takes me to a magistrate. The magistrate asks who saw the assault. Fifty men, in a shipyard, at midday. He says he cannot issue a warrant unless a white man comes forward to swear to it. My own account is worth nothing. Understand what that sentence means. They could have killed me in front of a thousand black witnesses and no one would have been arrested.

beats.title: Every Saturday Night
beats.modern: I learn to calk. Within a year I command the highest wages paid to any calker on the point, sometimes nine dollars a week. I find the work. I make the contracts. I collect the money with my own hands. Then every Saturday night I hand all of it to Master Hugh. Not because he earned it. Not because he had any part in it. Only because he can make me. A pirate on the open sea has exactly the same right.
beats.quote: solely because he had the power to compel me to give it up.

beats.title: Is This All
beats.modern: 1838. Every week I pour my wages into his hand, and he counts them, and looks up at me, and asks if that is all. Sometimes when I bring him six dollars he gives me six cents back to encourage me. It has the opposite effect. Handing me a piece of it is an admission that the whole of it was mine.
beats.quote: “Is this all?”

beats.title: September Third
beats.modern: The third of September, 1838. I left my chains and reached New York without being stopped once. How I did it, which way I went, what I travelled on, who helped me, I will not say. Not for effect. There are people still down there who will need that same door, and I am not going to shut it for the sake of telling a better story.

beats.title: Trust No Man
beats.modern: People ask me what it felt like to stand in a free state. I have never managed to answer it properly. The first hour is the highest I have ever been. Then the floor drops out. I am a stranger in the middle of thousands, including thousands of my own people, and I cannot tell one of them what I am, because kidnappers make a living waiting for men exactly like me and I do not know whose face belongs to which. So the rule I carried out of slavery was this: trust no man.
beats.quote: I felt like one who had escaped a den of hungry lions.

beats.title: Choosing A Name
beats.modern: By now I have been Bailey, then Stanley, then Johnson, shedding names the way you shed a coat when men are hunting you. New Bedford already has too many Johnsons. At the breakfast table I tell my host he can name me, on one condition: the Frederick stays. That part is not theirs to take. He has been reading Walter Scott and he suggests Douglass. That is the name I have gone by ever since.
beats.quote: I must hold on to that, to preserve a sense of my identity.

beats.title: The First Money
beats.modern: Third day in New Bedford I get work stowing a sloop with oil. Dirty, heavy, unfamiliar. I have never enjoyed a day's labor more in my life. Nobody is standing at the end of it waiting to take it off me. It is the first work whose reward was entirely my own, done for myself and my new wife, and it is where my life actually starts.

beats.title: Nantucket
beats.modern: Nantucket, the eleventh of August, 1841. They urge me to speak. I do not want to. I still feel like a slave, and the thought of addressing a room of white people sits on my chest like a weight. I get a few sentences out and something loosens, and then I say what I came to say with no trouble at all. I have been saying it ever since. You can judge the rest for yourself.

a-connecticut-yankee-in-king.title: A Connecticut Yankee in King Arthur's Court
a-connecticut-yankee-in-king.author: Mark Twain

beats.title: Hartford, Then Nothing
beats.modern: quick intro for the new followers: Hartford boy, dad was a blacksmith, uncle was a horse doctor, I run the arms factory now. guns, cannon, engines, anything you want, and if there's no way to build it I invent one. two thousand men under me. then a guy called Hercules caught me alongside the head with a crowbar and the whole world went dark. chat that's the last frame of the old stream.

beats.title: Bridgeport? Camelot.
beats.modern: wake up under a tree and there's a man on a horse in FULL plate, helmet like a nail keg, horse wearing a bedquilt. asks if I will "just." I tell him to go back to his circus. he charges me with a spear so I'm up the tree, and now apparently I'm his property? we walk an hour, I point at the skyline and go "Bridgeport?" he goes "Camelot." chat.
beats.quote: “Bridgeport?” said I, pointing. “Camelot,” said he.

beats.title: It's 528 And I'm Taking Over
beats.modern: the page kid mentions he was born in 513. I ask him again, slowly. he's not lying, nobody's lying, this is not an asylum, it is King Arthur's court and it is June 528. everyone I know won't be born for thirteen hundred years. and then, chat, I did the math the other way: I've got a thirteen-century head start on the smartest man alive. give me three months and I own this country.

beats.title: Merlin's Rerun
beats.modern: old man stands up and the whole hall visibly dies inside. it's Merlin. he has ONE story and he tells it word for word every single time he gets a barrel in him. the page just sighs "we shall have it again" and pretends to nap. by minute three the dogs are asleep, the guards are asleep, the rats are out walking around, and one of them is sitting on the KING'S HEAD eating cheese. nobody wakes up.
beats.quote: “Merlin, the mighty liar and magician, perdition singe him for the weariness he worketh with his one tale!

beats.title: Just Strip Him, Says Merlin
beats.modern: they've decided my clothes are enchanted and now they can't figure out how to execute me through the enchantment. big theological debate. then Merlin goes, guys. have you tried taking them off. so now I am naked in front of the entire Round Table, and I am the only person in the room who's embarrassed. they discuss me like produce. the queen's one review: she'd never seen legs quite like mine. thanks.
beats.quote: she had never seen anybody with legs just like mine before.

beats.title: I'm A Magician, Actually
beats.modern: the kid is on his knees terrified because I insulted Merlin out loud. so I look him dead in the eye: I laughed because I'm a magician too. known Merlin seven hundred years. he's died and come back thirteen times under thirteen different names. he's a one-night-stand act, provincial circuit, never got past the tutorial. now go tell the king I'm quietly cooking up a calamity and it goes off if anything happens to me.

beats.title: I Will Blot Out The Sun
beats.modern: they want me to NAME the calamity and I don't have one. and then it lands: there's a total eclipse due, and I know the exact hour. so I let the silence pile up, stood over that poor kid a full minute, and gave him the line of my life. he collapsed. I had to carry him out to the guards myself.
beats.quote: “Go back and tell the king that at that hour I will smother the whole world in the dead blackness of midnight; I will blot out the sun, and he shall never shine again;

beats.title: My Best Friend Got Me Killed
beats.modern: so they come for me a day EARLY and I'm chained to the stake before I can breathe. and Clarence squeezes through the crowd absolutely GLOWING, because he did it. he told them my sun-magic wouldn't be at full power till tomorrow, so kill me today. now he's begging me to only do a little darkness, the littlest little darkness, please don't hurt the sun. I couldn't tell him. he saved me so hard he killed me.

beats.title: The Eclipse Drops
beats.modern: monk's got the torch at my feet, he's droning Latin, and then he just STOPS. four thousand people look up at once. chat. IT'S STARTING. black rim creeping across the sun right on schedule. I got my arm up pointing at it, best pose of my career. Merlin screams apply the torch, the king screams I forbid it, and I say if any man moves, even the king, I blast him with lightning. everybody sat back down.

beats.title: One Percent Of The Upside
beats.modern: king offers me half the kingdom to give the sun back. HALF A KINGDOM. I turned it down. I asked for one percent of whatever growth I create for the state. keep your crown, keep the glory, I'll take equity. he was so relieved he unchained me on the spot and put my seat on the top step of the throne. I could not have stopped that eclipse if I wanted to, by the way. it was going to end on its own.
beats.quote: you shall appoint me your perpetual minister and executive, and give me for my services one per cent of such actual increase of revenue over and above its present amount as I may succeed in creating for the state.

beats.title: Merlin's Tower Goes Up
beats.modern: Merlin's been telling people I'm a fraud, so: public duel, my magic against his, his own tower is the target. I gave him first go. he draws a circle, burns a pinch of powder, waves his arms around like a windmill. nothing. meanwhile my lightning rod is quietly loading itself. I made three passes in the air. the tower LEFT THE PLANET. it rained masonry for a week. Merlin's stock: flat.

beats.title: The Boss, Elected By The Nation
beats.modern: they offered me a title. I said no. I don't want a name some duke hands down, I want the one the country gives me. a blacksmith said it in a village one day, half a joke, and in ten days the whole kingdom was using it. there are very few THEs in this world. The King. The Queen. and me.
beats.quote: This title, translated into modern speech, would be THE BOSS. Elected by the nation.

beats.title: Sagramor Heard That Wrong
beats.modern: Sir Dinadan told me the single worst joke in human history, the exact one I've hated my whole life, and then went off to joust. I blacked out from it. came to just as Gareth cratered him, and I said out loud "I hope to gracious he's killed." unfortunately Gareth ALSO cratered Sir Sagramor at that exact second, and Sagramor thinks I meant him. so that's a duel. in three or four years. he's got a grail run booked first.

beats.title: The Grail Is A Group Quest
beats.modern: everybody here takes a flier at the Holy Grail. it's a multi-year cruise. nobody knows where it is, nobody expects to find it, and none of them would know what to do with it if they tripped over it. every year an expedition goes out grailing and the next year a relief expedition goes out hunting for THEM. worlds of reputation in it. no money. they actually asked me to put in.

beats.title: The Nineteenth Century, Buried
beats.modern: four years of quiet building, chat. schools, factories, mines, a teacher-factory, a secret West Point, telephone wire strung at night so nobody asks questions. the nineteenth century is running full blast under this country's nose and nobody has noticed. it's a volcano with a clean blue sky over it. my hand is on the valve. I'm not turning it yet, one candle-power at a time, because the Church would be on my back inside a minute.

beats.title: Quest Giver With No Coordinates
beats.modern: so a girl shows up with forty-five captive princesses and three four-armed one-eyed ogres, and the king hands ME the quest. fine. I ask basic questions. how far? she can't count leagues, they all look alike. which direction? the road turns, therefore the castle HAS no direction, it is God's will that castles not have directions, and then four hundred more words of that. do you have a map? she thinks a map is something you boil with an onion.

beats.title: How To Put On Armor
beats.modern: gear tutorial, chat. blanket layer, chain mail shirt that pours like wet fishnet, steel shoes, spurs, greaves, cuisses, backplate, breastplate, a steel petticoat scalloped out behind so you can sit down, sword, stovepipes on the arms, iron gauntlets, and an iron rat-trap for your head. no pockets. anywhere. you end up packed in like a candle in a mould, and honestly there's more shell than meat in there.

beats.title: The Fly In The Helmet
beats.modern: the sun's been cooking the iron for hours and you start to itch. you are inside, your hands are outside, nothing but steel in between. it spreads until the whole territory is occupied. and THEN a fly gets in through the visor bars, the bars are stuck, and he works nose to lip to ear, biting, for miles. I gave up. Sandy unshipped the helmet and poured water down inside the armor like I was a barrel.

beats.title: Six Knights, One Pipe
beats.modern: six knights spot us in a meadow and mount up. and they come ALL AT ONCE, none of that honorable one-at-a-time business you read about, heads down, lances level, like a volley from a battery. beautiful sight. for a man up a tree. I waited till the iron wave was about to break over me and spouted a column of white smoke through my visor bars. wave came apart. now they're two hundred yards off, too scared of dragons to leave. Sandy walked over and collected their surrender.

beats.title: Morgan Stabs The Waiter
beats.modern: Morgan le Fay is talking to me like a flute, sweetest voice you ever heard, and a page kneels to hand her something, overbalances, and brushes her knee. she put a knife in him the way you'd swat a rat. kept talking. never dropped the thread. and while the servants carried him out she was checking their work, sent back for cleaner towels, and pointed out the one red speck on the floor they'd missed.

beats.title: She Hanged The Composer
beats.modern: the band opened dinner with what I can only describe as the original rough draft of a song that would need thirteen more centuries to become bad. cymbals, horns, harps, other horrors. it was new. it wanted rehearsal. and chat, after dinner, the queen had the composer hanged.
beats.quote: For some reason or other the queen had the composer hanged, after dinner.

beats.title: Why He Wouldn't Confess
beats.modern: the man on the rack finally says it: he DID kill the deer. so why take hours of that instead of confessing? and his own wife had been begging him to confess so he'd get a quick death. then it lands. the law takes a convicted man's property. they could torture him to death all day, but with no confession they couldn't take the roof off his wife and baby. he was buying them a house with his spine.

beats.title: Nine Years, Fifty Feet Apart
beats.modern: woman in the queen's dungeon looks middle-aged. she's twenty-seven. went in at eighteen on her wedding night for refusing a lord. her husband is in the next hole, fifty feet away. nine years. neither one ever learned whether the other was alive. they stopped asking years ago. I brought him to her, chat, and they looked at each other with a sort of weak animal curiosity, and then forgot the other one was in the room.

beats.title: Sponsored Knights
beats.modern: here comes one of mine down the road cursing his soul to rags, carrying a billboard in shining gold letters: USE PETERSON'S PROPHYLACTIC TOOTH-BRUSH. that's Sir Madok. his shield has a gauntlet gripping a toothbrush, motto TRY NOYOUDONT. he is hunting the stove-polish guy, who sent him on a three-hour cross-country ride to sell tooth-wash to five men who just did twenty years in a dungeon and have no teeth left.

beats.title: The Castle Is A Pigsty
beats.modern: Sandy whispers THE CASTLE, LO WHERE IT LOOMS. chat it's a pigsty. wattled fence. she explains it must be enchanted to my eyes only, so I play along and buy all forty-five "princesses" off the swineherds for sixteen pennies. then she runs down the hill sobbing with joy, throws herself on the hogs and calls them by their titles. we drove them home ten miles. I grabbed one by the tail and got told it is indelicate to drag a countess by her train.

beats.title: The Girl In The Slave Line
beats.modern: she was barely more than a kid, carrying a baby, and she stumbled from exhaustion so the master opened her back with a lash in the middle of the road. one of the chained men turned his face away and got flogged for it. our pilgrims watched and complimented the technique. they were kind people. they would not have let him do that to a horse. she was sold an hour later, and the man who turned his face away was her husband.

beats.title: Fireworks At The Fountain
beats.modern: the holy well went dry, Merlin's been sweating on it three days, so I set up a hogshead of rockets, four magazines of Greek fire, buried wires, and a Latin chant for the pre-show. then I stood up in front of that whole black valley and slowly pronounced a word. blue fire. another word. red. then green. then purple. then the demon's true name, the rockets go up, and the water comes out the chapel door. Merlin went home on a shutter.
beats.quote: “Constantinopolitanischerdudelsackspfeifenmachersgesellschafft!”

beats.title: What's My Right Hand Doing
beats.modern: a wandering magician shows up and starts telling the monks what the Sultan of Egypt is doing RIGHT NOW. accuracy: flawless, unfalsifiable, crowd is eating it. so I offer him two hundred silver pennies for one question. tell me what I am doing with my right hand. dead silence. he's got nothing. can read a man ten thousand miles away, can't read one standing three yards off.

beats.title: The Newsboy Arrives
beats.modern: I'm sitting through hour three of the king touching sick people for luck, bored out of my skull, and then through the window: CAMELOT WEEKLY HOSANNAH AND LITERARY VOLCANO, LATEST IRRUPTION, TWO CENTS. chat I nearly came apart. thirteen worthless centuries fell off me at once. and I was the only person in that entire hall who understood what had just walked into the world.
beats.quote: One greater than kings had arrived--the newsboy.

beats.title: Drilling The King To Slouch
beats.modern: taking the king out incognito and his WALK is blowing it. shoulders back, chin up, eyes on the horizon. sire, the cares of a kingdom don't bend a man. poverty does that. so we spent a whole day in a field practicing. chin down. eyes ten steps ahead. more shamble. and after all that, every mechanical detail was right and it still didn't work, because he's missing the one thing you cannot fake: the genuine spiritlessness.

beats.title: The Smallpox Hut
beats.modern: the hut is under the Church's curse so nobody has come near it in days. the woman begs us to run. the king goes up the ladder anyway and comes back down carrying a fifteen-year-old girl on his chest, dying of smallpox, so her mother can look at her one more time. no armor, no crowd, no reward, nothing to win. I have watched this man do brave things in steel. this was the first time he was great.

beats.title: Dowley Ratios Himself
beats.modern: the rich blacksmith has been dunking on me all dinner about wages, so I walk him through the pillory instead. how the mob starts with clods, then dead cats, then bricks. how an unpopular man just dies in it. everybody agrees, yes, terrible. and then: shame, Dowley, that you mentioned an hour ago you paid a man over the legal rate this week. whole table went white. I only meant to scare them. not to death.

beats.title: Sold For Seven Dollars
beats.modern: the nice lord who rescued us from that mob had his servants cuff us in the market square. put up the slaves and sell them. and here's the law, chat: the claimant doesn't have to prove you're a slave, YOU have to prove you're not. we couldn't. so they auctioned us. the King of England went for seven dollars. I went for nine. dull market. he was worth twelve.

beats.title: The Girl On The Gallows
beats.modern: she was eighteen. they pressed her husband into the navy without telling her, she lost the room, she begged until she couldn't, and then she stole a piece of cloth worth a quarter of a cent to feed the baby. the man she stole it from heard the sentence, screamed that he didn't know it was death, and took his own life before sundown. they had to pry the baby out of her arms. the priest told her he'd be its father till he died.

beats.title: Five Hundred Knights On Bicycles
beats.modern: they hang three slaves in front of me, and then they blindfold the KING and walk him under the rope, and I can't move, I can't speak. noose goes on him. and I looked down that road one last time and chat. CHAT. the cavalry came. Launcelot at the front, plumes streaming, sun flashing off five hundred sets of spokes. Clarence had been drilling them in secret for months, just for the entrance.
beats.quote: here they came, a-tilting!--five hundred mailed and belted knights on bicycles!

beats.title: Lasso Meta
beats.modern: Sagramor came back from grailing and cashed in that grudge. he's a tower of iron on an armored horse. I turned up in flesh-colored tights on a bare horse with no lance, no sword, nothing. dodged him three passes until he lost his temper and started chasing me, which is a game of tag I win every time. then I took the rope off my saddle horn, swung it wide, and yanked him clean out of the seat.

beats.title: Merlin Stole My Lasso
beats.modern: seven knights roped, Launcelot included. I'm sitting there drunk on it thinking knight-errantry is dead. then the bugle goes again and my lasso is GONE, Merlin lifted it under his robe. and here comes Sagramor with a sword and death in his smile, and the king says the man is weaponless, and Sagramor says he fights with what he brought. fine. I let him get to fifteen paces. one flash, one bang, revolver back in the holster before anybody blinked.

beats.title: I Challenge All Of England
beats.modern: nobody could find a wound on him so nobody understood. so I stayed where I stood and said it: I name none, I challenge all. not one at a time. in mass. it was a bluff, chat, and five hundred of them called it and came down on me at once. eleven shots in the cylinders. nine saddles emptied before I felt the wobble go through the crowd, then I just raised both barrels and they broke and ran.

beats.title: I Hanged My Own Author
beats.modern: three years on and England is unrecognizable. schools, colleges, newspapers, railways, telephones, slavery abolished, dukes working as train conductors. we even got authorship started. Sir Dinadan the Humorist published first, a whole volume of jokes I'd known for thirteen centuries. I'd have let it slide. but he put the lecturer one in. so I suppressed the book and hanged the author.
beats.quote: I suppressed the book and hanged the author.

beats.title: Royal Family Of Cats
beats.modern: I want a republic. Clarence wants a republic with a royal family on top, because a nation that has once known the joy of worshipping one will pine away without it. I said kings are dangerous. he said, then have cats. Tom the Seventh, by the grace of God, King. same divine right, same vanity, cheaper, and they hang nobody. inside forty years all Europe is governed by cats and we're the supplier. he had me completely sold and then went ME-E-E-YOW to prove it was a bit.

beats.title: Hello-Central
beats.modern: I used to call out in my sleep for a girl thirteen centuries from here. Sandy heard it every night, decided it was the name of someone I'd lost, and named our daughter after it as a surprise. then she said it out loud to me with her whole heart. HELLO-CENTRAL. I did not laugh. I am grateful for that every day of my life. it did rupture something internal, I could hear my bones clack for weeks. she never found out.

beats.title: The Interdict
beats.modern: sail home and the harbors are dead. no sails, no smoke, no bells. Canterbury empty on a Sunday. then I see a funeral with no priest walk straight past a church without going in, and I look up at the belfry and the bell is wrapped in black with its tongue tied back. and I understood. it wasn't invasion. invasion would be nothing next to this. the Church had struck.

beats.title: Launcelot Corners The Market
beats.modern: want to know what actually ended the Round Table, chat? not love. the stock-board. Launcelot quietly bought the London, Canterbury and Dover on the cheap, then bought twice as much again deliverable on call, and squeezed. Mordred and Agravaine got skinned alive in the settlement at 283. so they went to the king with the thing about Launcelot and the queen that everyone but the king already knew. a short squeeze burned down Camelot.

beats.title: The King Is Dead
beats.modern: the whole board went over while I was at sea. queen to the stake, Launcelot rescues her and cuts down Gareth and Gaheris in the blur without ever seeing who they were. civil war. Mordred takes the throne. two armies at Salisbury under a truce, and an adder bites a knight on the heel. he draws his sword at the snake. both hosts saw a blade come up and fell on each other for a whole day. Arthur got Mordred. Mordred got Arthur.

beats.title: Proclaim The Republic
beats.modern: Clarence says sit down and wait. no sir. defense isn't my line. we've got fifty-two boys, Merlin's cave, thirteen gatlings, electric fences and a forty-foot belt of buried torpedoes, and the whole Church is coming. so I dictated it, printed it, posted it, and signed it The Boss, dated from Merlin's Cave, which tells them exactly where to find us. that's the point. we strike, then it's their innings.
beats.quote: A Republic is hereby proclaimed, as being the natural estate of a nation when other authority has ceased.

beats.title: Fifty-Four Minds
beats.modern: I wrote them a surrender offer. reflect: we are well fortified and we number 54. fifty-four what, men? no. MINDS. the capablest in the world. throw down your arms and all is forgiven. read it to Clarence first, and he played the enemy commander, slapped the paper out of my hand and told me word for word what they'd send back. he was right. I tore it up and gave my sentimentality a permanent rest.

beats.title: Killed By A Dead Man
beats.modern: first one came in the dark and found the top wire with both hands. stood there upright in his armor like a statue, plumes moving a little in the night wind, smell of burning. second one crept up behind him, wondered why his friend wasn't moving on, said "why dreamest thou here, good Sir Mar--" and put a hand on his shoulder. one small soft moan and down. killed by a dead man. killed by a dead friend.

beats.title: Eleven Thousand
beats.modern: they came in silence because they wanted a surprise, so not one of them ever got to shout. the bodies stacked into a wall around us, three fences deep. then I hit the switch on fifty electric suns and the whole host froze in the glare for exactly one instant, and I used it. that was the sound, chat. one groan for eleven thousand men. then the ditch flooded, the thirteen gatlings opened, and ten minutes later fifty-four of us owned England.
beats.quote: There was a groan you could hear! It voiced the death-pang of eleven thousand men.

beats.title: I Am Merlin
beats.modern: here's the trap, and we built it ourselves. stay inside and our own dead poison us. step outside and we're just fifty-four men. the first wounded knight I bent down to help stabbed me. and the kind old peasant woman who turned up to cook for us was Merlin the entire time. he told us at midnight, laughing. then he reeled back into one of our own wires. his mouth is still open.
beats.quote: “Ye were conquerors; ye are conquered! These others are perishing --you also. Ye shall all die in this place--every one--except him. He sleepeth now--and shall sleep thirteen centuries. I am Merlin!”

beats.title: Man The Battlements
beats.modern: thirteen centuries later, dying in a rented room, and he's talking to a Sandy who isn't there. asking for her hand. asking someone to bring the baby so he can touch her hair and say goodbye. he says he's been having awful dreams, that the king was dead, that there was a revolution, that he was a creature out of some unborn age with an abyss of thirteen hundred years between him and everything he loved. then he hears a bugle. gg.

beats.title: The Roommate Does A Bit
beats.modern: my roommate is on the roof of our tower doing a full latin mass with his shaving bowl. holds it up. does the voice. blesses the mountains. then yells at me to come up the stairs like I'm a dog he owns. chat I have not slept. it is 8am and he is doing bits.

beats.title: You Could Have Knelt
beats.modern: and then he brings up my mother. asks why I wouldn't kneel and pray at her deathbed when she begged me with her last breath. chat she comes to me in dreams smelling of wax and wet ashes and I keep seeing the white bowl of green bile beside her bed. and he says it while SHAVING. casually. like weather.
beats.quote: There is something sinister in you....

beats.title: Cracked Lookingglass
beats.modern: he holds up a mirror he stole out of the maid's room so I can look at myself. hair on end. glass cracked down the middle. I told him: that's Irish art for you. a servant's cracked mirror. he thought it was a great line. chat it was not a line.
beats.quote: —It is a symbol of Irish art. The cracked lookingglass of a servant.

beats.title: Usurper
beats.modern: he asks for the key to the tower. the tower I pay the rent on. then he asks for beer money. I handed over both and walked. he's in the water shouting after me, a little seal head bobbing out there. I'm not sleeping there tonight and I can't go home either. one word for him, chat.
beats.quote: —He who stealeth from the poor lendeth to the Lord.

beats.title: History Is A Nightmare
beats.modern: my boss has me cornered at his desk explaining all of history to me. where it's going. God's big plan. so I told him history is a nightmare I'm trying to wake up from. outside the window the boys score a goal and start screaming. I pointed at the screaming. that's God. that's all of it.
beats.quote: —History, Stephen said, is a nightmare from which I am trying to awake.

beats.title: Never Let Them In
beats.modern: he chased me down to the gate. ran. just to land a joke. said Ireland is the only country that never persecuted the jews, and do I know why. because she never let them in. then he laughed so hard he choked on his own phlegm, waving his arms in the sun. chat that's my employer.
beats.quote: —Because she never let them in, Mr Deasy said solemnly.

beats.title: Shut Your Eyes And See
beats.modern: walking the beach alone doing philosophy at myself, as one does when unemployed. closed my eyes to check whether the world keeps existing when I stop looking at it. kept walking. crunch crunch crunch. opened them. still there. chat the world does not need me. noted.
beats.quote: Shut your eyes and see.

beats.title: New Streamer, Same Day
beats.modern: channel switch, chat. same city, same morning, different man. I'm Leopold Bloom and I eat the organs. kidneys, hearts, gizzards, the whole inside of the animal. grilled mutton kidney has a faint tang of urine and that is genuinely the appeal. wife's still in bed upstairs. cat is doing laps of the table leg. beautiful day.
beats.quote: Mr Leopold Bloom ate with relish the inner organs of beasts and fowls.

beats.title: The Cat Has Notes
beats.modern: the cat is speaking to me. mkgnao. then mrkgnao. then MRKRGNAO, escalating every single time milk fails to appear. people say cats are stupid, chat. they understand us perfectly. we're the ones who don't understand them. I wonder what I look like to her. tall as a tower? no. she could jump me.
beats.quote: They call them stupid. They understand what we say better than we understand them.

beats.title: Met Him Pike Hoses
beats.modern: wife wants a word explained out of her book. metempsychosis. I said it's Greek, transmigration of souls, you get born again as something else. she said tell us in plain words. chat she is reading a novel where a circus girl gets whipped by an italian and SHE wants plain words from ME.
beats.quote: —O, rocks! she said. Tell us in plain words.

beats.title: The Jakes Arc
beats.modern: out to the outhouse with the paper. reading the prize story, pacing myself, timing it perfectly, seated calm above my own rising smell. some man got three pounds thirteen and six for writing this. I could do that. me and the wife, by Mr and Mrs L. M. Bloom. anyway I tore it in half and wiped with it.
beats.quote: He read on, seated calm above his own rising smell.

beats.title: Dear Henry
beats.modern: she wrote back. Martha. writes to Henry Flower, who is me, because I am running a full alias for a pen pal affair I have never once acted on. she's angry about the stamps. she wants to punish me. she asks if I'm unhappy at home. and then the postscript: what perfume does your wife use. MARTHA.
beats.quote: Are you not happy in your home you poor little naughty boy?

beats.title: This Is My Body
beats.modern: off to the baths. going to lie in the warm water and look down the length of myself floating there, navel like a little bud, everything drifting soft in the stream like a lazy flower. this is my body, chat. it's not even noon and this is the best part of the day so far.

beats.title: If Little Rudy Had Lived
beats.modern: man in the funeral carriage will not stop talking about his son. good for him, honestly. something to hand on. I had a son. he lived eleven days. if Rudy had lived I'd be hearing his voice in the house right now, walking beside Molly in a little suit, me in his eyes. I could have helped him on in life. I could have.
beats.quote: If little Rudy had lived. See him grow up. Hear his voice in the house.

beats.title: There He Is, Airing His Quiff
beats.modern: and there he is on the street. white straw hat. Boylan. the man who is coming to my house at four o'clock today. everyone in the carriage leans out and waves at him. and chat, at that exact moment, I looked down and reviewed my own fingernails. left hand. then right hand. very thorough. lovely nails.

beats.title: Corpse Is Meat Gone Bad
beats.modern: there's a rat wriggling in under a gravestone. it'll strip whoever's under there, doesn't matter who they were in life. a corpse is meat gone bad. and what's cheese? corpse of milk. anyway the gates are still open so I'm leaving. they are not getting me this innings. warm beds, chat. warm fullblooded life.
beats.quote: A corpse is meat gone bad.

beats.title: The House Of Keys
beats.modern: pitching the ad, chat. two crossed keys at the top, the house of keys, little wink at the Manx parliament, innuendo of home rule, and the tourists eat it up. the foreman scratches his ribs and says we can do that. that's my whole job. I sell the small boxes in the newspaper.

beats.title: The Parable Of The Plums
beats.modern: told the newsroom my story. two old women climb the pillar, get too scared to look down, sit on their petticoats, eat plums, and spit the stones out through the railings onto Dublin. that's the whole story. the editor loved it. I gave it a title about Moses seeing the promised land he never gets to enter.
beats.quote: I call it A Pisgah Sight of Palestine or The Parable of The Plums.

beats.title: Elijah Is Coming
beats.modern: man hands me a leaflet in the street and for one second I read my own name in it. Bloo... me? no. blood of the lamb. it's a revival ad. Elijah is coming. chat I'm keeping this. remember this leaflet. it comes back.
beats.quote: Bloo... Me? No.

beats.title: The Seedcake
beats.modern: one glass of burgundy in a quiet pub and I'm on Howth head sixteen years ago. ferns, the bay asleep below us, her hair on my coat. she chewed a piece of seedcake soft and put it in my mouth and I ate it and it was joy. she said take me. ...two flies stuck buzzing on the window. me. and me now.
beats.quote: Softly she gave me in my mouth the seedcake warm and chewed.

beats.title: Safe!
beats.modern: straw hat. tan shoes. it's HIM. do not look up, do not look up. chat watch me become the busiest man in Ireland. searching my pockets. searching them again. what am I looking for. anything. paper. potato. purse. ah soap there I yes. gate. SAFE.

beats.title: The Hamlet Theory
beats.modern: library stream. my thesis: Shakespeare isn't the prince, he's the GHOST. wrote it after his own boy died, so writing it he stopped being anyone's son and became the father of his whole line, father of his own grandfather. the librarians are taking notes. nobody has offered me a single coin.

beats.title: A Man Passed Between Them
beats.modern: walking out of the library and a quiet man in black steps between me and Mulligan in the doorway. bows. says good day. Mulligan whispers he's the wandering jew and that he was looking at me. chat we have never spoken. we just passed through each other like a door and that was that.
beats.quote: A man passed out between them, bowing, greeting.

beats.title: Dilly Bought A Book
beats.modern: ran into my little sister at the second hand book cart. she bought a french primer for a penny and hid it when she saw me. asks if it's any good. chat there is no fire at home, no dinner, my books are pawned, and she is quietly teaching herself french. she has my eyes. she is drowning and I have money in my pocket.
beats.quote: She is drowning. Agenbite. Save her. Agenbite. All against us.

beats.title: Sonnez La Cloche
beats.modern: the lads in the hotel bar have talked the barmaid into snapping her garter against her own thigh. SMACK. huge cheer. and he's sitting right there watching, drinking, killing the hour before he comes to my house. chat I'm sitting where he can't see me. eating.

beats.title: Jingle Jaunty Jingle
beats.modern: he's gone. I can hear the car leaving down Bachelor's walk, jingle jaunty jingle, whip flick, horse trotting toward my street. chat I am sitting in a hotel dining room chewing my food while that sound gets further away. four o'clock. haw haw horn.

beats.title: Done.
beats.modern: standing at a shop window reading a hero's last words while the burgundy makes its way through me. waiting for a tram so nobody hears. here it comes. krandlkrankran. "when my country takes her place among the nations of the earth... let my epitaph be..." PPRRPFFRRPPFFFF. done.
beats.quote: Pprrpffrrppffff. Done.

beats.title: The Citizen And Garryowen
beats.modern: into the pub and there he is in the corner, the big patriot, holding court with himself, stack of newspapers, and a mangy dog that growls like it's owed money. "stand and deliver," he says. we're friends, we say. "pass, friends." chat I'm only here waiting on a man about a dead friend's insurance. this will go fine.
beats.quote: —Stand and deliver, says he.

beats.title: I Mean The Opposite Of Hatred
