beats.modern: ran the numbers on my sentence, chat. five for the bread. tried to leave, plus three. tried again, plus five. again, plus three. last time I was out four HOURS and it cost me three years. five became nineteen and none of the extra was for the bread. the loaf was just the entry fee.

beats.title: The Gendarmes Bring Me Back
beats.modern: okay so I robbed him. the one man on earth who fed me. cops catch me with the silver in my bag and drag me back to his door for the confirm. easiest case ever made. and this man walks up smiling and goes oh good you're here, you forgot the rest of it. and tells the cops to let me go. chat. CHAT.
beats.quote: I gave you the candlesticks too, which are of silver like the rest,

beats.title: I Buy Your Soul
beats.modern: he hands me the candlesticks. the actual silver. then he leans in quiet so the cops can't hear and says he's buying my soul off me and giving it to God, and that I promised to become an honest man. I promised NOTHING. he just wrote it into the save file and closed it. worst part is it worked.
beats.quote: It is your soul that I buy from you;

beats.title: Little Gervais
beats.modern: a kid walks by singing with his little coin. my boot comes down on it. he begs, I roar at him, he runs. then I look down and see silver shining and something in me just BREAKS. I ran that whole plain screaming his name into the dark. nobody answered. first time I cried in nineteen years and it wasn't for me.
beats.quote: “I am a wretch!”

beats.title: This Is The Surprise
beats.modern: story time, this part is before my POV. four rich students take four girls to dinner, promise them a big surprise, then leave the table and have a note delivered an hour later. our parents want us home, we're going to be respectable now, mourn quickly and replace us. p.s. dinner's paid for. three of the girls laughed it off. Fantine laughed too, then went home and remembered she had a baby.
beats.quote: The dinner is paid for.”

beats.title: Fifty-Seven Francs
beats.modern: she can't get hired anywhere with a kid, so she stops at an inn where two little girls are laughing on a swing and thinks: good mother, safe place. asks them to keep her daughter. wife says maybe. then the husband's voice comes out of the back room like a raid boss: not for less than seven a month, six months up front. she paid it. she thought she got lucky.

beats.title: Father Madeleine, Local Legend
beats.modern: new save, new name, new town. I invented a cheaper way to make glass beads and the whole region got rich off it. schools, hospital beds, a free clinic. they offer me mayor, I say no. king offers me a medal, I say no. town's official verdict: he's probably some kind of adventurer. sure. whatever stops you checking my papers.
beats.quote: “The two prime functionaries of the state are the nurse and the schoolmaster.”

beats.title: The Cart In The Mud
beats.modern: old man pinned under a wagon, mud swallowing it, nobody moves for twenty gold coins. then my inspector says, real slow, looking dead at me: only one man I ever knew could lift that. he was a convict. Toulon. chat he is FISHING. and the old man is screaming. so I got on my knees and lifted the cart in front of him.
beats.quote: “He was a convict.”

beats.title: Fired From My Own Factory
beats.modern: a woman on my floor had a kid she never mentioned. the town gossip took a paid trip to go LOOK at the child and came back to tell everyone. my supervisor hands her fifty francs and the door. in my name. I never heard a word about it. she didn't even come to me, chat. she decided the mayor gave her the money because he was kind and fired her because he was fair.

beats.title: The Hair, Then The Teeth
beats.modern: the innkeepers keep inventing bills. your kid is sick, they write. forty francs, they write. so she sells her hair. then a guy on a cart offers gold for her two front teeth and she runs from him screaming that he's a monster. that night she goes anyway. comes home smiling with blood in it and a black hole in her mouth. the kid was never sick. they made it up for the money.
beats.quote: The two teeth had been extracted.

beats.title: Snow Down Her Back
beats.modern: some guy in a good hat spends his whole evening insulting a woman in the street for sport, gets bored that she won't react, sneaks up behind her and shoves a fistful of snow down her bare back. she turns and claws his face. guess which one of them gets arrested. he wandered off during the paperwork.

beats.title: The Highest Law Is Conscience
beats.modern: six months in jail, says my inspector. she has a daughter, she says. so I say one word: I. I let her go. he goes white. he says the law was insulted. I tell him conscience outranks the law and she will not serve a single day. chat I just used the mayor account to override the cop in front of his own station and he will never forgive it.
beats.quote: “the highest law is conscience. I have heard this woman; I know what I am doing.”

beats.title: He Reported Me To Himself
beats.modern: my inspector walks into my office and confesses. to me. he says he got angry after the cart thing and wrote to the Prefecture that the mayor is an escaped convict named Jean Valjean. he is telling me this to my face. chat, he reported me, and then came to tell me he reported me, because not telling me would have been dishonest.
beats.quote: Wrath impelled me; I denounced you at the Prefecture!”

beats.title: They Caught Jean Valjean
beats.modern: here's the twist. the reply came back and it says the real Jean Valjean is already in custody. some confused old man who stole apples. four witnesses positively ID'd him. trial tomorrow in Arras, galleys for life, done. my inspector explains all of this to me cheerfully while I pretend to read paperwork. so I'm free forever. all I have to do is nothing.

beats.title: Fire Me, Sir
beats.modern: and then he asks to be fired. for it. he says if one of his own men had accused an honest mayor with no proof he'd have thrown him out of the service, so throw him out. I'm sitting there going please stop. this man's entire personality is a rulebook and he has just found himself in violation of it.

beats.title: It Is I
beats.modern: I sat in the back of that courtroom for one hour and my hair went white in it. then I stood up, said the three witnesses' names out loud, and told the judge to release the prisoner and arrest me instead. nobody in the room breathed. the prosecutor offered to call a doctor. I told him I'm not mad, you were simply about to make a very large mistake.
beats.quote: He is not the man whom you are in search of; it is I: I am Jean Valjean.”

beats.title: Fantine Finds Out
beats.modern: I made it back to her sickbed. I asked him for three days to go and get her daughter. three days. he laughs in my face and announces to the whole room that there is no mayor here, there's a convict called Jean Valjean and he's got him by the collar. she sits up. she looks at me. she reaches for something that isn't there. and that's the clip.

beats.title: I Advise You Not To Disturb Me
beats.modern: I tore an iron bar off the spare bed and looked at him. he backed to the door. I told him quietly not to disturb me right now. then I put her head on the pillow the way you'd do for a sleeping kid, tied her collar, smoothed her hair, closed her eyes, knelt and kissed her hand. then I turned round and told him I'm ready.
beats.quote: “I advise you not to disturb me at this moment.”

beats.title: Number 9,430
beats.modern: back in the galleys, new number. sailor's hanging off a yard over open water and nobody will go up. I ask permission, snap my ankle chain with one hammer blow and go get him. whole harbour screaming pardon that man. then on the way down I fall in the sea and never surface. paper next day: convict 9,430 drowned, body not recovered, name Jean Valjean. yeah. about that.

beats.title: The Bucket In The Woods
beats.modern: found her in the forest at night. eight years old, hauling a bucket bigger than she is, alone, in the dark. I take the handle without a word and we walk. I ask about her mother. she says other people have mothers, I have none, I don't think I ever had any. chat I promised a dead woman I'd find this kid and I found her carrying water in the woods at night.
beats.quote: Other people have mothers. I have none.”

beats.title: Catherine
beats.modern: there's a doll in the shop window she's been staring at for weeks and is never allowed to touch. I bought it. put it in her hands. she asked permission three separate times, from the woman who beats her, before she'd believe it. whole tavern went dead silent. she named it Catherine. chat that kid held that doll like it might be taken back.
beats.quote: “I shall call her Catherine,”

beats.title: The Wooden Shoe
beats.modern: christmas eve. the two daughters of the house set their pretty little shoes by the fire and mother fairy has already dropped a coin in each one. then way back in the dark corner of the hearth there's a third. a beat-up wooden clog covered in ash and dried mud. she put hers out too. hoping. it was empty. I put a gold piece in it and went to bed.
beats.quote: There was nothing in this wooden shoe.

beats.title: Fifteen Hundred Francs
beats.modern: innkeeper opens with a speech about how a father can't just hand his beloved foster daughter to a stranger, he'd need to know where she's going, he'd need to see a passport. I tell him he gets none of that. he reads the room in half a second and drops the whole act: I need fifteen hundred francs. I put the bills on the table under my thumb. go and fetch Cosette.

beats.title: Over The Wall
beats.modern: dead end alley, patrol closing, my inspector's voice bouncing off the walls telling them to search it. she whispers dad I'm scared, who's coming. I tell her it's the innkeeper's wife come to take her back. cruel. it worked, she went silent. rope round her under the arms, up the wall barefoot, her on my back along the top, down the roof, into a garden. she never made a sound.
beats.quote: “Search the blind alley! The Rue Droit-Mur is guarded!

beats.title: Buried Alive
beats.modern: to stay in the convent I had to leave it and come back in through the front door legally. the plan: get nailed into a coffin, ride out with a real funeral, get dug up by my guy before they fill it in. priest leaves. I'm alone. I'm fine. then thunder. it's dirt. it's dirt hitting the lid. second shovelful. third. one of my air holes is gone.
beats.quote: It was a shovelful of earth falling on the coffin.

beats.title: The Note In The Colonel's Hand
beats.modern: different stream, but you need this one. a rich kid's father dies and leaves him one scrap of paper. it says: the Emperor made me a baron at Waterloo, take the title. and then: a sergeant named Thénardier saved my life there, he keeps a little inn near Paris, if you ever meet him do all the good you can for him. the kid is Marius. the innkeeper is THAT innkeeper. hold that thought for years.
beats.quote: “At that same battle of Waterloo, a sergeant saved my life. The man’s name was Thénardier.

beats.title: The Red-Hot Chisel
beats.modern: walked into a charity call, it was a trap, and the man running it is the innkeeper wearing a new name. six of them. they want my signature on a ransom letter. I tell them my life isn't worth the trouble of defending, then I pick their own glowing chisel off the fire and lay it on my bare arm and hold it there. nobody in that room could look at me. I threw it out the window. do what you like.
beats.quote: “have no more fear of me than I have for you!”

beats.title: A Dog Scanning A Thief
beats.modern: there's a boy orbiting our bench in the park. every day. she's started noticing him. and I have spent my whole life being hunted so I know exactly what I look like right now: a dog watching a thief. so I moved the bench. then he found the street. so I moved the house. chat I know how this ends and I did it anyway.
beats.quote: It was a dog scanning a thief.

beats.title: I Adore You
beats.modern: the garden clip I never got to see. he tells her the truth: he's broke, his boots let water in, he can't follow her to England, he can't even pay for a passport. then he puts his forehead against a tree like a statue of despair for two hours while she cries behind him. then: do you love me. she says I adore you. and he gives her his word of honour that if she leaves he'll die. he meant it literally. that's the problem.
beats.quote: “I adore you!”

beats.title: Move Away From Your House
beats.modern: someone scratched an address into my garden wall in the night. fresh, plaster dust still on the nettles. I don't tell her. then I'm sitting out on the slope and a paper folded in four drops onto my knees from behind me: MOVE AWAY FROM YOUR HOUSE. I'm up instantly, nobody there, just something too big to be a child and too small to be a man vaulting the parapet.
beats.quote: “MOVE AWAY FROM YOUR HOUSE.”

beats.title: The Funeral That Became A War
beats.modern: they buried a general and the whole city turned out. rain, a red flag, someone yelling take him to the Pantheon. dragoons blocking the bridge. three shots from nobody knows where: one kills a squadron chief, one kills a deaf old woman closing her window. a voice screams they're starting too soon. and Paris just goes up. stones, muskets, paving torn out, barricades within the hour.
beats.quote: “They are beginning too soon!”

beats.title: Éponine's Last Clip
beats.modern: the innkeeper's eldest daughter. she took a musket ball through the HAND stopping it hitting him, and it went on into her, and she dragged herself to the barricade to die at his feet. she'd been carrying the letter from the girl he loves in her pocket the whole time. hands it over. asks one thing: kiss my forehead when I'm dead, I'll feel it. then, last words, almost cheerful: by the way, I think I was a little bit in love with you.
beats.quote: “And by the way, Monsieur Marius, I believe that I was a little bit in love with you.”

beats.title: The Blotter In The Mirror
beats.modern: I'm pacing the new place feeling GOOD, chat. quiet street, London in a week, she's safe, everything's fine. then I catch four lines in the mirror over the sideboard. it's her letter. she blotted it and left the book lying open and the mirror flipped it the right way round for me. my dearest, my father is making us leave. she has a him. I sat down in that chair and the light went out of the world.
beats.quote: The mirror reflected the writing.

beats.title: A Fifth Uniform Falls From Heaven
beats.modern: they had four spare uniforms and five men with families, and Marius was being made to choose which one stays and dies. every one of them shouting me, me, me. then a fifth uniform lands on the pile out of nowhere. fifth man saved. Marius looks up and it's me. I walked into a barricade to carry a boy home to my daughter, chat. that is the entire reason I'm here.

beats.title: Gavroche Outside The Wall
beats.modern: we're out of cartridges, so the smallest kid on the barricade climbs OUT with a basket and starts looting the dead in the open street, in front of the line, singing at them. every volley misses. he ducks, pops up, thumbs his nose, keeps singing, keeps filling the basket. we're all screaming at him to come back. then one bullet finds him. he sits up with blood on his face and starts the next verse anyway. he didn't get to finish it.

beats.title: You Are Free
beats.modern: they had my inspector tied up to be shot and I asked for the job. everyone assumed. I walk him out to the alley past Éponine's body, put the pistol under my arm and open a knife. he goes: a clasp-knife, yeah, that suits you better. take your revenge. so I cut the rope at his neck, his wrists, his feet. you are free. here's my address, by the way. he stood there like a broken statue, then shouted back down the lane: you annoy me, kill me instead.
beats.quote: “You are free.”

beats.title: Shoot Me
beats.modern: upstairs, last room, Enjolras alone with a broken gun barrel and no cartridges. twelve rifles on him. he throws the stub away, folds his arms and says shoot me. one guardsman lowers his gun saying it feels like shooting a flower. and then the drunk wakes up. Grantaire, asleep through the entire war, opens his eyes, understands everything instantly, stands up and shouts long live the Republic, I'm one of them. walks over. do you permit it? they died together.
beats.quote: “Long live the Republic! I’m one of them.”

beats.title: The Quagmire
beats.modern: carrying the boy out through the sewers. unconscious, bleeding, dead weight on my back. then the floor stops being floor. it's a sinkhole. slime to my calves, then my knees, then water at my chin with him held up above my head. one more step and it's over for both of us. and then my foot hits stone. there was a shelf down there. there was a shelf down there, chat.

beats.title: You Pay When You Go Out
beats.modern: there's a locked grating at the outlet and a man in the dark with the key. it's HIM. the innkeeper. he doesn't recognise me under the filth, he's decided I murdered the boy on my back, and he is thrilled about it. robs my pockets, takes everything down to the coppers, tells me I cut people's throats too cheap. then unlocks the gate like a turnstile. it's like the fair here, you pay on the way out.
beats.quote: “Now, my friend, you must leave. It’s like the fair here, you pay when you go out.

beats.title: Waiting Outside The Grating
beats.modern: step out of the sewer into clean air and he's standing right there. arms folded. of course he is. I say inspector, you have me, I've counted myself your prisoner since this morning, just grant me one favour. he doesn't answer. he kneels down instead and wipes the blood off the boy's face with his own handkerchief and takes his pulse. I say he's wounded. he says he's a dead man. I say: no. not yet.

beats.title: Javert Derailed
beats.modern: he let me go. drove me home, waited at my door, and left. then he went to the station and wrote the most Javert document in history: a numbered list of prison reforms. prisoners standing barefoot on cold flagstones. the bars on the canteen. ten sous docked for a broken thread. signed, inspector first class. then he walked back to the parapet above the rapids, set his hat on the stone, and stepped off.

beats.title: My Name Is Not Fauchelevent
beats.modern: day after the wedding I walk into her husband's house and hand him the whole thing. I'm not her father. I'm not related to her at all. I'm a peasant from Faverolles who pruned trees for a living. my name is not Fauchelevent, it's Jean Valjean. he asks who on earth could prove that. I say: me. since I'm telling you. nobody lies that calmly. he believed me.
beats.quote: My name is not Fauchelevent, but Jean Valjean.

beats.title: The Pendulum Winding Down
beats.modern: so I stop visiting. not all at once. every evening I walk towards her street and every evening I stop a little sooner. the corner. then the street before it. then the street before that. an old man going out at the same hour to not arrive. the neighbours decided I was simple. children followed me laughing. one thought the whole way home: what's the use.
beats.quote: One would have said that he was a pendulum which was no longer wound up,

beats.title: Blackmailed Into The Truth
beats.modern: the innkeeper turns up to sell Marius dirt on me. proof that I'm a murderer, he says. produces his evidence: a scrap of cloth he tore off the killer in the sewer that night. Marius has the matching coat upstairs. chat this man walked in to blackmail him and accidentally PROVED I carried him home. Marius pays him off to get out, then runs for a carriage shouting it was him, he saved my life, he carried me through the sewer.
beats.quote: It was he who saved my life!

beats.title: It Is Nothing To Die
beats.modern: they got there in time. both of them on their knees telling me I'm going to live. doctor takes my pulse and whispers two words to Marius: too late. and the only thing I can get out is that dying isn't the hard part. not living is. then I stood up, walked to the wall on my own legs, took down the little copper crucifix and set it on the table.
beats.quote: “It is nothing to die; it is dreadful not to live.”

beats.title: The Candlesticks Go Back
beats.modern: leaving her the two candlesticks off the mantelpiece. they're only silver but to me they're gold, they're diamonds, they turn any candle you put in them into a wax taper. I hope the man who gave them to me is pleased with what I did with them. bury me under a plain stone, chat. no name on it.
beats.quote: They are of silver, but to me they are gold, they are diamonds;

beats.title: Her Mother's Name
beats.modern: last thing. Cosette, it's time you knew your mother's name. she was called Fantine. kneel when you say it. she suffered as much as you have been happy, that's just how it got divided up. remember Montfermeil? the forest, the bucket, the first time I ever touched your hand and it was freezing. love each other always, there's nothing else in the world. come closer, both of you. let me put my hands on your heads. gg.
beats.quote: She was called Fantine. Remember that name—Fantine.

a-journey-to-the-centre.title: A Journey to the Centre of the Earth
a-journey-to-the-centre.author: Jules Verne

beats.title: The Parchment Falls Out
beats.modern: uncle kicks the door in screaming my name because he bought an old book. not a GOOD book. an old one. twelfth century Icelandic, unreadable, he's tapping his forehead going wonderful, wonderful. then a scrap of paper falls out of the pages covered in runes and chat I watched a man's whole personality reroute in real time. that scrap ends me. I just don't know it yet.

beats.title: Nobody Eats Until I Solve It
beats.modern: he's decided the scribble is a cipher and he WILL crack it. "until I discover the meaning of this sentence I will neither eat nor sleep." cool. inspiring. love that for you. then: "nor you neither." EXCUSE ME? he locked the front door and pocketed the key. me and the cook are hostages to a man's side quest.
beats.quote: Until I discover the meaning of this sentence I will neither eat nor sleep."

beats.title: Read It Backwards
beats.modern: day two. eyes fried, letters dancing, brain on fire. I start fanning myself with the cursed paper to not pass out, catch the BACK of it, and the ink has bled through. chat. you read it backwards. that's it. that's the whole puzzle. he's been raw-dogging alphabet math for two days and I solved it by being overheated.

beats.title: Perish The Fearful Secret
beats.modern: so I read it. and then I decided nobody on earth is ever knowing this. because if HE reads it he goes, and if he goes he takes me, and we do not come back. book in one hand, parchment in the other, walking to the fire. burning it. burning it right now— he walked in. he walked in.

beats.title: I Did It, Signed Arne
beats.modern: I caved for a bread roll. he reads it out: go down the crater at Sneffels that the shadow of Scartaris touches, before July, brave traveler, and you'll reach the centre of the earth. I DID IT. some sixteenth century alchemist left a dare in a book three hundred years ago and my uncle just accepted it on my behalf.
beats.quote: Descend into the crater of Yocul of Sneffels, which the shade of Scartaris caresses, before the kalends of July, audacious traveler, and you will reach the centre of the earth. I did it.

beats.title: Gretchen Is Not Helping
beats.modern: told my fiancée the plan, fully expecting backup. she said, out loud, with her whole chest: what a magnificent journey, if only I were a man. babe. BABE. you were my last save point. she is ENVIOUS. the household has voted and I am going into a volcano.
beats.quote: "What a magnificent journey. If I were only a man! A journey worthy of the nephew of Professor Hardwigg.

beats.title: Vertigo Bootcamp
beats.modern: I mentioned I get dizzy on tall things. so he took me to a church steeple with an outside staircase and asked, in the pitiless voice, if I was a coward. I went up on my hands and knees like a snake with my eyes shut. came down folded in half like a rheumatic old man. he did this to me for five days. day five I strolled up. worst part: it worked.

beats.title: Seasick Conqueror
beats.modern: eleven days at sea and the man who intends to conquer the interior of the earth cannot conquer a boat. flat on his back the entire crossing, groaning, unable to interrogate the captain about mountains. I was completely fine. chat I need you to know that I did not pity him. not once.

beats.title: Behold Mount Sneffels
beats.modern: we dock in Iceland and before he greets a single human being he hauls me to the quarterdeck, points north at a white two-peaked mountain, and whispers it like a password. then finger to the lips. scowl. we do NOT say the mountain's name out loud. we are being extremely normal about this.
beats.quote: "Behold he whispered in an awe-stricken voice, behold--Mount Sneffels!"

beats.title: Efter
beats.modern: hired a guide. Hans. duck-down hunter. moves approximately one muscle per hour, says one word per conversation. uncle tries to pay him up front and he says: after. then leaves. no questions. chat this man has agreed to walk into the centre of the earth for fourteen shillings a week and his only condition is that Saturday is payday.
beats.quote: "Efter."

beats.title: The Horse Says No
beats.modern: uncle tries to ride his pony across a sea inlet. pony sniffs the wave, says no. uncle whips it. pony spreads its legs, slides out from under him, and leaves him standing on two separate rocks like the Colossus of Rhodes. then Hans taps his shoulder and points at the FERRY. there was a ferry. there was always a ferry.

beats.title: Saknussemm Was Here
beats.modern: bottom of the crater. three holes, no way to pick. then uncle SCREAMS and I assume he's fallen in. no. he's frozen in front of a black slab tall enough to hold a statue, arms out, staring at a name carved into it three hundred years ago. still readable. "now, unbeliever, do you begin to have faith?" I could not produce one word.
beats.quote: "Arne Saknussemm!" cried my uncle, "now, unbeliever, do you begin to have faith?"

beats.title: The Shadow Hits The Pit
beats.modern: we needed direct sun to show us which of the three holes. six days of cloud and rain and I was quietly praying for one more so the whole thing gets postponed a year. Sunday the 28th the sky opens. noon exactly. the peak's shadow crawls across the floor and lands on the middle pit like a cursor. forward, he says. we went in at 1:13.

beats.title: Down The Rope
beats.modern: leaned over the shaft to look. hundred feet across, no bottom, nothing but throat. hair up, teeth chattering, I lose my centre of gravity and start to go over — and a hand catches me. Hans. doesn't speak, doesn't look at me, just puts me back. five days of steeple training and I nearly deleted myself on the tutorial.

beats.title: Last Look At The Sky
beats.modern: lamps lit, packs up, he says forward. and right as I stepped into the tunnel I looked back up the shaft and there was a little circle of Iceland sky. and I knew. that's the one. that's the last one I get. I stood there thinking is that really it. then I walked in anyway.

beats.title: The Trilobite Receipt
beats.modern: picked a fossil shell out of the wall and held it up to him. "trilobite. nothing more, I assure you." sir. SIR. a trilobite means we left the lava road. we are not on Saknussemm's route. and then he admits it — he's known for hours. he just kept walking with his eyes closed, because to him being wrong out loud costs more than dying of thirst.

beats.title: No Thoroughfare
beats.modern: six days down the wrong tunnel and then: wall. no left, no right, no over, no under. rock saying no in a language you can't argue with. and the water is gone. tomorrow there is not one drop between the three of us. he tells me my courage went with it. I'd have traded a diamond mine for a glass of water.
beats.quote: I would have bartered a diamond mine for a glass of pure spring water!

beats.title: The Last Mouthful
beats.modern: I'm on the floor at the crossroads, lips split, done, ready to be somebody's interesting fossil. he lifts me up and puts the flask to my mouth. one swallow. he'd been carrying that swallow for days. said he resisted it a hundred times because he knew I'd fall here. this man tortures me daily and then does that.
beats.quote: Twenty times, a hundred times, I have resisted the fearful desire to drink it. But--no--no, Harry, I saved it for you."

beats.title: One More Day
beats.modern: I said we turn around. he said: go, take Hans, I'll go on alone. and then he pitched me. Columbus asked his crew for three days and got a continent. he's asking me for one. one day to find water and if he doesn't he swears he takes us up. what am I supposed to say to that. we went down.
beats.quote: Now I, the Christopher Columbus of this subterranean region, only ask of you one more day.

beats.title: Hans Digs For Water
beats.modern: Hans vanishes into the dark with the lamp. I assume he's leaving us to die. he comes back and says two words: water, below. then he walks the granite with his ear on it until he finds the exact spot and starts swinging a crowbar. an hour of small patient hits. then it BLASTS through and slams the far wall. we drink. it's boiling. "never mind, it'll cool."
beats.quote: "Well, never mind," said my uncle, "it will soon get cool."

beats.title: Old Ocean Overhead
beats.modern: ran the numbers on the map. fifty leagues southeast of the coast means we're past the island. chat we are not under Iceland anymore. we are under the ATLANTIC. I announce this like it's terrible news and he rubs his hands together like I told him dinner's ready. whales over our heads. he says don't worry, they can't get through.

beats.title: Chat I Am Alone Down Here
beats.modern: walking out front examining granite, fully locked in, not looking back once. turn around. nobody. walk back fifteen minutes. nobody. shout, and the shout comes back at me from every direction at once and none of them are him. I told myself out loud there is only one road so we have to meet. I did not believe me.

beats.title: The River Is Gone
beats.modern: the stream was my thread. follow the water, find them, follow it all the way back to daylight if I have to. I knelt to splash my face and my hands hit dry shingle. it's not here. it was never in this tunnel. I took one wrong fork at the halt and walked away from the only thread I had. thirty leagues of rock on my shoulders like Atlas.

beats.title: Lights Out
beats.modern: lamp's failing. I watched the last thread of light shrink in the coil and I would not blink in case blinking cost me the end of it. then it went. not night-dark. deleted-dark. no light anywhere for a hundred miles to leak in. so I ran. screaming, falling, bleeding, tasting my own blood, until my legs quit under me.

beats.title: The Whispering Gallery
beats.modern: half dead against the wall and I hear voices coming out of the rock. figured I'd started hallucinating. then I hear my NAME. the tunnel bends sound like a wire and my ear happens to be resting on the one spot in the whole wall where it lands. I say uncle. and out of the granite: Harry, my boy, is that you?

beats.title: Forty Seconds
beats.modern: we timed it. he says my name and marks the second, I repeat it back, he marks the second it lands. forty seconds round trip. twenty each way. that's a league and a half of solid rock between me and them. he said the number cheerfully, like it was progress. it landed on me like a death knell.
beats.quote: "Forty seconds," said my uncle. "There has elapsed forty seconds between the two words.

beats.title: The Sea, The Sea
beats.modern: I crawl toward them, the floor drops, I fall down a well and wake up bandaged in a grotto four days later. there's LIGHT. there's WIND. there are WAVES. I stagger outside and there is an ocean. horizon, clouds, storms, a granite sky burning like a permanent aurora. a hundred miles underground. he names it on the spot, obviously.
beats.quote: "The sea--the sea," I cried.

beats.title: Forest Of Mushrooms
beats.modern: round a headland and there's a forest. straight trunks, tops like parasols, completely motionless in a stiff breeze. I'm already writing the discovery paper in my head. he glances at it for one second and says, in the flattest voice a human has produced, that it is a forest of mushrooms. forty feet tall. thousands of them. it is very dark under there.
beats.quote: "It is only," he said, in his coolest manner, "a forest of mushrooms."

beats.title: Blind Fish
beats.modern: Hans drops a line in the underground sea and pulls up a fish that's been extinct since the Devonian. living fossil. uncle nearly ascends. then he adds the detail: it has no eyes. not damaged, not blinded — never had them. nothing down here has ever needed them. we caught dozens over two hours. every single one. all of them.
beats.quote: "Not only blind," continued the Professor, "but absolutely without organs of sight."

beats.title: Something Bit The Crowbar
beats.modern: raft gets lifted clean out of the water and thrown twenty fathoms. Hans points. two hundred yards out, a black mass moving. then a sea lizard. then crocodile jaws. then two columns of spray going up like artillery. the SMALLEST thing out there could take the raft and all three of us in one bite. I picked up a rifle. against armour plate. sure.

beats.title: Tva
beats.modern: they charge each other instead of us. I'm counting five monsters out there — lizard, whale, croc, turtle, serpent. Hans holds up two fingers. "two." and he's right. it's ONE ichthyosaur with a porpoise snout and lizard head and croc teeth, and ONE plesiosaur wearing a turtle shell with thirty feet of swan neck. two animals in five costumes.
beats.quote: "Tva," he said.

beats.title: Only One Comes Back Up
beats.modern: three hours of them tearing each other apart, mountains of water breaking over us, hissing loud enough to shake the roof of the world. then both go under and leave a whirlpool that nearly takes us with it. silence. then a head surfaces. just the plesiosaur, dying, thirty feet of neck whipping the sea like a cut worm until it stops. the other one never came back up.

beats.title: The Island Was A Geyser
beats.modern: black mountain lying on the sea, spouting water five hundred feet up. I said turn west. he said advance. I called him foolhardy and mad and threatened to cut the sail, the full meltdown, and he did not answer me once. then Hans points and says: island. it's an island. the spout is a geyser. uncle laughing his head off. then he named it after me.
beats.quote: "Geyser," said Hans.

beats.title: Ball Lightning On The Powder
beats.modern: three days of storm where we can't hear each other scream. then a ball of fire the size of a shell drops onto the raft. rolls the bulwark. hops the provisions. lands on the POWDER BARREL. does not go off. then it magnetises every piece of iron on board and my boot nails weld to the deck while the thing circles my feet. tore my foot free right as it burst.

beats.title: The Needle Points North
beats.modern: storm dumps us on a beach. uncle is delighted, we've crossed. he sets the compass down, reads it, closes his eyes, rubs them, reads it again, and then he can't speak. just points. the needle says the sea is north. we never crossed anything. the wind turned mid-tempest and put us back on the shore we left. every hour on that raft was nothing.

beats.title: This Is A Human Head
beats.modern: walked inland and hit a plain of bones. three square miles of every animal that ever lived, drifted into barrows going out to the horizon. he's standing in it with his arms raised at the granite sky, mouth open, having the best day of his life. then he snatches something out of the dust and his voice goes shaky: Harry, this is a human head.
beats.quote: "Harry, my boy--Harry--this is a human head!"

beats.title: The Giant Shepherd
beats.modern: living mastodons. a whole herd of them, pulling down trees with their trunks. already too much. then he drops his voice to a whisper and tells me to look. quarter mile out, leaning on a trunk: twelve feet tall, head like a buffalo, hair in a mane, holding a branch like a crook. he is HERDING them. we ran. I have spent years since telling myself we did not see that.

beats.title: The Rusty Dagger
beats.modern: found something shining in the sand. a dagger. Spanish, sixteenth century steel, blade chewed to bits from being dragged across stone. somebody stood on this beach. we walk the cliff face reading every crack and under an overhang there's a granite tablet, rubbed smooth, with two worn letters. A. S. he was here. and I'm holding the tool he wrote it with.

beats.title: Blow It Up
beats.modern: the tunnel behind the initials is plugged by one enormous block of granite. no gap above, below, either side. pickaxes are a joke against it. so I said gunpowder. Hans hollowed a chamber, we packed fifty pounds of guncotton in and ran a wick out, and then we went to bed. six hours lying next to it knowing what's in the wall.

beats.title: We Drained The Sea
beats.modern: I lit it and ran. he counted me down off his chronometer like a man launching a firework. the rock didn't break, chat — the whole cliff drew aside like a curtain and behind it was a bottomless pit. and then the sea went in. the entire underground ocean poured down the hole and took the raft with it. we blew a drain in the bottom of the world.

beats.title: The Food Is Gone
beats.modern: took inventory while we were falling. instruments: gone except compass and chronometer. ladders, ropes, tools: gone. food: one piece of dried meat and some soaked mouldy biscuit. for three men, at a hundred miles an hour, going down. I sat there holding it and decided not to tell him yet, because his calm was the last supply we had and I didn't want to spend it.

beats.title: The Ape Gigans
beats.modern: fourteen feet of black-haired ape with saw teeth walks into the cave sniffing for me. fights a shark-crocodile over who gets to eat me. WINS. comes at me gory, breathing on my neck — and I woke up on the raft. it was a dream. and chat, the genuinely upsetting part is that this trip has made that a completely reasonable thing to dream.

beats.title: We Are Going Up
beats.modern: his voice in the pitch dark: don't you see what's happened, we're going up. I put my hand on the wall to check and pulled it back skinned to the meat. two fathoms a second. the sea we let loose hit the bottom of the gulf and now the whole shaft is a barrel and we are the shot.

beats.title: An Eruption Is Good News
beats.modern: water boiling under us. walls red hot to the touch. compass spinning pole to pole like it's possessed. I tell him it's an earthquake and we're finished. he says no, he's expecting something bigger. an eruption. and then he smiles at me from under his spectacles and calls it the most fortunate thing that could happen to us. and chat — he's right. a volcano is the only lift out.
beats.quote: "An eruption, Harry."

beats.title: Stromboli
beats.modern: spat out of a crater half naked into HEAT. olives. figs. grapes. we are supposed to be in the arctic. we grab a local kid and my uncle interrogates him in German, English, French, Italian, and then another dialect of Italian. finally the boy gives up one word and bolts: Stromboli. we went in under Iceland and came out in Sicily. that cone on the horizon is Etna.
beats.quote: "Stromboli," replied the rickety little shepherd,

beats.title: Farval
beats.modern: back in Hamburg he's a legend, waxwork offers, the whole thing. and Hans just leaves. wouldn't take a reward, wouldn't let us pay the debt, got homesick for Reykjavik. said one word — farewell — and went. the man carried us out of the earth for fourteen shillings a week and clocked off like it was any other shift.
beats.quote: "Farval," said he,

beats.title: The Compass Lied
beats.modern: six months later I'm tidying his minerals, pick up the old compass, and the needle points SOUTH. the poles are swapped. the ball of fire on the raft magnetised the whole thing backwards. we never sailed north. we went exactly where we thought we were going. the one thing that had been eating him for half a year, solved by me dusting a shelf.
beats.quote: "During the storm, upon the Central Sea, the ball of fire which made a magnet of the iron in our raft, turned our compass topsy-turvy."

beats.title: Stream's Over
beats.modern: uncle: happiest learned man alive, arguing with every scientist in Europe. me: married Gretchen. we entered the earth by one volcano and left by another twelve hundred leagues away, and nobody at home believed a word of it until Hans stood there in the room. gg. stream's over.

beats.title: Everyone Left For The Summer
beats.modern: chat the entire city just packed up and went to their summer houses and nobody invited him. not one person. eight years in Petersburg and he has zero friends, but he's memorised every stranger on his walking route like a friends list. he's not sad about a breakup. he's sad the server emptied out.

beats.title: They Painted My Friend Yellow
beats.modern: he has parasocial relationships with BUILDINGS. there's a little pink house he greets every day, very proud of itself, looks down on the ugly houses next to it. he walks past last week and it's been painted yellow. he says: the villains. the barbarians. he has not been able to bring himself to visit since.

beats.title: Girl On The Canal
beats.modern: midnight, empty embankment, a girl crying on the railing. a drunk in evening dress spots her and takes off after her at a full sprint. our guy happens to be carrying a big knotted stick. he crosses the road, raises it, the drunk reads the room and leaves. first W of his entire life. she takes his arm.

beats.title: Twenty Six And Never Once
beats.modern: forty seconds into the first conversation he's ever had with a woman, he volunteers this: I'm twenty-six, I've never spoken to anyone, I fall in love with people who don't exist, I run full romance arcs in my head about strangers. sir. SIR. she is a person you met on a bridge.
beats.quote: I don't know how to be silent when my heart is speaking.

beats.title: The One Condition
beats.modern: she agrees to meet him again tomorrow. one rule: do not fall in love with me. that's impossible anyway, she says. he swears immediately. she goes hush, don't swear, I can already tell you go up like gunpowder. chat she called it on night one. check the VOD.
beats.quote: you won't fall in love with me.... That's impossible, I assure you.

beats.title: Definition Of A Dreamer
beats.modern: she asks what he is and he answers like he's reading a species entry. a dreamer isn't a human being, it's an intermediate creature. lives in a grimy green corner. grows onto it like a snail. or, and these are his words, like the thing that's an animal and a house at the same time. bro classified himself as a tortoise.

beats.title: Where Did You Bury Your Best Days
beats.modern: and then the bit drops out from under him. he starts asking himself out loud where the years went. how fast they went. what he did with them. where he buried his best days, whether he lived at all. and the answer is nothing. none of it happened. it was all dreams. no punchline on this one, chat.
beats.quote: Where have you buried your best days? Have you lived or not?

beats.title: She Showed Up With A Bundle
beats.modern: her turn. a year ago the lodger upstairs said he was leaving for Moscow, so she packed every piece of clothing she owned into a bundle, climbed his stairs, and put it on his bed. he opened the door and thought she was a ghost. then he said the worst sentence available: I'm poor. how would we live.

beats.title: Why Isn't He You
beats.modern: he's been the emotional support friend for three nights straight. she turns to him and says, kindly, sincerely: you're better than him. you're kinder than him. why isn't he you. and then, same breath, I love him more than you. chat she does not know she is committing a murder.
beats.quote: Why isn't he you? Why isn't he like you?

beats.title: It's Impossible, But I Love You
beats.modern: the man he's been consoling her about never shows. she breaks down. and he cracks and says it out loud: it's impossible, but I love you. she goes, oh. what of it. I've known that for ages, I just assumed you liked me a lot. she has known THE WHOLE TIME.

beats.title: Then I Love You Too
beats.modern: and then it flips. she says she'll get over him, she's getting over him now, he laughed at her, he never loved her — and you did, and you're nobler, and I love you. she says it out loud. she means it in that minute. she cries into his shoulder and he holds her. chat. chat we won.

beats.title: It's Him
beats.modern: they spend the night picking rooms. he'll rent the top floor. granny comes too. they're arguing about which opera to see. then a young man walks past, stops, and looks at them. she goes rigid. it's him. she tears out of his arms, doubles back to kiss him once, and leads the other man away. he stands there until they're gone.

beats.title: A Whole Moment Of Happiness
beats.modern: the letter arrives in the morning. she's marrying him next week, please forgive her, please still be her brother, please like him. he looks around his room and sees it fifteen years ahead: same cobwebs, same servant, same him. and he doesn't curse her. he blesses her. then he asks the question the whole book was built for.
beats.quote: My God, a whole moment of happiness! Is that too little for the whole of a man's life?

beats.title: I Am A Sick Man
beats.modern: new POV, chat, and this one is a different animal entirely. forty year old ex-clerk, quit the second he inherited money, lives in a corner of Petersburg. opens his diary with: I am sick, I am spiteful, I am unattractive. thinks his liver's rotting. refuses to see a doctor purely out of spite. knows the spite only hurts him. does it anyway.
beats.quote: I am a sick man.... I am a spiteful man. I am an unattractive man.

beats.title: Forty Is Extreme Old Age
beats.modern: he announces that living past forty is bad manners, vulgar and immoral, and that only fools and worthless men do it. he says this at exactly forty. then immediately adds that he personally intends to make sixty. seventy. eighty. and then asks for a second to catch his breath.
beats.quote: To live longer than forty years is bad manners, is vulgar, immoral.

beats.title: The Mouse In The Hole
beats.modern: he explains the two categories of man. normal man gets insulted, lowers his horns, charges. he gets insulted and turns into a mouse: doubts, side questions, a whole stinking brew of it, everyone laughing, and then he creeps back into the hole. and there he reruns the clip for forty years, adding worse details every time. chat he invented the 3am shame spiral and he's fucking proud of it.

beats.title: Twice Two Makes Four
beats.modern: they tell him: nature doesn't take requests, a wall is a wall, two times two is four, be reconciled to it. and he says I know I can't headbutt through a wall. I'm just never going to be at peace about it. the man is picking a fight with arithmetic. he'd rather lose than agree.
beats.quote: what do I care for the laws of nature and arithmetic, when, for some reason I dislike those laws and the fact that twice two makes four?

beats.title: Enjoyment In A Toothache
beats.modern: someone jokes he'll be finding pleasure in toothache next. he says correct, had one for a month, and here's how it works. by day three you're not moaning from pain. you're moaning AT the household. everyone knows you're performing. you know they know. that's the whole pleasure. this man weaponised a molar.
beats.quote: Even in toothache there is enjoyment,"

beats.title: The Crystal Palace
beats.modern: they promise him the perfect future. a crystal palace. everything solved forever, nothing left to want. and he says that's exactly what terrifies him, because you can't stick your tongue out at it. a henhouse keeps the rain off too, he says, and I'm still not calling it a palace out of gratitude.
beats.quote: But meanwhile I will not take a hen-house for a mansion.

beats.title: Moved Like Furniture
beats.modern: he's standing near a billiard table, in the way. an officer takes him by the shoulders, physically relocates him to a different spot, and walks on without a word. doesn't insult him. doesn't even see him. and he says: I could have forgiven being hit. what I cannot forgive is being MOVED.
beats.quote: I could have forgiven blows, but I could not forgive his having moved me without noticing me.

beats.title: The Collision
beats.modern: two years of prep for this. he researched the man, wrote a whole novel unmasking him, drafted a duel letter, sold his coat collar, borrowed money for a decent hat, all so he could walk down the Nevsky and NOT step aside. finally does it. shoulders him. gets bounced off like a ball. declares total victory and goes home singing Italian opera. absolutely fucking unhinged.

beats.title: He Invited Himself
beats.modern: old schoolmates are arranging a farewell dinner for a guy he has despised since school. he was not invited. he interrupts their maths so his share gets counted in. they say where would we even have found you. he insists anyway. and he still owes one of them fifteen roubles. what the hell is wrong with this man.

beats.title: An Hour Early
beats.modern: they moved the dinner from five to six and nobody told him. so he's sitting alone in an empty private room from half past five, watching a waiter lay a table for other people, feeling worse with every fork. he's too embarrassed to keep asking the staff. they arrive an hour late and find it hilarious.

beats.title: The Toast
beats.modern: drunk, ignored, spiralling, he stands up to make his own speech. announces that he hates phrasemongers, hates men in corsets, hates ribald talk, loves truth and honesty. then toasts the guest of honour with go seduce the Circassian girls. table goes silent. somebody says he wants a punch in the face. he challenges a man to a duel and the whole room falls over laughing.
beats.quote: Seduce the Circassian girls, shoot the enemies of the fatherland and ... and ... to your health, Monsieur Zverkov!"

beats.title: Three Hours Of Pacing
beats.modern: they move to the sofa and stop acknowledging he exists. so he paces. table to stove, stove to table, thumping his heels on purpose so they have to hear it. eight o'clock to eleven. three hours. he sweats through his shirt three separate times. he knows he'll still be replaying this in forty years. he keeps pacing.

beats.title: Two Wide Open Eyes
beats.modern: he chases them to a brothel to slap someone and they've already scattered. hours later he wakes in the dark and there are two eyes on him, completely cold, completely detached. he hasn't said a single word to her all night. he asks her name just to make the looking stop. Liza. twenty. from Riga. two weeks in the house.

beats.title: The Grave Speech
beats.modern: then he does the cruellest thing in the whole volume. he narrates her own death to her: consumption, a wet grave in Volkovo, gravediggers swearing about the rain, nobody to mourn her, her name gone off the earth like she was never born. he admits he's showing off. it's a performance. she bites the pillow until her hand bleeds.
beats.quote: your name will vanish from the face of the earth--as though you had never existed, never been born at all!

beats.title: Her One Treasure
beats.modern: he panics at what he's done, gives her his address, says come to me. she stops him at the door, runs off, comes back glowing and puts a piece of paper in his hand. it's a love letter. a student who danced with her at a party and knows nothing about her life. she kept it. she needed him to know that somebody once wrote to her respectfully.

beats.title: I Was Laughing At You
beats.modern: she actually comes. finds him in a torn dressing gown mid-screaming-match with his servant. so he burns her down. tells her the sermon was sport, that he'd been humiliated at a dinner and needed something smaller to humiliate, that he was never saving anyone. she goes down into the chair like she's been hit with an axe.
beats.quote: I had been humiliated, so I wanted to humiliate; I had been treated like a rag, so I wanted to show my power....

beats.title: The Five Rouble Note
beats.modern: she works out the thing he can't stand: that he's the one who's unhappy. she holds him while he sobs. and he can't forgive being seen, so on her way out he forces money into her hand, deliberately, from spite. she leaves. he turns round and the note is lying on the table where she threw it.

beats.title: Anti-Hero
beats.modern: he never saw her again. and he closes by admitting there's no hero in these notes, only an anti-hero, and then turns it on the reader: we're all cripples, we're all divorced from real life, we all secretly prefer books to living. untie us and we'd beg to be tied back up. then he just stops writing.
beats.quote: we are all divorced from life, we are all cripples, every one of us, more or less.

beats.title: He's Getting Married
beats.modern: new story, two clerks sharing a flat. Vasya comes home in his best trousers, obviously bursting with news, and does the loud fake cough thing until his friend wakes up. Arkady pins him to the bed to get it out of him. news is: he's engaged. Arkady picks him up like a baby, carries him round the room pretending to rock him to sleep, then kisses his cheek.

beats.title: Death By Gratitude
beats.modern: Vasya's boss gave him copying work as a kindness. Vasya, drowning in gratitude for a job and a fiancée and a whole life he can't believe he's allowed, promises more than exists, doesn't finish, and convinces himself he'll be handed to the army for it. by morning he's standing in the director's office at attention. they ask what broke him. Arkady can only get one word out.
beats.quote: "Gra--gra--gratitude!"

beats.title: Not Fit For Military Service
beats.modern: the whole department is standing around him with no idea what to do. Vasya suddenly remembers what he came to report, steps forward, clicks his heel like a soldier and states that he has a physical defect, is small and weak, and is not fit for service, Your Excellency. the director starts crying. Vasya says present, wheels left, and marches out.
beats.quote: "I have a physical defect and am small and weak, and I am not fit for military service, Your Excellency,"

beats.title: The Curl Of Hair
beats.modern: they hug goodbye at the door before the hospital carriage takes him. Vasya presses a folded paper into Arkady's hand and begs him to look after it, bring it later, keep it safe. they take him away. Arkady opens it. it's a lock of Liza's hair he had never once gone anywhere without.

beats.title: Two Years Later, In Church
beats.modern: two years on, Arkady runs into Lizanka in a church. married. baby. nurse walking beside her. she says she's happy, thank God, not badly off, her husband is a kind man and she's fond of him. mid-sentence her voice gives out and she bows down to the floor so nobody can see her face.

beats.title: Compound Interest On A Child
beats.modern: children's party, New Year's Eve. the important guest everyone's fawning over steps into a side room and starts doing arithmetic on his fingers. three hundred thousand dowry. girl's eleven. five years at four percent, no, the father's sharper than that, call it eight, call it five hundred thousand. then he glances at the actual child and stops dead.

beats.title: Do You Know What Your Dolly Is Made Of
beats.modern: he goes over to her. kisses her head. asks what she's playing. tells her the doll is only rags. twice tries to send the poor red-haired boy out of the room. then, voice dropping softer and softer, asks whether she'll love him when he comes to see her papa and mamma. she's near tears. the boy takes her hand and starts crying with her.
beats.quote: "And will you love me, dear little girl, when I come and see your papa and mamma?"

beats.title: A Good Stroke Of Business
beats.modern: five years pass. the narrator walks past a church, sees the carriages, pushes into the crowd. the bride comes through: pale, preoccupied, eyes red from crying, and people in the crowd are saying she's only just sixteen. then he looks at the groom, recognises him, and shoves his way back out into the street. good stroke of business, he thinks.
beats.quote: People were saying that she was only just sixteen.

beats.title: The April Fool
beats.modern: a man who lets a whole tavern laugh at him for money tells them how he lost everything. he'd informed on his boss for a bribe, got caught, got tearfully forgiven, got engaged to the daughter. then on the first of April he decides it would be funny to hand over a formal letter of resignation as a prank. curls his hair, best coat, delivers it, then yells april fool like a kid shouting boo behind grandma's chair.

beats.title: The Starling
beats.modern: everyone laughs. wedding rings get ordered. weeks later the sack arrives. he runs to the boss going how, and the boss says calmly: you resigned. on the first of April. the letter was never taken back. then a page turns up with the birdcage he'd given the daughter and a note saying only, April 1st. he says he once meant to call that man a scoundrel to his face. he couldn't do it.

beats.title: He Got On The Horse
beats.modern: eleven year old boy, house full of adults using him as entertainment, one of them needling him about a horse nobody dares ride. something snaps. he's down the steps in one jump and has a foot in the stirrup before the grooms can move. Tancred rears, rips loose and goes off like a hurricane with fifty people screaming behind him.

beats.title: The Bee And The Letter
beats.modern: he's smuggled a letter into a bunch of flowers for the woman he's quietly, hopelessly in love with, and she takes the flowers without looking and sets them down. dead drop failed. then a bee turns up. she waves the flowers at it and the letter drops straight onto her open book. he shuts his eyes and fakes sleep while she reads it. her whole face changes.

beats.title: My Childhood Was Over
beats.modern: someone calls her name through the trees. she gets up, bends right down over him to check he's really asleep, and a kiss and her tears land on his hand. then a second one on his mouth, and she's gone before he can open his eyes. he lies in the grass shaking. the line he uses for it: my childhood was over from that moment.

beats.title: The Lodgers Invent The News
beats.modern: last one. an elderly clerk lives behind a screen in the cheapest corner of a boarding house, five roubles a month, bothers nobody. the other lodgers work out he'll believe literally anything, so they start feeding him fake office news: married clerks get promoted faster, they're docking pay for compulsory dancing lessons, there's going to be an exam. he starts walking softly. starts listening at doors. starts asking his boss whether it's true.

beats.title: They Cut Open The Mattress
beats.modern: he dies. they go through his things: two rags, socks, half a handkerchief, an old hat, some boot soles. then they shift the mattress and money hits the floor. there's a knife slit in it he cut himself. they send for scissors. coins keep coming, wrapped in paper, sorted by size, some of them a century old. final count: 2497 roubles and a half. he'd been living on nothing for twenty years.

beats.title: What If I'm Not Dead
beats.modern: the landlady wails that he cheated her, that he could have just handed it over and been looked after. and the book ends by putting words in a dead man's mouth. give over. stop whining. go to bed. it's nice lying here. though — look here — what if I get up.
beats.quote: what if I'm not dead, what if I get up, do you hear? What would happen then?"
